text: The James Webb Space Telescope was sent into space on December 25, 2021. Its massive main mirror is 6.5 meters wide, much larger than the mirror of the older Hubble telescope. It sits about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth, where it must stay extremely cold to work well. Webb is capable of seeing a kind of light that our eyes cannot see, which lets it look through clouds of dust. Its pictures show stars and planets in amazing detail. Scientists use what it sees to test their theories about how the first stars and galaxies in the universe formed, more than thirteen billion years ago.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “capable” mean?
qs.why: Capable means having the ability to do something. Webb can see a kind of light our eyes cannot. “Is not able” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “theories” mean?
options: facts that have already been fully proven
sets of ideas that try to explain how something happens
qs.why: Theories are ideas meant to explain how something happens. Scientists “test” them, which shows they are not yet fully proven facts.

qs.q: Why can Webb see through clouds of dust?
options: It is very close to Earth
Its mirror is smaller than Hubble's
It can see a kind of light that our eyes cannot see
It takes pictures only at night
qs.why: The passage says it sees light our eyes cannot see, “which lets it look through clouds of dust.” It is kept cold, not warm.

title: A New Life in Japan
text: When Lucas moved from Brazil to Japan for work, he found many things strange at first. People took off their shoes before entering a home, and few people ate while walking down the street. Initially, he was afraid of making mistakes, so he stayed quiet at the office. Then a co-worker named Yuki invited him to a festival in her town. Her family welcomed him warmly and showed him how to make rice cakes. That evening, he learned more about cultural habits than he had in a month of reading. He also started taking language lessons. Now he can hold a simple conversation in Japanese and has gained many new friends.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “Initially” mean?
options: by writing the first letter of his name
qs.why: Initially means at first, at the very beginning. Later, things changed after the festival.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “welcomed” mean?
options: greeted in a friendly way when he arrived
qs.why: Welcomed means said hello in a friendly way when he arrived. Yuki's family greeted him “warmly.”

qs.q: According to the passage, what helped Lucas learn the most about Japanese habits?
options: A month of reading about Japan
Spending an evening with Yuki's family at the festival
Taking off his shoes at work
Eating while walking down the street
qs.why: He learned more that evening “than he had in a month of reading,” so the festival with Yuki's family helped most.

title: Fixing the Old Car
text: Grace Mensah's old car stopped working on the highway one cold morning. She paid for a tow truck to take the vehicle to a small repair shop owned by a man named Viktor, an expert who had fixed cars for thirty years. He listened to the engine and found the problem quickly. A broken belt had stopped the engine. “I can replace it today,” he said, “with a new one from my shelf.” Viktor's shop was small, but it had all the right equipment, including a lift that could raise a car off the ground. The fee for the work was one hundred and twenty dollars, which Grace thought was fair.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “fee” mean?
options: the money paid for the work
the price of a new car
a tip left on the counter
qs.why: A fee is money paid for a service; here, $120 for fixing the car.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “expert” mean?
options: a beginner who is still learning
a person who knows a lot and is very skilled
qs.why: An expert knows a lot about something. Viktor had fixed cars for thirty years and found the problem quickly.

qs.q: What was wrong with Grace's car?
qs.why: Viktor found that “a broken belt had stopped the engine.”

title: Her First Marathon
text: Running a marathon is a huge challenge: the race is about 42 kilometers long. Fatima Hassan trained for eight months to achieve her goal of finishing her first one. The physical training was hard. She ran four times a week and built up the strength in her legs at the gym. But she says the mental part was even harder. “Around kilometer 30, your mind tells you to stop,” she said. On race day, a large crowd stood along the streets, cheering and holding signs. Fatima finished in four hours and forty minutes. She was not fast, but she did not stop once.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “mental” mean?
options: having to do with the body
having to do with the mind
qs.why: Mental means having to do with the mind; she explains that “your mind tells you to stop.” “The body” is what physical means.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “achieve” mean?
qs.why: Achieve means to succeed in reaching a goal through effort. Her goal was finishing, not winning; she “was not fast.”

qs.q: Which part of the marathon did Fatima find hardest?
options: Fighting the thought in her mind that she should stop
Running in front of a crowd
qs.why: She says the mental part was “even harder” than the physical training, because around kilometer 30 your mind tells you to stop.

title: The Bike Shop
text: Carlos Mendoza wanted to open a bicycle repair shop. He had saved some money, but not enough. So he went to the bank for a loan of twenty thousand dollars. He used it to buy tools and rent a space near the university. He saw the money he spent as an investment: he hoped the shop would make money for many years. In the first year, the shop's revenue was sixty thousand dollars. After paying rent, wages, and parts, he had a little left over. Slowly, he paid back his debt to the bank. Now, after four years, the shop is successful. Its purpose has stayed the same: to keep students riding.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “revenue” mean?
options: the money left after all costs were paid
the money he owed the bank
all the money the shop took in, before costs
qs.why: Revenue is all the money a business takes in before costs. The money left over after rent, wages and parts is profit, which was only “a little.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “debt” mean?
options: money he had to pay back
money the bank gave him for free
qs.why: A debt is money you must pay back. He “paid back his debt to the bank,” the loan.

qs.q: Why did Carlos get a loan from the bank?
options: The bank asked him to open a shop
He wanted to buy a house
His savings were not enough to start the shop
He needed to pay for school
qs.why: He “had saved some money, but not enough,” so he borrowed to buy tools and rent a space.

title: River Cleanup
text: On a bright Saturday, about fifty people met at the river near their town to clean its banks. The event was run by a small organization that cares for the local environment. Each person got gloves and a bag. In three hours, they removed more than two hundred kilograms of trash, including bottles, old tires, and fishing line. Fishing line is dangerous for birds, because it can wrap around their legs. The leader, Mei Lin, said the work has a real impact. “Five years ago, you could hardly see a heron here,” she said. “Now these big birds are widely seen along the river.” After the cleanup, everyone shared lunch under the trees.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “impact” mean?
options: the force of one thing hitting another
qs.why: Impact here means a strong effect; Mei Lin points to the birds coming back. The meaning “force of one thing hitting another” does not fit.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “removed” mean?
qs.why: Removed means took away. The volunteers took trash away from the river banks.

qs.q: What does Mei Lin suggest about the cleanups?
options: Herons are now harder to find
The river has no more trash
They have helped birds return to the river
Only five people come to them
qs.why: She says herons were hard to see five years ago but are now widely seen, showing the work has had an effect.

title: Grandmother's Songs
text: My grandmother is eighty-nine, and her memory is not as strong as it used to be. Some days she forgets what she ate for breakfast. Last week, when I visited, she did not recognize me at first. She thought I was her brother. It was emotional for me, and I had to step outside for a minute. But when I showed her old photos from her youth, she smiled and told me stories about dancing in Lagos in the 1950s. She remembered every song. I truly believe those happy years will stay with her forever, even if other things are lost.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “recognize” mean?
options: know who I was from seeing me before
officially say that I had done something good
qs.why: Recognize means to know someone because you have seen them before. She did not know who the writer was and thought he was her brother.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “youth” mean?
options: the time when she was young
qs.why: Youth here is the time of life when a person is young; the photos showed her younger years in the 1950s. “A young person” is a different use.

qs.q: What does the grandmother still remember well?
options: The day she visited the writer
Songs and stories from when she was young
qs.why: She forgets recent things like breakfast, but when shown old photos, she told stories and “remembered every song.”

title: The Lighthouse Keeper
text: For many years, a lighthouse stood on a rocky island off the coast, and a keeper lived inside it. In this story, the keeper is Elias, an old man with a gray beard. His main duty was to keep the lamp burning every night, so ships would know the location of the rocks. The wind on the island was constant; it never stopped blowing. When fog came, Elias used a loud horn to signal to the ships. Previously, when there was no light, many ships had crashed there. The stone tower stood strong through a hundred storms. In the coldest winters, even the water in his barrel froze solid.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “signal” mean?
options: make a sound to tell someone something
qs.why: To signal is to make a sound, movement or sign to tell someone something; the horn warned ships in the fog. “A light on a road” is a noun meaning.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “Previously” mean?
options: at an earlier time, before then
qs.why: Previously means at an earlier time. The sentence says “before the lighthouse was built.”

qs.q: Why was a lighthouse needed on the island?
options: Elias wanted a place to live
Ships had crashed on the rocks there before
The island had no stone for houses
Fog never came to the island
The wind made ships go faster
The town needed a lamp at night
qs.why: Before the lighthouse was built, “many ships had crashed there,” and its light showed where the rocks were.

title: A Strange Phone Call
text: One afternoon, Mrs. Ivanova got a phone call from a man who claimed to work for her bank. He said there was a problem with her account and requested her card number to fix it. Mrs. Ivanova suspected something was wrong. Her real bank had told her it would never ask for that number on the phone. She told the man she would call back and hung up. Then she called the number printed on her own bank card. The bank said the man had lied to her, and that this scheme had already fooled several people in her city. “Be careful,” the bank worker said. “Never share your card number with a caller.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “claimed” mean?
options: said it was true, though it was not proven
asked for money that was owed
qs.why: Claimed means said something is true without proof. The man said he worked for her bank, but it was a lie.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “scheme” mean?
options: a set of colors that go well together
a rule made by the bank
a secret plan to get money by breaking the rules
qs.why: A scheme here is a secret, dishonest plan to get money; it had fooled several people.

qs.q: How did Mrs. Ivanova know the call might be a trick?
options: The man had a strange voice
The man gave her his name
Her bank had said it would never ask for her card number by phone
Her friend warned her that day
qs.why: She suspected something was wrong because “her real bank had told her it would never ask for that number on the phone.”

title: Why Sleep Matters
text: Sleep is essential for good health. Health experts say most adults need at least seven hours a night. A lack of sleep affects how well we think, how we feel, and even how hungry we get. It can also add to stress, making small problems feel much bigger. The good news is that a few simple habits can help. Going to bed at the same time each night is one of the most effective changes. Another is to reduce screen time in the hour before bed. People who make these changes often find that their sleep improves significantly within a few weeks.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “affects” mean?
qs.why: Affects means has an influence on or causes a change in. Poor sleep changes how we think, feel and eat.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “significantly” mean?
options: by a large amount that you can notice
qs.why: Significantly means by a large, noticeable amount. “Only a little” is the opposite.

qs.q: Which habit does the passage name as one of the most effective?
options: Using a screen until you fall asleep
Going to bed at the same time each night
Taking long naps in the day
qs.why: The passage says going to bed at the same time each night “is one of the most effective changes.”

title: The Clock Museum
text: Our class visited the city museum to see its famous collection of old clocks. More than three hundred clocks were displayed in glass cases along the walls. Some were as small as a teacup, while others were taller than our teacher. The guide told us that one gold clock was the most valuable piece in the museum. It came from an era when clocks cost so much that most families could not own one. Nobody knows the exact year it was made, but experts think it is about three hundred years old. Its origin is also not certain, though the writing on it suggests it was made in France.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “era” mean?
options: a period of history known for something
qs.why: An era is a period of history known for a particular quality; here, a time when only rich families could own clocks.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “origin” mean?
options: the place where it came from
qs.why: Origin is where something comes from. The writing suggests France, but no one is sure.

qs.q: What is known about the gold clock?
options: It was made in France in a known year
Experts think it is about 300 years old, but the exact year is unknown
It is the smallest clock in the museum
It was owned by a poor family
It is taller than the teacher
qs.why: The passage says “nobody knows the exact year,” but experts think it is about three hundred years old. France is only suggested, not certain.

title: The Corner Garden
text: Three years ago, Rosa Delgado and her neighbors decided to establish a garden on an empty lot at the end of their street. Nobody was paid; the work was completely voluntary. At first, only four people came on Saturday mornings. Gradually, more families joined, and children began to help water the beds. Last summer, the small garden managed to yield more tomatoes and beans than the group could eat, so they gave the extra food to a local kitchen. Rosa says the best part is the enthusiasm of the kids, who run to check the plants after school. Everyone is asked to contribute something, even if it is just an hour of pulling weeds or a bag of seeds.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “voluntary” mean?
options: required by law, so people had to do it
done because people chose to, without being paid or forced
qs.why: The passage says nobody was paid, so people chose to help. “Required by law” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “yield” mean?
qs.why: The garden produced more tomatoes and beans than the group could eat. “Give way” is a different meaning of yield.

qs.q: Why did the group give food to a local kitchen?
options: The kitchen paid them for the vegetables.
The children did not like tomatoes and beans.
The city told them they had to.
The food was not good enough to sell.
The garden grew more food than the group could eat.
Rosa worked at the kitchen on weekends.
qs.why: They gave away the extra food because the harvest was bigger than they needed. Nothing says the kitchen paid them.

title: A Late Train Home
text: When the last train to Leeds stopped between two stations, there was confusion in Carriage C. The lights flickered, and nobody knew why the train had stopped. A man said he had an urgent meeting at nine and could not be late. For a moment it felt like chaos, with phones ringing and bags falling from the racks. Then the conductor, Amara Osei, walked through the train. She spoke calmly and tried to assure everyone that the problem was small: a signal had failed further down the line. She thanked people for their patience and promised hot drinks at the next station. The repair was swift, and twenty minutes later the train began to move again.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “assure” mean?
options: give orders in a loud voice
tell people something is true so they stop worrying
qs.why: Amara told passengers the problem was small so they would feel calm. “Warn about danger” is close to the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “swift” mean?
qs.why: Twenty minutes later the train moved again, so the repair was quick.

qs.q: Why did the train stop?
options: The lights in Carriage C broke.
A man needed to get off for a meeting.
The conductor stopped it to serve drinks.
The train ran out of power at a station.
A signal further down the line had failed.
qs.why: Amara explained that a signal had failed further down the line. The flickering lights happened, but they were not the cause.

title: Grandmother's Recipe Book
text: Every December, Mei Lin opens her grandmother's old recipe book. The pages are thin and stained with oil, and she keeps them in plastic sleeves to preserve them. The book is part of the family's heritage, carried from Guangzhou to San Francisco more than sixty years ago. Mei can still recall standing on a stool beside her grandmother, folding dumplings. Her grandmother was devoted to the family and cooked for everyone on every holiday. The dumplings have a distinctive taste, thanks to a little dried orange peel in the filling. Restaurants nearby sell similar food, but Mei's cousins say only her version tastes authentic, just like the ones they ate as children.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “preserve” mean?
options: cook in sugar to make jam
keep safe from damage so they last
qs.why: Mei keeps the thin pages in plastic so they will not be damaged. Cooking fruit in sugar is a different meaning of preserve.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “distinctive” mean?
qs.why: The orange peel gives the dumplings a special taste that people can recognize. “Very common” is the opposite.

qs.q: What gives the dumplings their special taste?
options: Oil from the old recipe book
A secret sauce from a restaurant
A little dried orange peel in the filling
qs.why: The passage says the taste comes from a little dried orange peel in the filling.

title: The New Science Teacher
text: Mr. Haddad joined Westfield School in September, and his classes quickly became the most popular in the building. His lessons were innovative: instead of reading from the textbook, students built small rockets from plastic bottles. He would demonstrate each step first, showing how air pressure pushes water out and lifts the bottle. He liked curious students who asked “why” again and again, and he would encourage quiet students to share their ideas too. One technique he used was asking groups to explain their mistakes to the class. At the end of each project, he gave written feedback, pointing out what worked and what to try next time.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “demonstrate” mean?
qs.why: He showed each step first so students could see how it worked. Marching in protest is a different meaning of demonstrate.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “feedback” mean?
options: a loud noise from a speaker
comments on the work to help students improve
qs.why: He pointed out what worked and what to try next time. The loud speaker noise is a different meaning of feedback.

qs.q: What made Mr. Haddad's lessons different from usual lessons?
options: He only taught the quiet students.
Students read the textbook out loud.
Students built and tested things instead of only reading the textbook.
He gave very long tests every week.
He did not allow students to make mistakes.
qs.why: His lessons were new because students built rockets instead of reading. He actually asked groups to explain their mistakes.

title: Running the City Marathon
text: Kwame Asante finished the city marathon for the third consecutive year this Sunday, but this race was the hardest. In March he hurt his knee and could barely walk for two weeks. His doctor told him to rest, and for a while he lost his motivation to train. What helped him overcome the injury was a group of older runners who met at the park every morning. They ran slowly, laughed a lot, and waited for him at every corner. With their support and his own determination, he got stronger week by week. His time on Sunday was his slowest ever, yet he calls it his greatest achievement.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “consecutive” mean?
options: one after another, with no break
qs.why: Third consecutive year means he ran it three years in a row. “Every other year” would mean there were breaks.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “barely” mean?
qs.why: After the injury he could almost not walk. “Without shoes” is a careless reading based on the word bare.

qs.q: Why does Kwame call his slowest race his greatest achievement?
options: He beat all the older runners.
He won a prize for his time.
It was the first marathon he ever ran.
His doctor ran the race with him.
He finished it after getting over an injury and losing his wish to train.
He finished faster than he expected.
qs.why: The race mattered because of what he overcame to finish it. It was his third race, not his first, and his time was slow.

title: Saving the River Otters
text: Thirty years ago, river otters had almost disappeared from many streams in the region. Their numbers began to decline when factories poured waste into the water and there were fewer fish to eat. Young otters are especially vulnerable in their first winter, when food is hard to find. A conservation group led by biologist Dr. Lena Novak spent years cleaning the riverbanks and planting trees along the water. Their goal was to restore the river to the clean state it was in long ago. Volunteers now observe the otters from small wooden huts, counting the animals and noting where they build their dens. The otters' survival now looks much more hopeful. Last spring, the team counted eleven pups, the most since records began.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “decline” mean?
qs.why: Otter numbers went down when the water became dirty. “Say no politely” is a different meaning of decline.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “vulnerable” mean?
qs.why: Young otters can easily be hurt or die in winter. “Very hungry” fits the scene but is not what the word means.

qs.q: What suggests that the group's work is succeeding?
options: The team counted more pups last spring than ever recorded.
Factories still pour waste into the river.
Young otters no longer need food in winter.
Volunteers have stopped counting the otters.
Dr. Novak has left the group.
Otters have moved away to other streams.
qs.why: Eleven pups was the most since records began, which shows the population is recovering.

title: Choosing a First Apartment
text: When Priya moved to Chicago for her first job, she had to find an apartment quickly. Her top priority was safety, followed by a short trip to work. She made a list of costs to estimate how much rent she could pay each month. Her dream apartment had a view of the lake, but it was not realistic on her salary. She planned to share with her friend Tess. Tess wanted a big kitchen; Priya wanted two bathrooms. In the end the two made a compromise: a place with one bathroom and a medium-sized kitchen, in a quiet building close to a train stop. The kitchen is adequate for two people who mostly cook simple meals. The location is convenient, since the grocery store is right across the street.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “realistic” mean?
options: possible with the money she really had
qs.why: She could not really afford the lake view on her salary. “Looking like a photo” is a different use of realistic.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “adequate” mean?
options: good enough, but not more than that
qs.why: The kitchen is good enough for two people who cook simple meals. “Too small to use” goes too far.

qs.q: What was Priya's most important need when looking for an apartment?
qs.why: The passage says her top priority was safety, followed by a short trip to work. The big kitchen was Tess's wish.

title: The Museum's New Wing
text: On Saturday, the Harbor City Museum opened its new wing with a short ceremony on the front steps. The wing is home to contemporary art, including paintings and sculptures made in the last twenty years. Its magnificent glass roof lets sunlight fall across the main hall. The museum hopes the new space will attract younger visitors who do not often go to galleries. One room is a tribute to Elena Ruiz, a local painter who taught free art classes to children for forty years. Several artists in the show say she was their first inspiration. Entry to the new wing will be free on the first Sunday of every month.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “contemporary” mean?
options: happening at the same time as an older event
on show for a short time only
modern; made in the present time
qs.why: The art was made in the last twenty years, so it is modern. Another meaning, “living at the same time as,” does not fit here.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “tribute” mean?
options: something done to show respect and thanks for someone
qs.why: The room honors Elena Ruiz for her years of teaching. Money paid to a ruler is an old, different meaning.

qs.q: Why does the new wing have a room about Elena Ruiz?
options: She paid for the glass roof.
She taught free art classes for many years and inspired several of the artists.
She is the youngest artist in the show.
She opened the museum on Saturday.
She sold all her paintings to the museum.
qs.why: She taught children free for forty years, and several artists say she inspired them.

title: A Phone Call from the Bank
text: Last month, Mr. Okafor got a call from a woman who said she worked for his bank. She told him someone was trying to withdraw money from his account and asked for his password to stop it. He felt suspicious, because the bank had always told customers it would never ask for a password. He refused to give it and hung up instantly. Then he called the number printed on the back of his bank card. A real staff member was able to confirm that the first call was fake and that his money was safe. She thanked him for protecting his privacy and told him to share personal details only with people he truly trusts.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “withdraw” mean?
options: take money out of an account
qs.why: The caller claimed someone was taking money out of his account. Putting money in is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “suspicious” mean?
options: not trusting; feeling that something wrong was happening
qs.why: He did not trust the caller because the bank never asks for passwords.

qs.q: What made Mr. Okafor doubt the caller?
options: The caller spoke in a strange accent.
The call came late at night.
He had no money in the account.
His bank had said it would never ask for a password.
qs.why: He felt suspicious because the bank had always told customers it would never ask for a password.

title: The Kite Festival
text: In many parts of Gujarat, India, people fly kites in the middle of January to celebrate the festival of Uttarayan. Ravi's family celebrates it annually on the roof of their building. Traditionally, the family makes sweets from sesame seeds and sugar the night before. On the day, everyone from grandparents to small cousins wants to participate. The sky fills with thousands of colorful kites, and the view is truly spectacular. Some people fly enormous kites that need two adults to hold the string. The atmosphere is noisy and happy: music plays, neighbors shout to each other across the rooftops, and nobody wants the day to end.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “atmosphere” mean?
options: the mood or feeling of a place
qs.why: Noisy, happy and with music describes the mood. The air around the earth is a different meaning.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “annually” mean?
qs.why: The family celebrates the festival every January, once a year.

qs.q: What happens the night before the festival?
options: Neighbors play music on the roofs.
The family makes sweets from sesame seeds and sugar.
Two adults test the biggest kite.
qs.why: The passage says sweets are made the night before. The music and kites happen on the festival day.

title: A Remote Village Clinic
text: The village of San Lucas sits high in the mountains, in a remote area three hours from the nearest town. For years, the only road was a dirt track that flooded in the rainy season. Families had to rely on one nurse, Carmen Quispe, who visited twice a month. Last year, a new clinic opened with a paved path and a ramp, so it is now accessible to older people and those who use wheelchairs. Two local students trained to assist Carmen by checking blood pressure and keeping records. The clinic has become vital to the village. When a farmer broke his leg in March, he was treated the same day and was able to recover at home.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “accessible” mean?
options: easy to reach and enter, even for people in wheelchairs
qs.why: The ramp and paved path let older people and wheelchair users get in.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “remote” mean?
options: far from towns and hard to reach
a device for changing TV channels
qs.why: San Lucas is three hours from the nearest town. A TV remote is a different meaning.

qs.q: How did the new clinic help the farmer with the broken leg?
options: He was flown to a big city hospital.
He waited for the nurse's next visit.
He trained to work at the clinic.
He got care the same day, close to home.
He did not need any treatment.
qs.why: Because the clinic was there, he was treated the same day and recovered at home instead of waiting or travelling.

title: The Chess Club Rivalry
text: For five years, the chess team at Lincoln High lost every match to its rival, Eastbrook Academy. This year, the coach, Ms. Tanaka, tried new tactics. Instead of waiting for mistakes, her players made bold moves early, attacking before Eastbrook was ready. Most people thought the odds were against Lincoln, since Eastbrook had two state champions. But the Lincoln players felt confident after weeks of practice. In the final game, Eastbrook's best player attacked hard, and Lincoln's youngest member, Omar, had to defend his queen for almost an hour. When Omar finally won, his teammates cheered so loudly that the judge asked them to leave the room.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “odds” mean?
options: how likely something was to happen
qs.why: People thought Lincoln was unlikely to win. “Strange events” is a careless reading of odd.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “tactics” mean?
options: planned ways of playing to win
qs.why: The coach changed how the team planned to win, by attacking early.

qs.q: Why did most people expect Lincoln to lose?
options: Omar was too young to play.
Eastbrook had two state champions and had beaten Lincoln for five years.
qs.why: The passage says Eastbrook had two state champions and had won every match for five years.

title: A Day at the Recycling Plant
text: Every day, trucks bring tons of plastic bottles to the Greenway recycling plant. First, machines divide the bottles into groups by color. A simple mechanism of fast belts and air jets pushes each bottle into the right bin. Workers then clean the plastic and melt it down to convert it into small pieces, which factories use to make new bottles or clothing. The plant is efficient: it uses heat from its own machines to warm the building in winter. It also has solar panels on the roof that generate about a third of the power it needs. The manager, Mr. Petrov, wants a sustainable business that can run for decades without harming the land around it.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “convert” mean?
qs.why: The plastic is melted and changed into small pieces. Changing someone's religion is a different meaning of convert.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “generate” mean?
qs.why: The solar panels produce about a third of the plant's power. “Use up” is the opposite.

qs.q: How does the plant save energy in winter?
options: It closes during the coldest months.
It burns old plastic for heat.
It buys power from another factory.
It uses heat from its own machines to warm the building.
It turns off the air jets.
qs.why: The passage says it uses heat from its own machines to warm the building in winter.

title: The Lost Wallet
text: Last Tuesday, a bus driver named Luis Moreno found a brown wallet under a seat. Inside were three hundred dollars and a driver's license. Luis could have kept the money, but he called the owner, an older woman named Ruth Cohen. She was so grateful that she cried on the phone. She tried to give him fifty dollars, but he insisted that he did not want anything. Later, the bus company chose to praise him in its newsletter, calling him a model of integrity. Luis was humble about it. “I'm just an ordinary guy,” he told reporters. “Anyone would do the same.” His wife laughed and said that was not true.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “integrity” mean?
options: being honest and having strong moral standards
qs.why: Returning all the money showed honesty. “Being whole” is a different meaning of integrity.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “humble” mean?
options: not proud; not thinking he was better than others
qs.why: He said he was just an ordinary guy instead of boasting. “Poor” is another use of humble that does not fit here.

qs.q: What does Luis's wife's laugh suggest?
options: She thinks Luis kept the fifty dollars.
She does not believe the story is true.
She is angry that he talked to reporters.
She wanted the money for herself.
She thinks Luis is not ordinary because he is rich.
She thinks not everyone would return the money.
qs.why: She said it was not true that anyone would do the same, so she believes his honesty is unusual.

title: Learning to Swim at Forty
text: Tomás Herrera never learned to swim as a child, and for years he felt anxious whenever his kids splashed in the pool. At forty, he finally signed up for lessons. On the first day, he stood in the shallow end, where the water reached only his waist, and his heart was pounding. His teacher, Grace, offered calm guidance: breathe out slowly, relax your shoulders, trust the water. It took courage just to put his face under. Over ten weeks his progress was slow but steady. Now he swims a full length of the pool without stopping. He regrets only one thing, he says: that he waited so long to try.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “shallow” mean?
qs.why: The water reached only his waist, so it was not deep. “Not serious” is a different meaning of shallow.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “steady” mean?
options: even and regular, without big stops
qs.why: His progress kept going at an even pace, even though it was slow.

qs.q: What does Tomás feel sorry about now?
options: That he chose Grace as his teacher
That he stood in the shallow end
That he waited so many years to learn
That his kids splashed in the pool
That he cannot swim a full length
That the lessons lasted ten weeks
qs.why: He says his only regret is that he waited so long to try. He can now swim a full length.

title: The Weather Station
text: On a hill above the town of Hollowmere, a small weather station records the temperature, wind and rain every ten minutes. Its tools are precise, measuring temperature to one tenth of a degree. Students from the local college use the data to predict storms. Last winter they noticed a strange phenomenon: fog formed in the valley on clear nights while the hilltop stayed clear. A rapid drop in temperature after sunset seemed to cause it. The students found that the fog tended to occur when the wind was very light. Their charts now indicate the nights when drivers on the valley road should take extra care.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “phenomenon” mean?
options: something that can be seen happening, especially something unusual
qs.why: The fog in the valley was an unusual event they observed. “A very successful person” is another use of the word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “occur” mean?
qs.why: The fog tended to happen on nights with light wind.

qs.q: When does the valley fog tend to form?
options: On clear nights when the wind is very light
When the hilltop is foggy too
Early in the morning in summer
When the temperature rises after sunset
qs.why: The passage links the fog to clear nights, a quick drop in temperature and very light wind. The temperature falls, not rises.

title: A Tiny Bakery's Big Year
text: When Aisha Rahman left her office job to open a bakery, her friends worried. A new venture like this could easily fail in its first year. She chose to invest her savings in a good oven and fresh ingredients instead of a fancy shop sign. Within months, the bakery built a reputation for the best cardamom buns in the neighborhood, and people waited in line on weekends. She began to earn enough to pay two part-time workers. Now she plans to expand into the empty shop next door, which will add space for twelve tables. It will take considerable work, but Aisha says she has never been happier.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “venture” mean?
options: a new business that involves risk
qs.why: Opening a bakery was a new, risky business. Her friends worried it could fail.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “reputation” mean?
options: what people generally think of it
qs.why: People came to believe it had the best cardamom buns, based on what they tasted.

qs.q: Why did people wait in line on weekends?
options: It had a fancy new shop sign.
The bakery was known for having the best cardamom buns nearby.
It was the only shop open on weekends.
Aisha's office friends told everyone to go.
qs.why: The bakery built a reputation for the best cardamom buns. Aisha chose not to spend money on a fancy sign.

title: The Old Lighthouse
text: On a rocky island off the coast stands an old lighthouse that is now a small museum. It was formerly the home of a keeper and his family, who lived there for nearly thirty years. The island was so isolated that supplies arrived by boat only once a month. A local legend says the keeper's daughter once rowed out in a storm to rescue three fishermen. Nobody knows if the story is true. When the light became automatic, the family had to abandon the island and move to the mainland. Today visitors climb the tower to look at the horizon, where ships pass slowly far out at sea.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “legend” mean?
options: an old, well-known story that may not be true
the key that explains a map
qs.why: The story about the daughter is old and nobody knows if it is true. The key on a map is a different meaning.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “abandon” mean?
qs.why: The family left the island and moved to the mainland for good.

qs.q: What does “Nobody knows if the story is true” tell the reader?
options: The fishermen died in the storm.
The keeper's daughter is still alive.
The rescue may not have really happened.
The museum has proof of the rescue.
The story was invented by visitors last year.
qs.why: The line shows the story is a legend, so it might not be true. It does not say the story is false or invented recently.

title: A Four-Day Work Week
text: Last year, a small design company in Melbourne tried a four-day work week. The proposal came from a junior worker, Jack Nguyen, who sent a short plan to the owners. Initially, the owners were not sure; they worried that clients would be unhappy. They agreed to test it for six months and then evaluate the results. Staff kept the same pay but had to finish their work in four days. To improve efficiency, they cut long meetings and answered emails at set times. The outcome surprised everyone: projects were finished on time, and fewer people called in sick. The company also made the schedule flexible, so parents could choose which day to take off.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “evaluate” mean?
options: judge carefully how good something is
qs.why: After six months the owners would look carefully at how well the plan worked.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “initially” mean?
qs.why: The owners were unsure at the start but later agreed to test the plan. “In the end” is the opposite.

qs.q: What was one change staff made to finish their work in four days?
options: They worked twelve hours each day.
They cut long meetings and answered emails at set times.
qs.why: The passage says they cut long meetings and answered emails at set times. Their pay stayed the same.

title: Moving to a New Country
text: When Yuki's family moved abroad to Germany for her mother's job, Yuki was eleven and spoke no German. The first months were hard. At school she felt a deep sense of isolation, sitting alone at lunch while other children chatted. She tried to cope by drawing in her notebook and writing long emails to friends in Osaka. Her teacher helped with the transition by pairing her with a classmate, Leni, who spoke a little English. The two girls learned to communicate with words, hand signs and many drawings. Slowly Yuki got used to the new routines, like cycling to school in the rain. Nowadays she even dreams in two languages.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “isolation” mean?
options: being alone and cut off from others
qs.why: She sat alone at lunch while others chatted, so she felt alone and separated.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “cope” mean?
qs.why: Drawing and writing to friends helped her manage a hard time. “Give up” is the opposite.

qs.q: How did Yuki's teacher help her?
options: She taught Yuki German after school.
She paired Yuki with a classmate who spoke some English.
She let Yuki eat lunch in the classroom.
She sent emails to Yuki's friends in Osaka.
She moved Yuki to a Japanese school.
qs.why: The teacher paired her with Leni, who spoke a little English.

title: Fixing the Bridge
text: In April, engineers closed the old Mill Street bridge after finding large cracks in its supports. They feared it could collapse under heavy trucks. The bridge is a key part of the town's infrastructure, carrying more than five thousand cars a day. Workers put up a barrier at both ends, and the town built a temporary metal bridge a little further down the river. Engineers will examine every beam before deciding whether to repair or replace the old bridge. For now, a speed limit of fifteen miles an hour is mandatory on the new bridge, and police are checking drivers' speed.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “collapse” mean?
options: fold up neatly to save space
fall down suddenly because it is weak
qs.why: The cracks meant the bridge might suddenly fall. Folding up is a different meaning of collapse.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “mandatory” mean?
options: required by a rule, so drivers must obey it
qs.why: Police are checking speed, so the limit must be followed. “Suggested” is the opposite.

qs.q: Why did the town build the metal bridge?
options: To replace the old bridge forever
To give police a place to check speed
So people could still cross the river while the old bridge was closed
Because engineers finished repairing the old bridge
qs.why: The old bridge was closed, so the temporary bridge let traffic keep crossing. It is temporary, not forever.

title: The Photography Contest
text: The library's photography contest is open to anyone over sixteen who lives in the county. Younger people are not eligible this year, but there will be a youth contest in the spring. Each person may submit up to three photos by email. To avoid bias, the judges see the photos without names, so every entry is anonymous until the winners are chosen. Last year's winning picture, by a grandfather named Faisal Karim, showed a gray heron standing on the edge of a frozen pond. The judges called it striking because of the bright orange sunset behind the bird. They said it showed excellent judgment about light and timing.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “anonymous” mean?
qs.why: The judges see the photos without names. “Very famous” is close to the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “striking” mean?
options: so unusual that it catches your attention right away
qs.why: The bright sunset behind the gray bird made the photo stand out. Hitting and refusing to work are other uses of strike.

qs.q: Why do the judges see the photos without names?
options: Because most people forget to add names
So the photos can be printed faster
Because the library lost the names
So they judge each photo fairly, without favoring anyone
qs.why: Hiding names is done “to avoid bias,” so judges cannot favor people they know.

title: The Night Market
text: Every Friday evening, the parking lot behind the Riverside mall turns into a night market. More than sixty stalls sell food from around the world, and the crowd is just as diverse as the menu. You can eat Filipino barbecue, Ethiopian lentils and Mexican corn while standing at a small table. The mood is casual; people wear sandals and chat with strangers in line. Some stalls offer elaborate dishes, like a Peruvian chicken plate with five sauces, while others sell simple fried dough. The market has become an important center of local commerce, helping new cooks test their recipes. Apart from an occasional rainy night, it is always busy, and the sellers are generous with free samples.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “casual” mean?
qs.why: Sandals and chatting with strangers show a relaxed mood. “By chance” is another meaning of casual.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “occasional” mean?
qs.why: Rainy nights happen only now and then. “For a special event” is a careless reading based on occasion.

qs.q: How does the market help new cooks?
options: They are paid by the mall.
They can cook only on rainy nights.
They can try out their recipes on real customers.
qs.why: The passage says the market helps new cooks test their recipes.

title: The Debate Team Disagreement
text: Before the regional final, the debate team at Ridgeview High faced a problem: they could not agree on how to begin their speech. Daniel wanted to open with a funny story, while Fatima thought a list of facts was more logical. The two began to argue in the library, and the tension grew so strong that nobody else wanted to speak. Their coach, Mr. Lindqvist, asked each of them to explain their stance in two minutes without being interrupted. Then the team voted, and there was a clear consensus. Almost everyone liked a mix: start with a short story, then move quickly to facts. That plan helped resolve the fight, and they won the round.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “stance” mean?
options: the way you stand with your feet
qs.why: Each student explained what they thought about how to start. The way you stand is a different meaning.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “consensus” mean?
options: a count of all the people
agreement among all or most of the group
qs.why: After the vote almost everyone agreed on the mix. “A count of people” is a careless reading, like census.

qs.q: What plan did the team finally choose?
options: Begin with a short story, then move quickly to facts.
Begin with a long list of facts.
Let the coach write the speech.
Skip the opening and start with questions.
qs.why: Most members liked a mix: a short story first, then facts.

title: A Hike Across the Lava
text: Last summer, Sofia and her brother joined a guided hike to explore a lava field in Iceland. The guide, Bjorn, was strict about safety: stay on the marked path, and never walk toward the steam vents. He explained that some gases from the ground can be toxic and make people very ill. The heat near the newer lava was intense, even though the air was cool. At the top of the ridge, they stopped to marvel at the view: black rock stretched for miles, with green moss growing in the cracks. Sofia said the sheer size of the land made her feel tiny. They walked back slowly, tired but thrilled.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “sheer” mean?
options: complete and total; used to show how great something is
qs.why: “The sheer size” stresses how huge the land was. “Very steep” and “thin” are other meanings of sheer.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “marvel” mean?
options: look at with great surprise and admiration
qs.why: They stopped to enjoy and wonder at the amazing view.

qs.q: Why did Bjorn tell the group never to walk toward the steam vents?
options: The vents were closed for repairs.
The moss near the vents was rare.
Gases there can be poisonous and make people very ill.
The view was better from the path.
The group was too tired to walk far.
The air near the vents was too cold.
qs.why: He explained that some gases from the ground can be toxic.

title: Changes to School Lunch
text: This fall, the Oakdale school district decided to implement a new lunch plan. Its main goal is to eliminate sugary drinks from school cafeterias and serve water and milk instead. Nurses had noticed that many students drank an excessive amount of soda, sometimes three cans a day. The new menu still includes treats, but in moderate amounts, such as a small cookie on Fridays. Some parents have offered criticism, saying children should be free to choose what they drink. Others believe the change will be beneficial, especially for students' teeth and energy in afternoon classes. The district will survey families in June to see how the plan is working.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “excessive” mean?
options: more than is normal or reasonable
qs.why: Three cans of soda a day is far too much. “Very small” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “moderate” mean?
options: not too much and not too little
qs.why: A small cookie on Fridays is a reasonable, limited amount of treats.

qs.q: What is the main goal of the new lunch plan?
options: To make lunch free for everyone
To let children choose any drink
To serve lunch later in the afternoon
To remove sugary drinks from school cafeterias
qs.why: The passage says the main goal is to eliminate sugary drinks. Treats are still served in small amounts.

title: Finding Lost Cousins
text: When Nadia Khoury's grandmother turned ninety, Nadia decided to trace the family's history. She started with an old shoebox of letters. The first clue was a postcard from Brazil, written in Arabic in 1924. Nadia read through the letters thoroughly, noting every name and date. To obtain more facts, she wrote to a church in São Paulo and asked for copies of its old records. The records would reveal something unexpected: her great-grandfather had a twin brother who stayed in Brazil and opened a fabric shop. Last year, Nadia flew to São Paulo and met twenty cousins she had never known about.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “trace” mean?
options: copy a drawing by going over its lines
find where something came from by following it back
qs.why: Nadia followed her family's history back through letters and records. Copying a drawing is a different meaning of trace.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “thoroughly” mean?
qs.why: She paid attention to every name and date. “Only partly” is the opposite.

qs.q: What surprising fact did the records show?
options: Her grandmother was born in São Paulo.
Her great-grandfather had a twin brother who stayed in Brazil.
The postcard was written in Portuguese.
Her great-grandfather opened a fabric shop.
The church had lost all its records.
qs.why: The records revealed the twin brother. It was the twin, not the great-grandfather, who opened the shop.

title: The Noise Upstairs
text: For months, the people in apartment 4B played loud music late at night. Mrs. Ito, who lives below, knocked on their door twice, but a young man answered and was rude, shutting the door in her face. Finally, the building manager, Mr. Diallo, invited both sides to a meeting. He stayed neutral and let each person speak. Mrs. Ito spoke frankly: she had not slept well in weeks. The young man, Kofi, explained that he works night shifts and practices guitar when he gets home. He offered an apology for the way he had acted. Together they found a way to settle the problem: Kofi now plays with headphones after ten o'clock. The respect between them is now mutual.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “neutral” mean?
qs.why: Mr. Diallo let each person speak without supporting one side. “No bright color” is another meaning of neutral.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “settle” mean?
options: move to live in a new place
qs.why: They agreed on headphones after ten o'clock, which ended the problem.

qs.q: Why did Kofi play music late at night?
options: He wanted to annoy Mrs. Ito.
He did not know anyone lived below.
He was having parties every night.
Mr. Diallo told him it was allowed.
He works night shifts and practices guitar when he gets home.
qs.why: Kofi explained that he works night shifts and practices when he gets home.

title: Saving for a First Car
text: Maya, a nursing student in Toronto, wants to buy a used car before her hospital training starts in September. That date is her deadline, because the hospital is far from any bus line. Each month she saves roughly two hundred dollars from her part-time job at a pharmacy. It means a real sacrifice: no new clothes and very few meals out. Still, she worries that her savings will not be sufficient. Because of inflation, the price of used cars has gone up over the past year, so the same money buys less. Her father suggested a more practical choice: a smaller, older car that is cheap to repair and uses less gas.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “inflation” mean?
options: a general rise in prices, so money buys less
qs.why: Car prices have gone up, so her money buys less. Filling tires with air is a different meaning of inflation.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “sufficient” mean?
qs.why: She worries she will not have enough money for a car.

qs.q: Why is September Maya's deadline?
options: Her hospital training starts then, and the hospital is far from buses.
Car prices will drop in September.
Her job at the pharmacy ends then.
Her father will lend her money then.
She will finish her nursing degree then.
The car shop closes in September.
qs.why: Her training starts in September and the hospital is far from any bus line, so she needs a car by then.

title: The Community Choir
text: The Eastside Community Choir has forty members, from teenagers to a woman of eighty-two. Their director, Hana Kowalski, is passionate about music and believes anyone can learn to sing. Her practices are demanding: two hours every Tuesday, plus work at home. Joining the choir is a real commitment, and members promise to miss no more than two practices before a concert. At the spring concert, the choir sang a song in four parts, with each group singing a different line simultaneously. The result was impressive; the audience stood and clapped for a full minute. Afterward, the singing seemed to inspire many listeners, who asked how they could join.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “demanding” mean?
options: needing a lot of time and effort
qs.why: Two hours a week plus home practice takes a lot of time and effort. “Short and easy” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “simultaneously” mean?
qs.why: Each group sang its own line at the same time as the others. “One after another” is a careless reading.

qs.q: What can you tell about how the audience felt about the concert?
options: They thought it was too long.
They were bored by the four parts.
They only came to see the director.
They wanted the choir to practice more.
They liked it very much, and some even wanted to sing too.
qs.why: They stood and clapped for a full minute, and many asked how to join.

title: A Critic Meets a Tart
text: Marisol Vega has been an epicure since childhood, when her grandmother taught her to taste the difference between real vanilla and the cheap imitation some bakers secretly use to adulterate cakes they sell as 'pure vanilla.' Now she writes a weekly food column, and last month she visited a tiny bakery on Fulton Street. The owner, a quiet man named Tomasz, served her a slice of plum tart so toothsome that she asked for the recipe on the spot. He only laughed and slipped a small almond cookie into her bag as lagniappe. Marisol is usually abstemious, skipping dessert most nights and drinking only water with dinner, but that afternoon she ate two slices and watched the regulars quaff strong coffee at the counter while they argued happily about football. Her column the next week was the warmest she had written all year.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “adulterate” mean?
options: decorate with extra layers of cream
bake for too long until dry
make richer by adding real vanilla
sell at a higher price than usual
make worse by secretly mixing in something cheaper
qs.why: Some bakers secretly mix cheap imitation vanilla into cakes they sell as pure vanilla, which lowers their quality. It does not mean making them richer, which is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “lagniappe” mean?
options: a sample she had asked to try
a small extra gift given for free
a coupon for her next visit
qs.why: Tomasz slipped a free cookie into her bag on top of what she had; she had not asked for it or paid for it.

qs.q: Why was it unusual that Marisol ate two slices that afternoon?
options: Her doctor had told her never to eat sugar.
She normally eats and drinks very moderately and skips dessert.
She had disliked plum tart as a child.
The owner did not want to sell her a second slice.
She was planning to write a bad review.
She had never visited a bakery before.
qs.why: The passage says she is usually abstemious, skipping dessert and drinking only water, so two slices broke her normal habit.

title: One Goal in the Last Minute
text: The Riverside under-twelve soccer team lost their first match of the season 5–0, a result that seemed to chasten even the loudest players. Coach Adaeze Okafor did not shout. She worked indefatigably with them all week, arriving before dawn to set out cones and staying until the field lights went off. Her ebullience was hard to resist; she cheered every good pass in practice as if it had won a trophy. By the second match, a new bonhomie had grown among the boys and girls, who now shared snacks and gave each other high fives after every drill. The game stayed scoreless until the final minute, when a miscue by the other team's goalkeeper left the ball loose in front of the net. Riverside's striker tapped it in for a 1–0 win. The players exulted, running in circles and hugging their coach, who laughed until she cried.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “chasten” mean?
options: make them want to quit the team
make them more humble and quiet
make them proud of their effort
qs.why: After a 5–0 loss even the loudest players were humbled. It did not make them louder or prouder.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “miscue” mean?
qs.why: The goalkeeper's error left the ball loose, which let Riverside score; it was an accident, not a trick.

qs.q: What best explains the change in the team between the two matches?
options: The coach shouted at the players after the first loss.
Older, more skilled players joined the team.
The players practiced less and rested more.
The coach's tireless work and cheerful energy brought the players closer together.
The striker trained alone every morning.
The referee favored Riverside in the second match.
qs.why: The passage stresses her tireless practices and her cheer, after which a friendly team spirit grew. It says outright that she did not shout.

title: The Shell Collector
text: Hamid Rostami left school at fifteen to work in his uncle's print shop, but he became an autodidact of rare skill, reading every book on geology he could borrow from the library. By forty he was an expert on a recondite subject: the tiny fossil shells found in the cliffs near his town. Professors who once ignored him began to write letters asking him to explicate his findings. In a lecture at the local museum, he propounded a bold theory that the cliffs had once been the floor of a shallow, warm sea. To support it, he adduced dozens of shells that closely matched kinds still living in tropical waters today. His explanation was so pellucid that even the schoolchildren in the front row nodded along, and one girl went home and started her own collection.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “recondite” mean?
options: little known and hard to understand without special knowledge
qs.why: Tiny fossil shells are a narrow subject few people know about. The shells come from cliffs, but the word does not mean buried or hidden underground.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “adduced” mean?
qs.why: He used the shells 'to support' his theory, so he presented them as proof, not simply collected or displayed them.

qs.q: What does the passage suggest about Hamid's lack of formal schooling?
options: It made professors refuse to listen to him for the rest of his life.
It did not stop him from becoming a respected expert.
It meant his theory about the cliffs was wrong.
It forced him to give up geology for printing.
It made his lecture too difficult for children.
It is the reason he worked at the museum.
qs.why: Professors who once ignored him later wrote asking for his explanations, showing he earned respect despite leaving school early.

title: Hard Times at the Workshop
text: When sales at the Okonkwo furniture company fell for the third year in a row, the founder's son, Emeka, had to retrench. He closed one of the two workshops and cut his own emolument by half before touching anyone else's pay. Some perquisites disappeared too, such as the free lunch on Fridays and the company van that workers could borrow on weekends. Several employees called him a skinflint behind his back, but others noticed that he still drove his old, rusty car. His father had been famous for being munificent, giving large sums to the town's hospital and library, and Emeka feared being remembered as the son who let it all fall apart. Yet he remembered the years before the business took off, when the family was so impecunious that dinner was often just bread and soup. He knew careful saving now could keep forty families employed.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “retrench” mean?
options: move the business to a new town
cut back spending and reduce the business
hire more workers to raise sales
sell the company to a rival
dig new foundations for a workshop
qs.why: He closed a workshop and cut pay and benefits, all ways of spending less because of money trouble.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “perquisites” mean?
options: extra benefits that come with the job
qs.why: The free Friday lunch and the borrowable van are extras on top of pay, not the pay itself.

qs.q: Why do some employees pay attention to Emeka's old, rusty car?
options: It proves the company is about to close.
It shows he has lost interest in the business.
It is one of the benefits that was taken away.
It shows he is as generous as his father.
It means he plans to sell the company van.
It suggests he is not keeping money for himself while cutting costs.
qs.why: Against the charge that he is stingy, the old car shows he is not spending on himself, which fits his cutting his own pay first.

title: Change on Delmar Avenue
text: When the first coffee shop selling forty-dollar bags of beans opened on Delmar Avenue, longtime residents had their misgivings. Within five years, the neighborhood began to gentrify quickly: old laundromats became yoga studios, and rents nearly doubled. New businesses burgeoned along the main street, and city leaders praised the 'revival.' But disgruntlement grew among families who had lived there for decades and could now barely afford their apartments. At one public meeting, a retired bus driver named Luis Moreno warned that the area was being homogenized, its corner shops and family restaurants replaced by the same chain stores found in every other city. Some called him a naysayer who feared all change. Luis disagreed. 'I'm not against new things,' he said. 'I just want my grandchildren to be able to live here too.'

qs.q: In the passage, what does “homogenized” mean?
options: made the same as everywhere else, losing what made it different
made more expensive to live in
qs.why: Luis means unique local shops were being replaced with the same chains found in every city. Rents did rise, but that is not what this word describes.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “naysayer” mean?
options: a person who always expects plans to fail and argues against them
a person who agrees with every new idea
a new resident of the area
a person who owns a chain store
a person who refuses to vote
qs.why: His critics claimed he opposed all change; Luis answered that he was not against new things.

qs.q: What is Luis's main concern?
options: That coffee shops and yoga studios are unhealthy.
That the city should ban all new businesses.
That the main street has become too quiet.
That he cannot buy property cheaply.
That the bus routes have been changed.
That families like his may no longer be able to afford to live in the area.
qs.why: His final words say he wants his grandchildren to be able to live there, and the passage notes rising rents squeezing long-time families.

title: The Treasurer's Trial
text: The bank's former treasurer, Gordon Pratt, was arraigned on a gray Monday morning and charged with taking nearly two million dollars from customer accounts. At his trial that autumn, his lawyer insisted the files would exculpate him, claiming a computer error had moved the money. On the witness stand, when the prosecutor asked where the funds had gone, Pratt prevaricated, talking about 'complex transfers' and 'timing issues' without ever giving a clear answer. Then the prosecutor revealed a darker detail: Pratt had tried to suborn a young clerk, offering her ten thousand dollars to tell the court she had made the transfers herself. The clerk refused and went straight to the police. Her recording of his phone call showed incontrovertibly that Pratt knew exactly what he was doing. By the end of the trial, the local paper was calling him 'the embezzler of Elm Street.'

qs.q: In the passage, what does “prevaricated” mean?
options: asked for more time to prepare
avoided a direct, honest answer by speaking vaguely
qs.why: On the stand he talked about vague 'complex transfers' without a clear answer. He did speak, so 'refused to speak' is wrong.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “suborn” mean?
options: hire someone as an honest witness
train someone to make bank transfers
secretly pay someone to do something illegal, such as lie in court
qs.why: He offered the clerk money to give false testimony, which is exactly this kind of illegal bribe.

qs.q: What showed beyond doubt that Pratt knew what he was doing?
options: A report proving a computer error moved the money.
The clerk admitting that she made the transfers.
His lawyer turning against him in court.
His own confession to the judge.
The clerk's recording of his call offering her money to lie.
An investigation by the local newspaper.
qs.why: The clerk's recording of his phone call showed incontrovertibly that he knew what he was doing. The computer-error story was only his lawyer's claim.

title: Rain on the Long Train
text: For the first two hours, the train crossed farmland where wheat fields undulated in the wind like a golden sea. The afternoon heat was fierce, and passengers sweltered in the old carriages, fanning themselves with maps and newspapers. Even the children grew somnolent, their heads drooping onto their parents' shoulders. Then, near the mountains, the sky turned dark purple, and a sudden cloudburst hit the roof so hard that conversation stopped. Ten minutes later the rain was gone, and the air smelled of wet earth. As evening came, the train climbed past serried rows of pine trees standing as close as soldiers. Kenji Watanabe, traveling alone to visit his sister, watched the lambent glow of a farmhouse lamp flicker across the valley and felt, for the first time in months, completely at peace.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “serried” mean?
qs.why: The trees stand 'as close as soldiers,' which describes tightly packed rows, the opposite of spread apart.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “lambent” mean?
qs.why: The lamp's light flickers gently across the valley, a soft, uneven glow rather than a steady or harsh one.

qs.q: How does the mood of the journey change?
options: It moves from peaceful to frightening and stays tense.
It stays hot and uncomfortable from start to finish.
It becomes lonely and sad once Kenji is alone.
It moves from cheerful to boring as the children sleep.
It moves from hot and tiring, through a sudden storm, to calm and peaceful.
It becomes dangerous when the train reaches the mountains.
qs.why: The heat makes people tired, a brief heavy rain passes, and the evening ends with Kenji feeling completely at peace.

title: The Girl at the Piano
text: Priya Raman's precocity showed itself early: at four, she could play any song she heard on the radio, though she was completely untutored and could not read a single note. Her parents worried about how to raise her. Her grandmother warned them not to mollycoddle the girl or protect her from every disappointment. 'Let her fail sometimes,' she said. So they found a strict teacher, Mr. Halloran, who made Priya practice scales for an hour each day. At first she hated it. She was scatterbrained about everything except music, leaving her shoes in the garden and her homework on the bus. But slowly the routine habituated her to hard work, and by nine she was practicing without being asked. Her first prize at a regional competition heartened the whole family, especially her grandmother, who sat in the front row smiling.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “mollycoddle” mean?
options: send away to a special school
treat too gently and protect too much
qs.why: The grandmother explains it herself: do not protect her from every disappointment, let her fail sometimes.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “untutored” mean?
options: had had no lessons or formal training
was taught only by her grandmother
qs.why: She played by ear but could not read music, because no one had taught her. She clearly had talent, so 'no talent' is wrong.

qs.q: What changed Priya most over the years?
options: Her grandmother gave her piano lessons.
She stopped being forgetful about everything.
Winning a prize made her love music for the first time.
A daily routine with a strict teacher made her used to hard work.
Her parents protected her from every failure.
She learned to read notes before she was four.
qs.why: The passage says the routine slowly made her used to hard work until she practiced without being asked.

title: Trouble on the Fourth Floor
text: The marketing department at Halvorsen Foods had become so factious that the two teams on the fourth floor barely spoke to each other. Everyone knew the cause. Victor Lindqvist, the department's deputy head, was famous for his careerism, and he would do anything to rise. His sycophancy toward the chief executive was embarrassing to watch; he laughed at her weakest jokes and praised every idea she mentioned. Meanwhile, his machinations behind the scenes kept the teams fighting, since a divided department was easier to control. He relied on a small circle of apparatchiks who repeated his views in every meeting without question. When a new director arrived, she saw within a week that Victor's only goal was to aggrandize himself. Her first decision was to merge the two teams and put a quiet, honest analyst in charge.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “sycophancy” mean?
options: honest admiration for a good leader
insincere flattery of a powerful person to win favor
qs.why: Laughing at her weakest jokes and praising every idea is fake flattery aimed at someone with power, not honest admiration.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “apparatchiks” mean?
options: independent experts who advise the company
loyal followers who repeat a leader's views without question
qs.why: They 'repeated his views in every meeting without question,' which is the mark of an unthinking loyal follower.

qs.q: Why did Victor keep the two teams fighting?
options: He wanted the teams to compete for higher sales.
The chief executive asked him to do it.
He personally disliked both team leaders.
He hoped the teams would be merged.
He believed conflict made people more creative.
A divided department was easier for him to control.
qs.why: The passage states it directly: a divided department was easier to control.

title: Recovery in the Orchard
text: After six weeks in the hospital with a severe lung infection, Rafael Torres came home to convalesce at his daughter's farmhouse. The illness had debilitated him badly; he could barely climb the porch steps without resting. His doctors were worried about his emaciation, since he had lost nearly thirty pounds, and they ordered three full meals a day. For the first weeks, a deep lassitude kept him in bed until noon, staring at the ceiling. His daughter believed in the recuperative power of fresh air, so each afternoon she helped him to a chair in the orchard. Slowly, things changed. He began eating his granddaughter's pancakes with real appetite, and one morning the family found him in the garden pulling weeds, enervated by the effort but smiling for the first time since spring.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “lassitude” mean?
options: tiredness and a lack of energy or interest
a habit of sleeping late for fun
qs.why: He lay in bed until noon staring at the ceiling, which shows weariness and no interest in doing anything, not pain or fever.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “recuperative” mean?
options: helping someone get back health and strength
qs.why: She took him to the orchard because she believed fresh air would help him recover.

qs.q: What does the scene of Rafael pulling weeds show?
options: He was growing stronger, though the work still tired him.
He had fully recovered and no longer felt tired.
He was bored and wanted to leave the farm.
His daughter was forcing him to do chores.
He no longer needed to eat full meals.
He was ignoring his doctors' orders to rest.
qs.why: He was working and smiling, a clear sign of progress, but he was still drained by the effort, so he was not fully well.

title: The Night of the Penguin
text: When the lead actor's train was delayed, the director of the small Brightwater Theatre walked onto the stage and announced that tonight's show would be unrehearsed: she would ask the audience for ideas, and the cast would invent a play around them. The crowd loved it. Someone shouted 'a lost penguin,' and the actors began at once, speaking extempore as they built the story. Abdul Karim, a large man with a stentorian voice, played a ship's captain who declaimed long speeches to the sea, gesticulating wildly with both arms. The youngest actor, Lena, stole the night with a quick witticism about penguins wearing tuxedos to work. By the final bow, several people said it was the best evening they had ever spent in that theatre, and the director wondered whether the delayed train had been a gift.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “stentorian” mean?
qs.why: A captain shouting long speeches to the sea fits a huge, booming voice.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “extempore” mean?
options: without preparation, making it up on the spot
qs.why: The actors invented the play from the audience's ideas at once, with no script and no practice.

qs.q: Why might the director think the delayed train 'had been a gift'?
options: The lead actor arrived in time for the final bow.
The theatre sold more tickets because of the delay.
She disliked the play they had planned to perform.
The train company paid the theatre for the trouble.
The delay led to an evening the audience enjoyed more than a normal show.
It gave the cast an extra night to rehearse.
qs.why: Because the actor was missing, the cast improvised, and several people called it the best evening they had spent there.

title: The Strictest Lab
text: Dr. Ingrid Solberg was the most punctilious scientist in the building. Every test tube in her lab was labeled with the date, the time and the name of the person who prepared it, and she checked the labels herself each Friday. New students found the stringency of her rules exhausting at first, but they soon understood why: a single mixed-up sample could ruin a year of work. She was just as strict about writing. When her students sent her drafts of their papers, she emended them fastidiously, fixing every misplaced comma and doubtful number. She also prized concision, often cutting a ten-page draft down to six. 'Say it once, and say it clearly,' she liked to tell them. Some students grumbled that she cared about every nicety of grammar, but their papers were almost always accepted by the first journal they tried.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “stringency” mean?
options: how few of them there were
how strict and demanding they were
qs.why: Students found the rules exhausting because they were so strict, and the reason given is that one mistake could ruin a year of work.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “concision” mean?
options: saying things clearly using only the words that are needed
qs.why: She cut ten pages to six and told students to say things once and clearly.

qs.q: What do the results of her strictness suggest?
options: It made students leave her lab in large numbers.
It caused many papers to be rejected.
It helped her students produce strong work.
It mattered only for test tubes, not writing.
It showed she did not trust her students to work.
It slowed the lab so much that little research was done.
qs.why: Her students' papers were almost always accepted by the first journal they tried, and they came to understand why her rules mattered.

title: Uncle Kofi's Holidays
text: Every December, the whole Mensah family gathered at Uncle Kofi's house, and every year he took charge of the children. He was avuncular in the truest sense, patient with the little ones and happy to answer their endless questions about the stars. He also had a puckish streak. One year he hid every left shoe in the house inside the freezer; another year he replaced the sugar in the bowl with salt just before his brother made tea. The adults pretended to be angry, but the badinage between Kofi and his brothers was the best part of the holiday. Over dinner, they traded one wisecrack after another while the children laughed until their stomachs hurt. Even Grandma, who rarely smiled, would shake her head jovially and say that the house had never been so mirthful.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “puckish” mean?
