options: playful and fond of harmless tricks
qs.why: Hiding shoes in the freezer and swapping sugar for salt are harmless jokes, not cruel acts.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “badinage” mean?
qs.why: The adults only pretended to be angry, and the brothers traded jokes, so their talk was playful teasing.

qs.q: How did the adults really feel about Kofi's tricks?
options: They were truly angry and asked him to stop.
They enjoyed them, even though they acted annoyed.
They found them childish and left early.
They did not notice them at all.
They thought the tricks scared the children.
They blamed the children for the tricks.
qs.why: The passage says the adults 'pretended' to be angry and that the joking was the best part of the holiday.

title: Saving Kestrel Rock
text: For two centuries, the small island of Kestrel Rock suffered from the depredations of rats that had arrived on whaling ships. The rats ate seabird eggs by the thousands, and their baneful effect on the island's wildlife was plain: of eleven nesting species, only four remained. Some scientists feared the damage was irremediable. Then, in a five-year project, conservation workers set out to extirpate the rats completely, checking every cave and cliff for survivors. Visitors were also banned from certain beaches, since careless tourists had begun to despoil them with litter and broken glass. The work succeeded. Today, with the rats gone, the birds are returning, and the island's plants grow untrammeled across the hills. Several species once thought lost have nested there again, proving that some harm can be undone after all.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “extirpate” mean?
options: remove them completely so that none are left
feed them to keep them away from nests
qs.why: Workers searched every cave and cliff for survivors, and the passage ends 'with the rats gone,' so the aim was total removal.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “untrammeled” mean?
options: in neat rows planted by workers
freely, without anything holding them back
qs.why: With the rats gone and visitors limited, plants spread freely. 'Trampled' only sounds similar.

qs.q: What do the returning birds show about the scientists' early fears?
options: The scientists were right that nothing could be done.
The damage was not as permanent as some had feared.
The rats were never really the problem.
Tourists caused more harm than the rats.
Only four species will ever nest there.
The birds came back before the rats were removed.
qs.why: Some scientists feared the harm could not be fixed, but the passage ends by saying it can be undone after all.

title: Letter from the Lighthouse
text: Dear Clara, I write from the lighthouse on a stormy night, with a strange presentiment that the fishing boats will need our light more than usual. With the wind howling, I have felt disquieted all evening, and I cannot settle by the fire. The gulls cry plaintively outside the window, as though calling for someone who will not come. Father looks careworn these days; the long winters have added lines to his face, and he sleeps too little. Yesterday the harbor master came to forewarn us that a great storm was moving up the coast, so we have filled every lamp and checked every window. Still, I take comfort in Father's unfaltering courage. He has climbed those iron stairs every night for thirty years, and he says he will climb them tonight as well. Write soon. Your loving sister, Margit

qs.q: In the passage, what does “presentiment” mean?
options: an official report about the weather
a memory of an earlier storm
a written plan for the night
a promise made to her sister
a feeling that something is about to happen
qs.why: Margit senses that the boats will need the light more than usual; it is a feeling about what is coming, not a report or a memory.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “careworn” mean?
options: tired and sad after a long time of worry
qs.why: The lines on his face and his lack of sleep after long hard winters show long worry and strain.

qs.q: What does Margit find most comforting?
options: The harbor master's promise that the storm will miss them.
Her father's steady courage in doing his duty every night.
The sound of the gulls outside the window.
Sitting warm and calm beside the fire.
Knowing the fishing boats stayed in the harbor.
Her sister's plan to visit soon.
qs.why: She writes, 'I take comfort in Father's unfaltering courage,' then describes him climbing the stairs every night for thirty years.

title: The Bridge Meeting
text: At the town meeting about the delayed bridge repair, residents wanted one simple answer: when would the bridge open? The engineering company's spokesman, Mr. Fairbanks, began to equivocate almost immediately. He spoke of 'dynamic schedules' and 'ongoing reviews,' a long circumlocution that left the crowd more confused than before. When a teacher asked whether the bridge would be ready before winter, he answered evasively that 'many factors were still in play.' Then the town's head engineer, Deborah Achebe, stood up. She was known as a plainspoken woman, and she answered forthrightly: 'No. It will not be ready until April, because the steel arrived late.' The room went quiet, then broke into applause. Mr. Fairbanks spoke only guardedly for the rest of the evening, choosing each word as if it might explode.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “circumlocution” mean?
options: a drawing of the new bridge
using many words to avoid saying something directly
qs.why: His talk of 'dynamic schedules' and 'ongoing reviews' was long and roundabout and left people more confused.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “guardedly” mean?
qs.why: He chose 'each word as if it might explode,' meaning he spoke with great caution. It has nothing to do with real guards.

qs.q: Why did the crowd applaud?
options: The bridge would open before winter after all.
Mr. Fairbanks apologized for the delay.
The teacher's question was very funny.
The company promised to pay for the delay.
Deborah announced that the steel had arrived early.
Deborah finally gave a clear, honest answer, even though it was bad news.
qs.why: Her answer was a direct 'No' with a date and reason, which the crowd valued after the spokesman's vague replies.

title: A Day at the Wildlife Park
text: Our visit to the wildlife park began at the elephant house, where a young pachyderm named Tika followed her mother through a muddy pool. In the farm section, two lambs gamboled across the grass, kicking up their heels. The children's favorite, though, was the bear keeper, Mr. Brandt, a thickset man with a gray beard and an almost ursine way of moving, slow and heavy but surprisingly gentle. He let the kids watch through glass as two young otters cavorted in their pond, sliding down a rock again and again. Last came the lions, cared for by Mrs. Ruiz, a tall woman with a leonine mane of white hair. The old male lion lay in the sun and barely opened an eye at the crowd. My daughter, Amara, decided on the spot that she wanted to work at the park when she grew up.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “ursine” mean?
qs.why: Mr. Brandt, the bear keeper, moves 'slow and heavy but surprisingly gentle,' which compares him to a bear.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “cavorted” mean?
options: jumped and played around in a lively way
qs.why: The otters slid down a rock again and again, which is lively, playful movement.

qs.q: What links the descriptions of the two keepers?
options: Both are described as old and slow.
Both are known for being strict with children.
Both are afraid of the animals they care for.
Each one is said to look or move like the animal they care for.
qs.why: The bear keeper moves like a bear and the lion keeper has lion-like hair, a deliberate match with their animals.

title: A Novelist's Rise and Fall
text: In her twenties, the novelist Rosa Delgado was lionized by the literary world. Magazines put her face on their covers, and one famous critic wrote an encomium so glowing that her publisher printed it on the back of every copy. Ten years later, the same critic lambasted her third novel as 'lazy, vain and empty.' Other reviewers soon joined in, and a polemicist known for his attacks on popular writers published a vituperative essay calling her 'the most overrated author of the decade.' Rosa stopped reading reviews altogether. She moved to a small coastal town and spent four years on her next book. When it finally appeared, even the critics who had excoriated her admitted it was her best work, and the novel won a national prize that spring.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “encomium” mean?
options: a piece of writing full of very high praise
a short summary of the book
an advertisement written by her publisher
qs.why: It was 'so glowing' that the publisher printed it on the book, which means it praised her highly.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “lionized” mean?
options: treated as a celebrity and given great attention and praise
qs.why: Her face was put on magazine covers and critics praised her, signs of being celebrated.

qs.q: What does Rosa's story suggest about critics' opinions?
options: They are always fair and accurate.
They never affect how a writer works.
They only praise writers who live in cities.
Once negative, they can never become positive again.
They can change sharply over time.
They matter less than magazine covers.
qs.why: The same critic who praised her later attacked her, and those who attacked her later called her new book her best.

title: Midnight at the Patel House
text: The college graduation party at the Patel house was meant to be a quiet dinner, but by nine o'clock it had turned almost bacchanalian. Cousins arrived from three cities, a neighbor brought a sound system, and someone hung flashing lights from every tree. Amid all the razzmatazz, the young graduates caroused in the backyard, clinking bottles of beer, singing loudly and dancing on the picnic table. Older relatives overindulged too, especially on Aunt Leela's famous sweets, which vanished within an hour. Only Ravi's grandfather, a doctor who had spent his career warning patients about intemperance, stayed calm and sipped his tea. When he finally asked everyone to lower the music at midnight, a few teenagers called him a spoilsport. He simply smiled, reminding them that the neighbors had to work in the morning, and the party ended peacefully soon after.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “razzmatazz” mean?
qs.why: The sound system and flashing lights in every tree are noisy, showy excitement.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “spoilsport” mean?
options: someone who is bad at sports
the loudest guest at a party
someone who ruins other people's fun
qs.why: The teenagers said this when he asked them to turn down the music, which ended part of their fun.

qs.q: Why does the grandfather's calm behavior fit his background?
options: He was the one who planned the party.
He was too tired to dance.
He was allergic to Aunt Leela's sweets.
He had spent his career warning people about a lack of self-control.
He wanted the neighbors to complain.
qs.why: As a doctor he warned patients about intemperance, so it fits that he stayed moderate while others overdid it.

title: The Poet's Assistant
text: In the last years of his life, the poet Yusuf Demir was nearly blind, so he dictated his work to an amanuensis, a young student named Selin who wrote down every word. Many of his poems mixed Turkish with old Persian phrases, and Selin had to transliterate the Persian words into Latin letters so that his publisher in Istanbul could read them. It was slow, delicate work, because a single careless mistake could garble a line beyond understanding. When tired, Yusuf also had a habit of eliding sounds and even whole small words, swallowing the ends of his phrases. At first this disconcerted Selin, who was never sure what he had meant. But her doggedness won out. Over three years she learned his voice so well that she could finish his sentences, and his final book was published with her name beside his.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “transliterate” mean?
options: write in a different alphabet, keeping the same sounds
qs.why: She changed the Persian words into Latin letters so they could be read, not into Turkish meanings, which would be translating.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “disconcerted” mean?
options: made her feel uneasy and unsure
qs.why: She was 'never sure what he had meant,' which left her uneasy and unsure how to proceed.

qs.q: What shows that Selin succeeded in her work?
options: She learned to read Persian before she met him.
She convinced him to stop dropping words.
She came to know his voice well enough to finish his sentences.
She wrote the final book on her own.
The publisher hired her to translate other poets.
qs.why: After three years she could finish his sentences, and her name was printed beside his on the final book.

title: The Tailor's Loan
text: When Grace Mwangi opened her tailoring shop, no bank considered her creditworthy; she owned no property and had never borrowed before. The only lender willing to help charged usurious rates, nearly sixty percent a year, and a friend warned her that such a loan could be ruinously expensive. Grace refused it. Instead, she joined a savings group of twelve women who each put money into a shared fund every week and took turns borrowing from it at low cost. Her first loan bought two sewing machines. She amortized it over eighteen months, paying a small amount every Friday, and she was careful never to overextend herself by taking orders she could not finish on time. Ten years later, her shop employs nine people, and she helps other women in her village escape the indigence she once feared.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “usurious” mean?
qs.why: Nearly sixty percent a year is an extreme rate, which is why her friend warned it could ruin her.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “amortized” mean?
options: paid it all back at once
paid it off little by little through regular payments
used it to borrow even more
had it forgiven by the group
qs.why: She paid 'a small amount every Friday' for eighteen months.

qs.q: Why did Grace join the savings group?
options: It let her borrow at low cost instead of taking an expensive loan.
A bank required her to join before lending.
She wanted to lend money to the other women at high rates.
She needed help sewing large orders.
The lender with high rates told her to join.
She already owned property to share.
qs.why: Banks would not lend to her and the only lender was far too costly, so the group's low-cost loans were her better option.

title: The Tonic Man of Millbrook
text: In the summer of 1874, a man calling himself Doctor Horatio Vance arrived in the river town of Millbrook with a wagon full of colored bottles. He was a mountebank of the old school, selling a 'miracle tonic' that he swore could cure everything from baldness to broken hearts. His legerdemain was impressive: he could make a coin vanish from a child's palm and reappear inside a sealed bottle, and the crowd gasped every time. He was also a gifted fabulist, telling tales of ancient kings who had once drunk his tonic. By appealing to people's cupidity, he inveigled the mayor into putting his savings into a 'tonic factory' that promised huge profits. The imposture ended when a visitor recognized him as Harold Vint, a former barber from Ohio. By morning, Vance and the mayor's money were gone.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “cupidity” mean?
qs.why: He won the mayor over with a factory that 'promised huge profits,' playing on greed. 'Love' is a careless guess from Cupid.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “inveigled” mean?
options: tricked him into it through flattery or deception
qs.why: Vance used false promises to get the mayor to hand over his savings, which is persuasion by trickery.

qs.q: How was Vance's false identity discovered?
options: The mayor tested the tonic in a laboratory.
A child saw how the coin trick worked.
A visitor recognized him as a former barber.
He confessed after drinking his own tonic.
The tonic factory was inspected by police.
He was caught stealing a wagon.
qs.why: The imposture ended when a visitor recognized him as Harold Vint, a former barber from Ohio.

title: Champions of 1972
text: The sports hall where the old Westbrook basketball team gathered for their reunion had fallen into decrepitude: the paint peeled, and rain dripped through the roof into buckets. Yet the twelve septuagenarians who arrived that Saturday did not seem to mind. These quondam champions had won the state title in 1972, and they walked slowly across the timeworn wooden floor, pointing out the spot where Danny Cho had made the winning shot. Nobody was doddering, exactly, though one man used a cane and another needed help with the stairs. When Danny himself walked in, white-haired and slightly bent, the room broke into unfeigned cheers. He picked up a ball, took aim from the free-throw line and missed by a mile. Everyone laughed, Danny loudest of all.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “quondam” mean?
qs.why: They won the title in 1972, more than fifty years earlier, so they are champions of the past, not the present.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “unfeigned” mean?
qs.why: The men loved Danny and his famous shot, so their cheers were genuine, not pretended.

qs.q: How does the hall's poor condition relate to the men's mood?
options: It makes them want to leave early.
It does not spoil their happiness at being together.
It makes them angry at the school.
It reminds them that they lost the title.
It stops them from walking on the floor.
It makes Danny refuse to take a shot.
qs.why: The passage says that despite the peeling paint and leaking roof, they 'did not seem to mind,' and the visit ends in laughter.

title: The Parking Space
text: The contretemps began over a parking space. Mr. Albrecht, a tetchy retired accountant, believed the spot in front of his house belonged to him, even though it was on a public street. When his new neighbor, Fatima Haddad, parked there one evening, he left a sharp note on her windshield. She found the note a small discourtesy and ignored it. The next morning, he stood on his porch and glowered at her as she left for work. Fatima disliked conflict, so she decided to conciliate him. She baked a lemon cake, knocked on his door and introduced herself properly. To propitiate him further, she offered to park around the corner on weekdays. Mr. Albrecht was so surprised that he forgot to be grumpy. Within a month, he was watering her plants whenever she traveled.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “contretemps” mean?
options: a parking ticket from the city
qs.why: It was a small quarrel over a parking spot, settled within a month with a cake, not a legal case or a long feud.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “glowered” mean?
qs.why: He was annoyed she had taken 'his' spot, so his stare from the porch was an angry one.

qs.q: What ended the dispute?
options: A police officer explaining that the street was public.
Mr. Albrecht moving to a new house.
Fatima's friendly actions, such as the cake and her offer about parking.
Fatima leaving him an angry note in return.
A city rule giving him the parking spot.
qs.why: She baked a cake, introduced herself and offered to park elsewhere on weekdays, which surprised him out of his grumpiness.

title: Dawn at the Port
text: With the strike deadline only hours away, talks between the port workers and the shipping company had reached a parlous state. Both sides were playing a game of brinkmanship, each refusing to move in the hope that the other would give in at the last minute. The imminence of a shutdown worried everyone in the city, since much of its food and medicine arrived through the port. At ten o'clock, the company's lawyer made an impolitic remark, calling the workers' demands 'childish,' and the union leaders nearly walked out. It was the mediator, a levelheaded woman named Ruth Abara, who saved the night. She reminded both sides of the exigency they faced: ships full of supplies were already waiting offshore. By dawn, they had signed a deal, and the first cranes began to move.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “brinkmanship” mean?
options: pushing a dangerous situation to the edge to force the other side to give in
sailing ships close to the shore
giving up early to avoid trouble
building trust between the two sides
qs.why: Each side refused to move, hoping the other would give in at the last minute, which is risky edge-pushing, not compromise.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “impolitic” mean?
options: having nothing to do with politics
unwise and likely to offend people
qs.why: Calling the workers 'childish' insulted them and nearly ended the talks.

qs.q: What argument helped Ruth Abara bring the sides to a deal?
options: She threatened to call the police.
She promised the workers much higher pay.
She asked the lawyer to leave the room.
She told them the strike was illegal.
She offered to delay the deadline by a week.
She reminded them of the urgent need, with supply ships already waiting.
qs.why: The passage says she reminded both sides of the urgent situation: ships full of supplies were waiting offshore.

title: Dressed for the Gala
text: Before the museum gala, Julian spent nearly an hour primping in front of the mirror, adjusting his silk scarf and polishing his shoes. His sister teased him for being foppish, but he insisted that tonight was important. At the gala, though, he was surprised by the guests. Many of the wealthiest people wore simple dark suits and plain dresses, without a single extra accoutrement. Meanwhile, a few other guests arrived covered in frippery: feathered hats, sparkling capes, gold-painted canes. The decorations followed the same pattern. The organizers had hung chintzy plastic chandeliers to save money, and the flashing lights around the stage seemed meretricious beside the quiet beauty of the paintings on the walls. On the way home, Julian took off his scarf, folded it carefully and decided that next time he would dress more simply.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “chintzy” mean?
qs.why: They were plastic and bought 'to save money,' so they looked cheap. A flower pattern is a different meaning of a related word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “meretricious” mean?
options: showy but with no real value
qs.why: The flashing lights looked flashy and empty compared with the 'quiet beauty' of the paintings. It does not mean deserving merit.

qs.q: What did Julian seem to learn at the gala?
options: Only rich people should attend galas.
Silk scarves are no longer in fashion.
Museums should spend more on decorations.
Real elegance often looks simple rather than showy.
The guests in feathered hats were the best dressed.
His sister was wrong to tease him.
qs.why: He saw the wealthiest guests dressed plainly while showy outfits and lights looked cheap, and he decided to dress more simply.

title: The Worst Sentence Contest
text: Every spring, Professor Oyelaran asks her first-year writing students to read aloud the worst sentence they wrote in high school. The results are always funny. One student read a poem of pure doggerel about her cat, rhyming 'cat' with 'hat,' 'mat' and 'that' six times. Another shared an essay so prolix that it took three pages to say that summer is hot. A third admitted to a sententious ending in which he warned readers that 'only those who respect their elders shall ever know true happiness.' The professor's favorite was a grandiloquent opening about 'the eternal, thundering ocean of human destiny,' followed immediately by the line 'and then I ate a sandwich,' a perfect case of bathos. 'Your early writing was jejune,' she tells them kindly, 'but that is how everyone begins.'

qs.q: In the passage, what does “sententious” mean?
options: preachy, as if lecturing others about right and wrong
qs.why: The ending tells readers how to live in a self-righteous tone. 'Long sentences' is a careless guess from the look of the word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “bathos” mean?
options: a sudden, funny drop from something grand to something ordinary
qs.why: The grand 'ocean of human destiny' is followed at once by eating a sandwich, a comic fall from lofty to trivial.

qs.q: What is the professor's attitude toward her students' early writing?
options: She sees weak early writing as a normal stage, not something to be ashamed of.
She thinks students who wrote badly should leave the class.
She believes high school teachers did a terrible job.
She thinks poems are worse than essays.
She wants students to write the way they did in high school.
She is angry that the sentences are so bad.
qs.why: She speaks 'kindly' and says 'that is how everyone begins,' treating it as a normal starting point.

title: Madame Zora Knows
text: At the edge of the autumn fair stood a striped tent with a sign that read 'Madame Zora Knows.' Inside, the light was dim, and colored lanterns threw shifting, phantasmagoric shapes across the walls. Madame Zora, who by day ran the dry-cleaning shop on Pine Street, spoke in sibylline phrases that seemed to hide warnings: 'Beware the door that opens twice.' Her advice was always gnomic, short and wise-sounding, but nobody could say exactly what it meant. Visitors loved the transmogrification of the quiet shopkeeper into a mysterious prophet with silver rings on every finger. Most of them knew her predictions were chimerical. Still, they kept coming back each year, perhaps because of the ineluctable human wish to know what tomorrow will bring.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “transmogrification” mean?
options: a small change in her clothes
a complete and strange change into something very different
a move to a new town
qs.why: A quiet dry-cleaner becoming a mysterious prophet is a total, surprising change, not a small one.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “chimerical” mean?
qs.why: Visitors 'knew' her predictions were not real, yet came anyway; the predictions existed only in imagination.

qs.q: According to the passage, why do visitors keep coming back?
options: People have a natural wish to know the future, even if they doubt her.
They believe every prediction she makes.
The fair requires them to visit the tent.
Her advice is clear and practical.
They want to buy her silver rings.
qs.why: The final sentence explains it: the unavoidable human wish to know what tomorrow will bring, even though most knew her predictions were not real.

title: Are We There Yet?
text: By the third hour of the drive to Lake Tahoma, the Kowalski family car had become a moving complaint box. Ten-year-old Max kvetched about everything: the heat, the music, the way his sister was breathing. His sister, Zoe, sat sullenly with her headphones on, refusing to speak to anyone. When their father announced a 'scenic detour,' Max kicked the seat petulantly and demanded snacks. Even Grandpa, normally cheerful, was growing dyspeptic after a long night of poor sleep, and his voice took on a querulous tone as he asked, for the tenth time, whether they were lost. Only their mother remained calm. 'We're not lost, we're exploring,' she said breezily, and she turned up the radio. An hour later, the lake appeared through the trees, bright blue and still, and the complaining stopped at once.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “dyspeptic” mean?
options: sick to his stomach from the car ride
qs.why: Grandpa, after poor sleep, starts complaining about being lost, which shows a bad mood. The passage never mentions stomach trouble, another meaning of the word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “breezily” mean?
qs.why: She stays calm and makes light of the situation; the word describes her manner, not the wind.

qs.q: What finally ended the complaining?
options: Their mother turned off the radio.
They turned around and drove home.
The beautiful lake came into view.
qs.why: The last sentence says that when the lake appeared through the trees, the complaining stopped at once.

title: Nia's Puppy Plan
text: For months, eight-year-old Nia had been importunate about getting a puppy, asking at breakfast, at dinner and in notes slipped under her parents' door. She tried to wheedle her father with compliments about his cooking, and she even tried to finagle a deal with her grandmother, offering to give up dessert for a year if Grandma would buy a dog for her birthday. Her mother demurred, gently pointing out that their apartment was small and that nobody was home during the day. But Nia had a plan. She wangled an invitation to spend a weekend helping at the animal shelter where her aunt worked, and she came home with a notebook full of facts about feeding, walking and training. Her parents, impressed, grew more acquiescent. By spring, a scruffy brown terrier named Biscuit was asleep at the foot of her bed.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “importunate” mean?
options: asking again and again, to the point of being annoying
qs.why: She asked at breakfast, at dinner and in notes under the door, which is constant, pushy asking.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “demurred” mean?
qs.why: She 'gently' pointed out problems with space and time, a mild objection rather than anger or agreement.

qs.q: What most likely convinced Nia's parents?
options: Her grandmother bought the dog anyway.
She gave up dessert for a year.
She showed she had learned how to care for a dog.
Her aunt brought a dog home for her.
They moved to a larger apartment.
Her father liked her compliments about his cooking.
qs.why: After the shelter weekend she came home with notes on feeding, walking and training, and the passage says her parents were 'impressed.'

title: The New Manager
text: When Priya became manager of the small design team, she knew her predecessor had been popular. At her first meeting, one colleague was blunt: "We liked the old way, and we don't see why anything should change." Priya did not get angry. She asked everyone for constructive ideas instead of just complaints. She also promised transparency, explaining that she would share the budget and the reasons behind every big decision. At first, some workers were reluctant to speak up in meetings. But after a few weeks, when they saw that she really listened and acted on their suggestions, the room grew louder and more relaxed. By spring, even the man who had spoken first admitted that a few changes had helped.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “predecessor” mean?
options: the person who will take the job after her
her boss at the main office
the person who had the job before her
a worker she hired on her first day
an older relative who taught her the job
the newest member of the team
qs.why: A predecessor is the person who held a job before someone else. It is not the person who comes after (that is a successor).

qs.q: In the passage, what does “blunt” mean?
options: saying exactly what he thought, without trying to be polite
qs.why: The colleague said directly that the team did not want change, with no attempt to soften it. “Not sharp” is a different meaning of blunt, used for knives.

qs.q: Why did the team become more relaxed over time?
options: Priya brought back the old way of working.
The man who spoke first left the team.
Priya made strict new rules for meetings.
The team was given a much bigger budget.
They saw that Priya listened and used their ideas.
Their old manager came back to help.
qs.why: The passage says the room relaxed when workers saw that she really listened and acted on their suggestions. Nothing says the old way returned or anyone left.

title: A Hardy Little Plant
text: High on the steep sides of mountains, where the wind never seems to stop, a small purple-pink flower called moss campion grows in tight cushions. It is a hardy plant that can survive freezing nights and months under snow. Its leaves are packed so closely together that they hold warm air near the ground. Because of this, it can thrive where taller plants quickly die. Hikers often see the bright cushions scattered across the rocks like dropped buttons. Warm, sunny days are not abundant up there, so the plant grows very slowly, and a large cushion may be many years old. Even so, the plant is fragile in one way: a single careless boot can crush years of growth. That is why walkers are asked to stay on the path.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “hardy” mean?
options: strong enough to survive hard conditions
qs.why: The plant survives freezing nights and months under snow, so “hardy” means tough enough for difficult conditions. It does not mean the plant feels hard.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “scattered” mean?
options: spread out here and there over a wide area
qs.why: The cushions are seen across the rocks “like dropped buttons,” that is, spread out with spaces between them, not in rows or in one spot.

qs.q: Why are walkers asked to stay on the path?
options: The plant is poisonous to touch.
The steep slopes are closed in winter.
The flowers need footprints to spread their seeds.
Stepping on the plant can destroy many years of slow growth.
The wind is too strong away from the path.
Only scientists are allowed to count the plants.
qs.why: The plant grows very slowly, and one careless boot can crush years of growth. The wind is mentioned, but not as the reason for staying on the path.

title: Grandma's Pepper Soup
text: Whenever anyone in the Okafor family caught a cold, Grandma Ada made her pepper soup. It was, supposedly, a remedy that could cure anything from a sore throat to a broken heart. Her grandson Tobi was fond of the soup, but he wondered whether it really worked. For a school project, he decided to verify the claim. He kept a simple chart showing how many days each family member's cold lasted, with and without the soup. The results were mixed, and he told Grandma so. She laughed, handed him a spoon, and told him to stir the pot while she added the spices. "Maybe it doesn't cure colds," Tobi said later, "but it makes everyone feel looked after." Grandma took that as the best compliment she had ever received.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “remedy” mean?
options: a kind of soup from West Africa
a treatment that fixes an illness or problem
qs.why: The soup was said to cure colds and sore throats, so a remedy here is a treatment or cure. The soup is a family recipe, but that is not what the word means.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “supposedly” mean?
options: according to what people said, though it might not be true
qs.why: The family said the soup cured everything, but Tobi doubted it, so the claim was only what people believed. It was not certain.

qs.q: What did Tobi decide in the end?
options: The soup cures colds faster than medicine.
The soup may not cure colds, but it helps people feel cared for.
The soup made colds last longer.
Grandma should stop making the soup.
Only the spices in the soup really work.
His chart was wrong and he should start again.
qs.why: His results were mixed, and he said the soup makes everyone feel looked after even if it does not cure colds.

title: Testing an Idea
text: Lena noticed that the tomato plants on the sunny side of the community garden produced more fruit. Her hypothesis was simple: more sunlight leads to more tomatoes. To test it, she measured sunlight in each bed with a small meter and counted the tomatoes every week. When she began to analyze her notes, she found a clear correlation: the sunnier beds did grow more fruit. But an older gardener pointed out that the sunny beds were also the ones closest to the water tap, so they got watered more often. Lena realized she might be mistaken about the cause. Before she could conclude anything, she would need to give every bed the same amount of water and measure again, as accurately as she could.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “correlation” mean?
options: proof that one thing causes another
a link where one thing changes when another changes
a sudden change in the weather
qs.why: More sun went together with more fruit, which is a correlation. The passage shows this does not prove the sun was the cause.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “conclude” mean?
options: decide that something is true after looking at the facts
guess without looking at any facts
qs.why: Lena could not yet decide what caused the extra fruit. “Finish” is another meaning of conclude, but she was not trying to end the project.

qs.q: Why did Lena think she might be wrong?
options: She had counted the tomatoes only once.
The sunny beds were also watered more, so water might be the cause.
The shady beds actually grew more fruit.
The older gardener did not believe in tests.
She had planted the beds on different days.
qs.why: The sunny beds were closest to the tap and got more water, so she could not tell whether sun or water made the difference.

title: Stranded Overnight
text: When a snowstorm closed the airport in Denver, hundreds of travelers were stranded overnight. Marco had been flying home for his sister's wedding. At first, his frustration grew with every delay shown on the screen. Then the airline began to notify passengers by text message that all flights were canceled until morning. Staff promptly handed out blankets and water, and a nearby hotel opened its lobby to families with small children. The airline also promised to compensate everyone for meals. What Marco remembers most, though, is the hospitality of strangers. A woman from Ohio shared her snacks, and a group of students taught him a card game that lasted until three in the morning. He made it to the wedding the next afternoon, tired but smiling.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “compensate” mean?
options: pay people back for their costs
sell food to people at the airport
qs.why: The airline promised to cover what travelers spent on meals, which means paying them back for a cost.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “hospitality” mean?
options: a feeling of being very tired
sadness about being away from home
friendly and generous treatment of others
qs.why: Strangers shared snacks and games with Marco, which is kind, generous treatment. The word sounds like “hospital” and “hotel,” but it does not mean a building.

qs.q: What does Marco remember most about the night?
options: How kind the other travelers were to him
The blankets handed out by airline staff
The free hotel room he was given
The text messages from the airline
Being angry at the airline all night
qs.why: The passage says what he remembers most is the hospitality of strangers. He did not miss the wedding, and the hotel lobby was for families with children.

title: The Long Race
text: Running a marathon takes more than fast legs; it takes endurance. Amara had trained for six months, slowly adding miles each week. On race day, she reached the halfway point feeling strong, a milestone she celebrated with a quick wave to her parents. Around mile twenty, however, fatigue hit her hard. Her legs felt heavy, and her mind told her to stop. She remembered her coach's advice: drink water at every station, even if you think you have ample energy left, and strive to keep a steady pace instead of racing ahead. Amara was persistent. When a pain in her right foot slowed her near the end, she kept going. She crossed the finish line in four hours and twelve minutes, and her first words were, "When's the next one?"

qs.q: In the passage, what does “fatigue” mean?
options: a sharp pain in the foot
a feeling of being extremely tired
qs.why: Her legs felt heavy and she wanted to stop, which describes extreme tiredness. The foot pain came later and is a separate problem.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “ample” mean?
qs.why: The coach meant: drink even when you feel you have plenty of energy. Ample means more than enough, the opposite of “not quite enough.”

qs.q: What was the coach's advice?
options: Run faster in the first half of the race.
Stop when your legs start to feel heavy.
Drink water only when you feel thirsty.
Drink at every station and keep an even pace.
Wave to your family to stay strong.
Skip the water stations to save time.
qs.why: The coach said to drink at every station and keep a steady pace instead of racing ahead.

title: Building a Famous Bridge
text: Building the Brooklyn Bridge in New York was a huge undertaking. Construction began in 1870, and the bridge's length was unprecedented: when it opened, it was the longest suspension bridge in the world. The designer, John Roebling, had died in 1869, so his son Washington took over. Then Washington became seriously ill and could no longer visit the site. His wife, Emily, became the link between him and the workers, carrying his instructions and learning the engineering herself. This obstacle could have stopped the project, but it did not. The bridge's eventual opening came in 1883, thirteen years after work began. It was a great feat of engineering, and the Roebling family became renowned for it.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “unprecedented” mean?
qs.why: No suspension bridge in the world was as long at the time, so its length had never been reached before.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “eventual” mean?
options: happening at the end of a long process
qs.why: The opening came in 1883, at the end of thirteen years of work. Eventual does not mean “possible,” even though a similar word means that in some other languages.

qs.q: What role did Emily Roebling play?
options: She designed the bridge after John Roebling died.
She paid for most of the building work.
She stopped the project when her husband became ill.
She carried her husband's instructions to the workers and learned engineering.
She replaced workers who became sick.
She was the city official who planned the opening.
qs.why: When Washington was too ill to visit the site, Emily linked him to the workers and learned the engineering herself.

title: Saving for a Bike
text: Twelve-year-old Diego wanted a new mountain bike that cost three hundred dollars. His parents made him an offer: for every dollar he saved, they would add fifty cents. That incentive made saving feel faster. Diego began walking dogs for neighbors and saved steadily, about fifteen dollars a week. The hardest part was the temptation of the snack shop near school. He made a sensible rule: one treat on Fridays only. When his phone screen cracked, the repair cost forty dollars, which hurt. To offset the loss, he took on two extra dogs for a month. By early summer he had a small surplus, enough for a helmet and a bright red bell. He says the bell is his favorite part.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “incentive” mean?
options: something that encourages you to do something
qs.why: The extra fifty cents for each dollar encouraged Diego to save. It was not a free gift, because he had to save first.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “offset” mean?
options: hide a mistake from his parents
pay someone else to fix it
make up for a loss with a gain of about the same size
qs.why: He earned extra money from two more dogs to balance out the forty dollars the repair cost.

qs.q: What did Diego do after his phone screen cracked?
options: He gave up on buying the bike.
His parents paid for the repair.
He worked more for a month to earn back the money.
He stopped buying his Friday treat.
He sold his old bike to pay for it.
He spent his helmet money on the repair.
qs.why: He took on two extra dogs for a month to make up the forty dollars. His parents only added money to his savings.

title: The Class Debate
text: Ms. Haddad's class held a debate: should the school day start an hour later? Jun spoke first, full of big words and dramatic pauses, but it was mostly rhetoric; he never gave a single fact. Ruth took a different path. She tried to persuade the class with studies from sleep scientists showing that many teenagers naturally fall asleep later at night. Her sources were credible because they came from universities and health groups. When someone asked whether feeling tired was just subjective, she offered to clarify: the studies measured test scores and attendance, not only how students felt. By the end, it was evident which side had won the room. Even Jun voted for Ruth.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “rhetoric” mean?
options: a question asked to the class
words meant to impress, without much real content
qs.why: Jun used big words and dramatic pauses but gave no facts, which is rhetoric: impressive-sounding language with little substance.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “subjective” mean?
options: the topic of a school lesson
based on personal feelings rather than facts
shared by everyone in the class
qs.why: The question was whether tiredness was only a personal feeling. Ruth answered that the studies also measured facts like test scores.

qs.q: Why did Ruth win the debate?
options: She supported her side with reliable facts from studies.
She spoke louder and longer than Jun.
She used more dramatic pauses than Jun.
The teacher chose her side before the debate.
She promised everyone a later school start.
Jun forgot to give his speech.
qs.why: Ruth used trusted studies with measured results, while Jun gave no facts at all.

title: The Empty Lot
text: For years, the corner lot on Maple Street sat vacant, filled with weeds and broken bottles. Then Mrs. Nguyen, a retired teacher, decided to initiate a clean-up. She knocked on doors and asked neighbors to cooperate for just one Saturday. Twenty people came with gloves and bags. They carried away old tires, plastic, and other debris, filling a whole truck. Afterward, the neighbors collectively decided to turn the lot into a garden, with each family taking care of one small bed. Now there are tomatoes, sunflowers, and a bench where older residents sit in the evening. "It was a lot of work," Mrs. Nguyen says, "but seeing children pick strawberries here makes it all worthwhile."

qs.q: In the passage, what does “initiate” mean?
qs.why: Mrs. Nguyen was the one who got the clean-up going, so initiate means start it. She did not just join someone else's plan.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “collectively” mean?
qs.why: The neighbors made the decision together as a group. The word looks like “collecting,” but it is not about money.

qs.q: How is the garden looked after now?
options: Mrs. Nguyen does all the work alone.
The city pays workers to care for it.
Older residents water it every evening.
Children are in charge of all the plants.
Each family takes care of its own small bed.
A truck comes every Saturday to clean it.
qs.why: The passage says each family takes care of one small bed. Older residents sit on the bench, but they are not said to water it.

title: Joining a Medicine Study
text: When Mr. Ibrahim's back pain became prolonged, lasting more than six months, his doctor suggested that he consult a specialist. The specialist explained that a new medicine might relieve the pain, but it was still being tested. Before joining the study, Mr. Ibrahim had to undergo several blood tests and a heart check. The nurse was honest with him: some patients had suffered adverse effects, such as stomach problems and dizziness. Mr. Ibrahim was cautious. He asked many questions, read every page of the information sheet, and talked it over with his daughter. In the end, he agreed to join. "If it helps me," he said, "and helps the next person too, then I think it is worth trying."

qs.q: In the passage, what does “undergo” mean?
qs.why: He had to go through blood tests and a heart check before joining the study.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “adverse” mean?
qs.why: The examples, stomach problems and dizziness, are harmful effects. Adverse is the opposite of helpful.

qs.q: Why did Mr. Ibrahim decide to join the study?
options: The nurse promised there would be no side effects.
His daughter told him he had to join.
The medicine had already been proven safe.
He would be paid a large amount of money.
He hoped it would help both him and future patients.
His pain had suddenly become much worse.
qs.why: He said it was worth trying if it helped him and the next person too. The nurse actually warned him about side effects.

title: The Ghost of the Mountains
text: The snow leopard is a solitary animal; apart from mothers with cubs, it lives and hunts alone in the high mountains of Central and South Asia. Its main prey are wild sheep and goats, which it follows across rocky slopes. Its long, thick tail helps it balance on narrow ledges and can be wrapped around its body for warmth. The cat is remarkably hard to see. Its grey, spotted coat blends with the rocks so well that many people who live in its vicinity have never seen one. Scientists now use hidden cameras to catch a glimpse of it. When it hunts, its instinct is to creep close without a sound and then spring forward.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “solitary” mean?
qs.why: The passage explains that, apart from mothers with cubs, it lives and hunts alone. It is hard to see, but solitary is about being alone.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “vicinity” mean?
qs.why: People who live near the snow leopard, in the same area, still rarely see it.

qs.q: Why do many people never see a snow leopard?
options: It only comes out on moonless nights.
Its coat matches the colors of the rocks.
It runs faster than any other animal.
It sleeps through the whole winter.
qs.why: The passage says its grey, spotted coat blends with the rocks. Nothing is said about night, groups, or sleeping through winter.

title: Working From Home
text: When Sofia's company let staff work remotely, she was thrilled. She enjoyed the autonomy of planning her own day, starting early and taking a long walk at lunch. Without a long bus ride, she could work more efficiently and finish reports faster than before. But after a few months, problems appeared. Her neighbor's barking dog and the pile of laundry would distract her, and she missed chatting with people in the office kitchen. Her manager noticed that Sofia had become withdrawn in video meetings, keeping her camera off and rarely speaking. Together they agreed on a mix: two days in the office, three at home. Now Sofia routinely meets a friend from work for coffee on Tuesdays, and she says she feels like herself again.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “autonomy” mean?
options: freedom to make her own decisions
qs.why: She enjoyed planning her own day, which is the freedom to decide for herself.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “withdrawn” mean?
options: quiet and not wanting to talk with others
qs.why: She kept her camera off and rarely spoke, so she had become quiet and closed off. “Removed” and “taken out” are other meanings of the word.

qs.q: What did Sofia and her manager agree to do?
options: She works from home every day.
She works some days in the office and some at home.
She goes back to the office full time.
She takes a long break from her job.
She moves to a desk far from the kitchen.
She turns her camera on at every meeting.
qs.why: They agreed on two days in the office and three at home.

title: When Coffee Prices Jump
text: Coffee is a major commodity, traded all around the world, and its price can be surprisingly volatile. Brazil grows more coffee than any other country, so bad weather there affects everyone. When frost or drought damages the crops, a shortage can follow within months. Consequently, the price of coffee beans may rise quickly. Many café owners buy their beans wholesale, in large sacks. A sudden surge in those costs can squeeze a small business. Leila, who roasts her own beans for her café in Chicago, explains that she cannot change her menu prices every week. "Instead, I buy extra raw beans when prices are low and store them," she says. "They keep for months. It doesn't always work, but it helps."

qs.q: In the passage, what does “volatile” mean?
qs.why: The price can jump when bad weather hits Brazil, so it changes suddenly. “Turning easily into a gas” is a science meaning of volatile, not the one used here.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “wholesale” mean?
options: in large amounts at a lower price
qs.why: Café owners buy beans in large sacks from big suppliers, which is buying wholesale.

qs.q: How does Leila deal with changing bean prices?
options: She changes her menu prices every week.
She grows her own coffee in Chicago.
She buys extra beans when prices are low and stores them.
She buys beans only from Brazil.
She stops selling coffee when prices rise.
She buys one small bag at a time.
qs.why: Leila says she cannot change menu prices weekly, so she stocks up when beans are cheap.

title: Letters in the Attic
text: While cleaning her late grandfather's attic, Hana found a box of old correspondence tied with string. The writing on most of the letters was faint, the ink faded to pale brown. One envelope was marked "Confidential: open only after I am gone." Inside was a revelation: her grandfather, a quiet shopkeeper, had once been a jazz pianist who toured Japan in the 1950s. He had never chosen to disclose this to anyone in the family. Hana's mother cried when she read it. "He always hummed while he worked," she said. "Now I know why." In another letter, he wrote of a plan to write a memoir about his years on the road, but he never did. So Hana collected the letters into a small book for his grandchildren.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “revelation” mean?
options: a surprising fact that had been kept secret
qs.why: The envelope revealed a secret no one knew: that he had been a jazz pianist.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “disclose” mean?
qs.why: He had never told the family about his music career. Disclose means to make secret information known, not to close something.

qs.q: Why did Hana's mother say, “Now I know why”?
options: His humming made sense once she learned he had been a musician.
She finally understood why he kept so many letters.
She learned why he had become a shopkeeper.
She found out why he had moved to Japan.
She understood why he wanted to write a book.
She learned why the ink had faded.
qs.why: She connected his habit of humming at work with the secret that he had once been a jazz pianist.

title: A Town Goes Solar
text: The island town of Puerto Claro once got almost all its electricity from a diesel plant. Fuel arrived by ship, and every storm that delayed the boats meant power cuts. The town council wanted to reduce its reliance on fuel from overseas, but many people doubted that renewable energy was feasible on such a small budget. A group of engineers studied the island and found that sun and wind together could supply most of its needs. With help from a national grant, the town put solar panels on school roofs and two wind turbines on the hill. Five years later, fuel costs have dropped substantially. The diesel plant still runs on calm, cloudy days, but the council believes the new system is viable and can sustain the town for decades.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “reliance” mean?
qs.why: The town depended on fuel brought by ship and wanted to depend on it less.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “substantially” mean?
qs.why: Five years after the change, fuel costs have fallen by a large amount.

qs.q: Why did the town want a new energy source?
options: The diesel plant had completely stopped working.
The national government ordered the change.
The town had a very large budget to spend.
Fuel came by ship, and storms caused power cuts.
Engineers said diesel was against the law.
The schools wanted solar panels on their roofs.
qs.why: Storms delayed the fuel boats and caused power cuts, so the council wanted to rely less on imported fuel.

title: The Hat-Eating Goat
text: Farmer Bianchi's goat, Pepe, had one great talent: being stubborn. Every morning he refused to leave the barn until he had eaten the farmer's hat. It was an absurd habit, but no one could stop it. One day, Bianchi's nephew, Luca, came to visit. He laughed and began to mock his uncle, calling him "the man who works for a goat." The next morning, Luca marched into the barn without a hat, sure he would win. Pepe did not hesitate. He glanced at Luca once, walked past him, and ate the sandwich sticking out of his jacket pocket. Luca stood there in utter shock. Bianchi just smiled and handed him a spare hat for tomorrow.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “mock” mean?
options: make fun of in an unkind way
qs.why: Luca laughed and called his uncle “the man who works for a goat,” which is making fun of him.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “utter” mean?
qs.why: Here utter is an adjective that adds force: Luca was completely shocked. As a verb, utter means “to say,” but that is not how it is used here.

qs.q: How did Pepe outsmart Luca?
options: Pepe stayed in the barn all day.
Pepe ate Luca's hat after all.
Pepe chased Luca out of the barn.
Luca had no hat, so Pepe ate his sandwich instead.
Pepe ate the spare hat Bianchi was holding.
Pepe refused to eat anything that morning.
qs.why: Luca came without a hat to beat the goat, but Pepe simply ate the sandwich in his pocket.

title: The Little Rover That Could
text: In 2004, NASA landed a rover named Opportunity on Mars. Engineers had planned for it to work for about ninety Martian days. No one could anticipate how long it would actually last. The little robot proved robust, surviving freezing nights, dust, and rocky ground. It went on to exceed its planned life many times over, working for almost fifteen years and driving more than forty-five kilometers. Each day, scientists on Earth would dispatch new commands, telling it where to drive and which rocks to study. Then, in 2018, a huge dust storm covered the planet. Opportunity could not endure months without sunlight on its solar panels, and its batteries ran down. Inevitably, contact was lost. The team said goodbye in early 2019.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “exceed” mean?
qs.why: It was planned for about ninety days but worked for almost fifteen years, going far beyond its planned life.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “robust” mean?
options: strong and able to work in hard conditions
qs.why: The rover survived freezing nights, dust, and rocky ground, so it was strong and tough.

qs.q: Why did Opportunity stop working?
options: It drove off a rocky cliff.
NASA decided to turn it off after ninety days.
Dust blocked the sunlight its solar panels needed.
Its wheels froze during a cold night.
It ran out of rocks to study.
qs.why: During the 2018 dust storm, its solar panels got no sunlight for months, so its batteries ran down.

title: A Moment on the Field
text: For fifty years, the Hillside and Riverside high school soccer teams have had a fierce rivalry. Fans paint their faces and fill the stands for every match. This year's final was tense, tied 1–1 with ten minutes left. Then Riverside's goalkeeper, Kofi, fell and hurt his ankle badly. The stadium went quiet. Hillside's captain, Tariq, walked over, knelt beside him, and put a hand on his shoulder while the medical staff worked. It was a small gesture, but the crowd noticed. Hillside fans, usually loud and teasing, clapped for Kofi as he was helped off. A local newspaper later called it a moment of solidarity between two towns that rarely agree on anything. Kofi said the other side had been sympathetic, which meant more to him than the score.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “fierce” mean?
options: wild and ready to attack, like an animal
qs.why: The two teams have competed hard for fifty years, with packed stands, so the rivalry is very strong and intense, not about a wild animal.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “gesture” mean?
options: a loud cheer from the crowd
a movement of the body that shows a feeling
a goal scored late in a match
qs.why: Mei's hand on Kofi's shoulder was a small movement that showed she cared.

qs.q: Why did the Hillside fans start clapping?
options: They were moved by Tariq's kindness and wanted to support Kofi.
Hillside had just scored the winning goal.
Kofi had made an amazing save.
The match had ended in a tie.
The newspaper asked them to clap.
Mei waved to them to cheer louder.
qs.why: After Mei's kind action, the usually teasing fans clapped for the injured goalkeeper as he left the field.

title: The Yellow Taco Truck
text: Tomás and Liza sold Filipino-Mexican tacos from a bright yellow food truck. They had found a niche: no one else in their city served adobo tacos with mango salsa. Customers loved them, and soon the line stretched down the block. The couple were ambitious; they dreamed of opening three restaurants within five years. First, they needed help. They began to recruit cooks, but they were selective, hiring only people who loved both kinds of cooking. One prospective employee, a young chef named Ray, cooked them his grandmother's lumpia during his interview. He was hired on the spot. "We don't want a monopoly on this food," Liza says. "We want the whole city eating well, even if other trucks copy us."

qs.q: In the passage, what does “niche” mean?
options: a small hollow in a wall
a large market that everyone shares
a special area of business that suits a small group
a parking spot for the truck
qs.why: They sold something no one else in the city offered, a special corner of the market. A hollow in a wall is another meaning of niche.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “prospective” mean?
options: hoping or expected to become one in the future
qs.why: Ray was not yet an employee; he was interviewing to become one.

qs.q: What does Liza mean when she talks about a monopoly?
options: They want to be the only ones selling this food.
They plan to buy all the other food trucks.
They will stop selling tacos soon.
They want the city to ban copying.
They are happy for other trucks to make similar food.
They are worried about losing their best cooks.
qs.why: She says they do not want full control of this food and want the whole city eating well, even if others copy them.

title: Keepers of the Light
text: Before modern technology, lighthouses were a key part of maritime safety. Each one warned ships of a hazard, such as rocks or a sandbar near the shore. Some lighthouses stood on small islands, where a lone keeper lived, sometimes for months without visitors. The job required great devotion. On stormy nights, the keeper had to keep the lamp burning continuously, climbing the stairs to add oil and clean the glass. When dense fog rolled in and the light could not be seen, keepers rang a bell or sounded a horn instead. Today, almost all lighthouses in the United States run automatically, but many people still visit them to imagine that quiet, watchful life.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “lone” mean?
options: the only one, with no others there
qs.why: There was a single keeper living in the tower. Lone means “only one”; it does not by itself say he felt sad.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “dense” mean?
options: thick, with parts packed closely together
qs.why: The fog was so thick that the light could not be seen. “Slow to understand” is an informal meaning of dense, not this one.

qs.q: What did keepers do when fog hid the light?
options: They turned the lamp off to save oil.
They rowed out to guide the ships.
They left the tower until the fog cleared.
They added extra lamps to the tower.
They rang a bell or sounded a horn.
They sent letters to warn the ships.
qs.why: The passage says that when fog hid the light, keepers used a bell or horn instead.

title: The Phone Deal
text: When fifteen-year-old Zainab's grades slipped, her father decided to restrict her phone use to one hour a day. Zainab was upset. She thought the rule was arbitrary: why one hour, and not two? Her father was resistant to changing it, but he agreed to sit down and negotiate. Zainab came prepared with a plan. She would leave her phone in the kitchen during homework, and he would not impose any limit on weekends, as long as her grades improved. Her father was surprised by her maturity. Instead of shouting or slamming doors, she had listened, made a fair offer, and kept her voice calm. They wrote the deal on a sticky note and put it on the fridge. Two months later, her grades were back up.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “arbitrary” mean?
qs.why: Zainab asked why the limit was one hour and not two, meaning the number seemed picked at random. A rule can be strict without being arbitrary.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “impose” mean?
qs.why: Under the deal, her father would not force any limit on her phone during weekends.

qs.q: What surprised Zainab's father?
options: She agreed to give up her phone completely.
She asked for two hours instead of one.
Her grades improved in a single week.
She stayed calm and offered a fair plan.
She refused to talk about the rule.
She put the phone in her bedroom.
qs.why: He was surprised that she listened, made a fair offer, and kept calm instead of shouting.

title: A Disease That Spreads Fast
text: Measles is one of the most infectious diseases known. The virus spreads through the air and can stay in a room for up to two hours after a sick person leaves. Before a vaccine became available in 1963, the disease was prevalent; in the United States, nearly all children caught it by age fifteen. Mortality was highest among young children and those who were already weak or poorly fed. Today, two doses of the measles vaccine are about 97 percent effective, which greatly lowers the likelihood of catching it. When an outbreak does happen, health workers move fast. A timely response, such as offering vaccines to everyone nearby, can stop the virus from reaching new neighborhoods.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “prevalent” mean?
qs.why: Nearly all children caught measles, so it was very common.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “timely” mean?
qs.why: A response that comes fast enough can stop the virus before it reaches new areas.

qs.q: Why do health workers act quickly during an outbreak?
options: The vaccine stops working after a few days.
Fast action, like offering vaccines nearby, can stop the spread.
The virus disappears from rooms after two hours.
Measles cannot spread through the air.
The vaccine is only given during outbreaks.
qs.why: The passage says a timely response, such as vaccinating people nearby, can stop the virus from reaching new neighborhoods.

title: Eighty Dollars Short
text: At the end of a busy Saturday, the cash register at Rivera Bakery was eighty dollars short. The owner, Mrs. Rivera, had a suspicion that someone had taken the money, but she did not want to accuse anyone without proof. She asked her three workers to stay and count the drawer again. Nothing changed. That night, a young cashier named Owen could not sleep; his conscience kept bothering him. The next morning he came in early to confess. He had not stolen anything, but he had given a customer change for a hundred-dollar bill when the customer had paid with a twenty. It was an honest oversight. Mrs. Rivera thanked him for being accountable and showed him how to check every large bill.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “oversight” mean?
options: the job of watching over workers
a mistake made by not paying attention
qs.why: Owen gave the wrong change without meaning to, a mistake from not paying attention. “Watching over” is another meaning of oversight, but not the one here.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “suspicion” mean?
options: a feeling that someone did wrong, without proof
a plan to catch a thief
qs.why: Mrs. Rivera thought someone might have taken the money, but she had no proof.

qs.q: What really happened to the missing money?
options: Owen took the money from the drawer.
A customer stole it from the register.
Owen gave a customer too much change by mistake.
Mrs. Rivera counted the drawer wrong.
One of the other workers hid it.
The bakery was paid with a fake bill.
qs.why: Owen gave change for a hundred-dollar bill when the customer paid with a twenty, eighty dollars too much.

title: Evening in Marrakech
text: Nadia had seen photographs of Jemaa el-Fnaa, the great square in Marrakech, Morocco, but nothing prepared her for the real thing. By evening, the square was lively with musicians, storytellers, and smoke rising from dozens of food stalls. There was an abundance of oranges, dates, olives, and spices piled into small mountains. To Nadia, who had grown up in a small town in Canada, the smells seemed exotic and wonderful. She stood still and let herself gaze at the scene for a long time, and the colors and lanterns were so vivid that she later painted them from memory. Watching the sun set behind the tall tower of a nearby mosque, she felt a quiet awe.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “gaze” mean?
options: look quickly and then turn away
look steadily for a long time
qs.why: She stood still and looked at the scene for a long time. A quick look would be a glance.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “abundance” mean?
qs.why: The fruit and spices were piled into small mountains, which shows a very large amount.

qs.q: What shows that the scene made a strong impression on Nadia?
options: She later painted it from memory.
She bought spices to take home.
She left quickly because of the smoke.
She took many photographs of the square.
She joined the musicians and storytellers.
She decided to move to Morocco.
qs.why: The colors were so vivid that she painted them later from memory. The passage says she had seen photos before, not that she took them.

title: Grandpa Moves In
text: After her grandfather's knee surgery, Rosa asked him to stay in her apartment for a while. He agreed, though he felt a little obliged to say yes so that she would stop worrying. Rosa was a tenant, so she checked with her landlord first; he was happy to allow a guest. At first, the two were not very compatible roommates. Grandpa woke at five and played the radio, while Rosa liked to sleep late. But they learned to adapt. He bought headphones, and she started joining him for early walks. Over the months, their affection for each other only grew. When he finally moved back home, he left a note on the table that said simply, "Thank you for everything." Rosa could feel his gratitude in every word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “obliged” mean?
options: feeling he had to, because it was expected
qs.why: He said yes partly because he felt he should, so Rosa would stop worrying. “Much obliged” can mean thankful, but that is not the meaning here.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “compatible” mean?
options: able to live together well without problems
qs.why: Their different sleep habits caused problems at first, so they did not fit well together as roommates.

qs.q: How did Rosa and her grandfather solve their problems?
options: Rosa moved to a different room in the building.
The landlord made new rules for them.
Both changed their habits a little.
Grandpa went home after one week.
Rosa asked him to stop playing the radio.
qs.why: He bought headphones and she joined his early walks, so each of them adapted.

title: A Lucky Accident
text: In 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming came back from a holiday to find that mold had grown on one of his dishes of bacteria. He had not added it intentionally; it was a coincidence that a tiny bit of mold had landed there. But Fleming noticed something strange: around the mold, the bacteria had died. At that time, even a small cut could lead to a lethal infection. His curiosity led him to study the mold, which made a substance he named penicillin. Even so, it took more than ten years for its true value to emerge. In the 1940s, a team at Oxford led by Howard Florey, working with Ernst Chain, turned it into a medicine that doctors could use on patients. The breakthrough saved millions of lives.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “coincidence” mean?
options: something that happened by chance, not by plan
qs.why: Fleming did not add the mold; it landed on the dish by chance.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “emerge” mean?
qs.why: It took more than ten years for people to understand and recognize how valuable penicillin was.

qs.q: What did Florey and Chain add to Fleming's discovery?
options: They found the mold on Fleming's dish.
They proved that mold kills all bacteria.
They turned penicillin into a medicine that could be used on patients.
They grew the first bacteria in a dish.
qs.why: Fleming found and named penicillin; the Oxford team led by Florey and Chain turned it into a medicine doctors could use on patients.

title: The Library Vote
text: The town library in Millbrook was falling apart: the roof leaked, and the children's room had no heating. The library board decided to propose a small new tax to pay for repairs. Because the town's rules required voters to approve any new tax, the question went to a referendum in November. Some residents chose to oppose it, arguing that families were already paying enough. Others pointed out that the town would levy only about two dollars a month per household. For weeks, the public discourse was polite and thoughtful, filling the newspaper's letters page and a packed meeting in the school gym. Early surveys were favorable, and on voting day the tax passed with 58 percent of the vote. Repairs begin next spring.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “levy” mean?
qs.why: The town would officially collect about two dollars a month from each household as a tax.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “discourse” mean?
qs.why: People discussed the tax thoughtfully in letters and at a public meeting.

qs.q: Why did the library tax go to a public vote?
options: The library board could not agree among themselves.
Residents asked for a vote at the gym meeting.
The town's rules said voters must approve any new tax.
Early surveys showed people were against it.
The roof repairs were too expensive for the state.
qs.why: The passage says town rules required voters to approve any new tax, so it went to a referendum.

title: Bringing a Piano Back
text: When Mateo's great-aunt moved to a smaller home, she gave him her old piano. It had not been played in thirty years. A repairman named Mr. Adeyemi came to look at it. After a thorough check of every key and string, he had good news: the wooden case was still intact, with no cracks. The ivory keys, however, were fragile and had to be handled with great care. Mr. Adeyemi did not want to modify the piano too much, because its age was part of its charm. He replaced the worn strings but chose to incorporate the original pedals and brass hinges into the repair. When he finished, Mateo played a simple tune. The sound was splendid, warm and full, filling the whole house.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “intact” mean?
qs.why: The frame had no cracks, so it was whole and undamaged. It was old, not brand new.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “incorporate” mean?
options: include as part of the whole
qs.why: He kept the original pedals and handles and made them part of the repaired piano. “Start a company” is a business meaning of incorporate.

qs.q: Why did Mr. Adeyemi avoid changing the piano too much?
options: He felt its age made it special.
The new parts were too expensive.
Mateo asked him not to touch it.
The wooden frame was badly cracked.
He did not know how to fix old pianos.
The great-aunt wanted it back soon.
qs.why: The passage says its age was part of its charm, so he kept as much of the original as he could.

title: Why Island Animals Are at Risk
text: Animals that live on islands are especially prone to extinction. Many of them are confined to a single small island, so one disaster can wipe out the whole species. Island animals also often developed over thousands of years without large hunters around, which makes them easy targets when new animals arrive. The dodo of Mauritius is the most famous example. It could not fly and had little fear of people. After sailors arrived around 1600, bringing rats, pigs, and other destructive animals that ate its eggs, the dodo disappeared in less than a hundred years. Today, some islands work hard to curb the number of rats and cats. New Zealand, for instance, has cleared rats from many small islands, and some rare birds there have been fortunate enough to recover.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “prone” mean?
qs.why: Island animals are likely to die out for the reasons the passage gives. “Lying flat” is another meaning of prone.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “curb” mean?
qs.why: Islands try to keep down the number of rats and cats. As a noun, curb can mean the edge of a street, but here it is a verb.

qs.q: Why did the dodo die out?
options: A single storm destroyed its island.
It flew away to other islands.
Sailors moved it to New Zealand.
It was hunted by large animals that lived on Mauritius.
Animals brought by sailors ate its eggs, and it had no defenses.
It could not find enough food after a long drought.
qs.why: Rats, pigs, and other animals brought by sailors ate its eggs, and the bird could not fly or fear danger.

title: The Bread Business
text: When Amara Osei opened her bakery in a small river town, friends warned her that bread was not a lucrative business. They were right about the money, at least at first. Her mornings began at four, and shaping two hundred rolls by hand was tedious work that left her arms sore by sunrise. Still, Amara was pragmatic. Instead of dreaming about a second shop, she bought one versatile oven that could bake bread at dawn, roast vegetables at noon, and dry fruit overnight. She added soup and sandwiches to the menu, and lunch crowds began to grow. Her brother, who had reluctantly agreed to help on weekends, soon asked for more hours. Five years later, the bakery supports two families. "It is not a fortune," Amara says, "but it is a livelihood, and it is ours."

qs.q: In the passage, what does “lucrative” mean?
qs.why: Her friends meant bread would not earn much, and the next line says “they were right about the money.” It is about profit, not popularity.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “versatile” mean?
options: easy to move from place to place
able to be used for many different jobs
qs.why: The oven bakes bread, roasts vegetables, and dries fruit, so it can do many jobs. “Built for one special purpose” is the opposite.

qs.q: What best explains Amara's success?
options: She made practical choices, like buying one useful oven and adding lunch dishes.
She opened a second shop early on.
Her brother paid for most of the business.
She got rich quickly by selling expensive bread.
She ignored her friends and only baked bread.
She moved her bakery to a bigger city.
qs.why: She skipped the second shop, bought a multi-use oven, and added soup and sandwiches. The passage says she did not dream of a second shop, and it is “not a fortune.”

title: The Bright Coral Patch
text: For years, divers off a small island in the Pacific had noticed something odd: one patch of coral stayed bright while the reefs around it turned pale in hot summers. Marine biologist Lucía Ferreira decided to treat the story as a question rather than a legend. "People love to speculate," she said, "but I wanted empirical answers." Her team spent two years measuring water temperature, light, and currents every hour. The work was rigorous; each sample was checked twice by different people. The data showed that the anomaly had a plausible cause. A cold underwater stream rose near the patch, cooling the water by about one degree. To be sure, the team tried to replicate the effect in tanks, pumping cooler water over coral samples. Those samples stayed healthy too, while coral in warmer tanks lost its color.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “empirical” mean?
options: based on careful measurement and observation
qs.why: She wanted answers from data, and her team then measured the water for two years. “Based on expert opinion” is close, but the point is measuring, not opinion.
