qs.q: In the passage, what does “anomaly” mean?
options: something different from what is normal
the usual pattern on the reef
qs.why: The anomaly is the one patch that stayed bright when other reefs turned pale, which is not what normally happens. “The usual pattern” is the opposite.

qs.q: What did the tank experiment add to the study?
options: It showed that light, not temperature, was the real cause.
It found that the cold stream was growing weaker.
It proved the coral patch was a different kind of coral.
It showed the divers had been mistaken all along.
It showed that cooler water could keep coral healthy, supporting the explanation.
It made measuring the water at the reef unnecessary.
qs.why: Coral given cooler water stayed healthy while coral in warmer tanks lost color, which backs up the cold-stream explanation. Nothing in the passage blames light.

title: A Letter About Dumplings
text: Dear Mei, thank you for the heartfelt letter you sent after the New Year dinner. I read it three times, and each time I felt a wave of nostalgia for the noisy kitchens of my own childhood. You asked why I still make dumplings by hand when the shop sells good ones. In our family it is customary for the oldest woman to fold the first dumpling of the year, and my mother did it until she was ninety. I know it sounds sentimental, but holding the dough connects me to a lineage of cooks I never met, women who fed their families through hard winters. The bamboo steamer you saw on the shelf belonged to my grandmother. I cherish it more than anything else I own. Next year, I want you beside me when I fold the first one. With love, Grandma Lin

qs.q: In the passage, what does “lineage” mean?
options: a set of old kitchen tools
the line of family members who came before her
qs.why: She means the women in her family before her, cooks she “never met.” “Her children and grandchildren” is a near miss: those come after her, not before.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “customary” mean?
options: the usual practice in the family
made to order for a customer
qs.why: Folding the first dumpling is what the family has always done, as her mother did until ninety. It is a habit, not a law.

qs.q: Why does Grandma still make dumplings by hand?
options: She cannot afford to buy dumplings.
Mei asked her to teach the skill.
It makes her feel connected to the women in her family who cooked before her.
Her doctor told her to keep her hands busy.
She wants to sell them at the market.
qs.why: She says holding the dough connects her to earlier cooks in her family. She even admits the shop sells good ones.

title: Breaking Three Hours
text: Kofi Mensah had run marathons for six years, but his times had hit a plateau. No matter how hard he trained, he finished in about three hours and ten minutes. His coach suggested a new plan: fewer miles, more rest, and one hard hill session each week. The hills were relentless, a long climb outside the city that never seemed to flatten. By the final climb, Kofi was so weary that he could barely lift his knees. Some weeks he wanted to quit. But he had always been resilient; after a bad race, he would sulk for one evening and be back on the road the next morning. At the spring marathon, he reached the last mile with almost nothing left. He managed to muster one final burst of speed and crossed the line in two hours and fifty-eight minutes, a goal he had tried to attain for years.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “plateau” mean?
options: a period when his progress stopped and stayed the same
a flat, high area of land
qs.why: His times stayed at about 3:10 no matter how hard he trained, so his progress had stopped. “A flat, high area of land” is another meaning of the word, not this one.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “muster” mean?
options: to find enough of something, like strength
qs.why: With almost nothing left, he found enough energy for one last burst of speed. He was not saving or hiding it.

qs.q: What finally helped Kofi break out of his slump?
options: Running many more miles each week
Taking several weeks off from running
A new plan with fewer miles, more rest, and weekly hill work
A new pair of racing shoes
Choosing a flatter, easier race course
Training with a faster group of runners
qs.why: His coach's new plan cut the miles, added rest, and added hills. Running harder alone had not helped before.

title: The Spread of Print
text: Before the advent of the printing press in Europe, most books were copied by hand, a slow process that made them rare and costly. Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg began printing with metal type in the German city of Mainz. The idea was not entirely new. Printing from carved wooden blocks had been used in China for centuries, and it was an important precursor of later printing methods. But Gutenberg's system was fast, and what followed was a proliferation of print shops across Europe; by 1500, there were presses in more than two hundred towns and cities. Over time, copying most books by hand became obsolete, though some scribes still found work. The change shaped European life profoundly. Pamphlets, maps, and printed books became common, and later, newspapers would become ubiquitous in cities, sold on almost every street corner.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “advent” mean?
options: the arrival or start of something new
the end of an old system
qs.why: “Before the advent of the printing press” means before the press arrived. Advent can also name a holiday season, but that is not the meaning here.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “obsolete” mean?
options: no longer used because something newer replaced it
slow but still the main method
qs.why: Printing replaced hand copying for most books. It was not banned, since some scribes still found work.

qs.q: According to the passage, how is Gutenberg's work connected to China?
options: Gutenberg learned printing while living in China.
China copied Gutenberg's metal type system.
China banned printing for many centuries.
Chinese scribes copied Gutenberg's books by hand.
Gutenberg's first press was built in China.
Chinese woodblock printing came earlier and helped lead to later printing.
qs.why: Woodblock printing had been used in China for centuries and is called an important precursor of later printing. The passage never says Gutenberg went to China.

title: A Day at the Clinic
text: Dr. Priya Raman sees about twenty patients a day at a rural clinic, and many arrive worried. Last Tuesday, a farmer named Tomás showed her a lump on his arm. After an exam and a scan, she told him it was benign, a harmless bundle of fat that needed no treatment. Next came an elderly woman with painful knees. Dr. Raman suggested gentle exercise and a cream to alleviate the ache, explaining that studies have tested its efficacy and found that it helps many people. Before cleaning a deep cut on a boy's hand, she laid out sterile tools on a fresh tray. "Older people and small children are more susceptible to infection," she explained to his mother, "so we take every precaution." By evening, Dr. Raman was tired but satisfied. "Most days," she said, "my job is to calm fears as much as to treat illness."

qs.q: In the passage, what does “benign” mean?
qs.why: She calls the lump harmless and says it needs no treatment. “Kind and friendly” is another meaning of benign, used for people, not lumps.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “efficacy” mean?
options: how well it works to do what it should
qs.why: Studies found the cream “helps many people,” so they tested whether it works. Safety is a different question.

qs.q: What does Dr. Raman suggest about her work?
options: Calming patients' worries is as important as treating them.
Most of her patients have serious illnesses.
She prefers treating children to treating adults.
She wishes the clinic had more modern tools.
She rarely needs to clean her tools.
Older patients are her hardest cases.
qs.why: She says her job is to “calm fears as much as to treat illness,” and many patients arrive worried. The day she describes was mostly about minor problems.

title: Saving the Old Library
text: When the town council of Eastbrook announced plans to tear down its old stone library, the backlash came quickly. Hundreds of letters arrived within a week, and a group of retired teachers began meeting every Saturday to find a way to salvage the building. They gathered signatures, raised money for an engineer's report, and asked the council to reconsider. The engineer found that the walls were sound; only the roof needed replacing. At the next public meeting, the turnout was the largest anyone could remember, with people standing along the back wall. After two hours of discussion, the council voted unanimously to repair the library instead. Next spring, the town will hold a small festival to commemorate the building's 150th birthday, and the teachers who saved it have been invited to cut the ribbon.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “backlash” mean?
options: a quick vote by the council
a sudden crack in a wall
a strong negative reaction from many people
a fine paid by the town
a loud argument between two people
qs.why: Hundreds of angry letters arrived after the plan was announced. People reacted against the plan, not in support of it.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “salvage” mean?
options: to save it from being destroyed
to move it to a new place
to decorate it for a festival
qs.why: The teachers wanted to keep the library from being torn down. “Tear it down safely” is what the council planned, not what they wanted.

qs.q: What did the engineer's report show?
options: The building had to be torn down.
The library needed a new foundation.
Repairs would cost more than a new building.
The roof was fine, but the walls were cracking.
The walls were strong, and only the roof needed replacing.
The building was younger than people thought.
qs.why: The passage says “the walls were sound; only the roof needed replacing.” The reverse, a good roof with cracked walls, is the tempting mix-up.

title: Turning Back on the Ridge
text: The trail across the northern ridge is one of the most rugged in the national park, all loose rock and steep drops. When Hana and her father set out to traverse it last August, the guidebook described it as "a full day for fit hikers." From the parking lot, the ridge looked daunting, a jagged line against the sky. The first hours were worth the effort. They passed a picturesque lake ringed with wildflowers and stopped to eat lunch on a flat rock. Then, around two o'clock, dark clouds began to gather behind the peaks, and a low rumble rolled across the valley. The ominous sound made her father stop. "We can finish another day," he said. Turning back felt disappointing, but it was the prudent choice: within an hour, hail was bouncing off the trail they had planned to cross.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “ominous” mean?
options: warning that something bad was coming
qs.why: The rumble with dark clouds meant a storm was near, and hail soon followed. It was not harmless.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “prudent” mean?
qs.why: Turning back kept them safe from the hail, so it was careful and wise. Pushing on would have been the daring choice.

qs.q: Why did Hana's father decide to turn back?
options: Hana was too tired to keep walking.
They had run out of food.
Park rangers had closed the trail.
Dark clouds and a low rumble suggested a storm was coming.
He wanted to spend more time at the lake.
The guidebook said the trail was too dangerous.
qs.why: He stopped after the clouds gathered and the rumble rolled across the valley. The guidebook only said it was a full day for fit hikers.

title: A Message From the Bank
text: The message looked official. It carried the bank's logo and warned Daniel Okafor that his account would be frozen unless he confirmed his details through a link. Daniel was skeptical; his bank had never contacted him that way before. He noticed that the sender's address ended in a dubious string of numbers, and the message was full of small spelling errors. Instead of clicking, he called the number printed on the back of his card. The bank confirmed that the message was fraudulent and thanked him for reporting it. Criminals, the bank officer explained, use fake prizes, refunds, and urgent warnings to lure people into handing over passwords. The deception works because people act quickly when they are scared. Her advice was simple: be wary of any message that demands fast action, and always contact the company directly using a number you already trust.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “dubious” mean?
options: suspicious and not to be trusted
qs.why: The odd string of numbers was a warning sign that the message was not real. It made the address look untrustworthy, not official.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “lure” mean?
options: to force people using physical strength
to teach people how to do something
to stop people from doing something
to pay people to stay away
to tempt or pull people into doing something
qs.why: Criminals tempt people with prizes and refunds to get them to give up passwords. They are not using force.

qs.q: According to the bank officer, why does this kind of trick often work?
options: Bank messages always look exactly the same.
Most people do not have bank cards.
People act quickly without thinking when they are scared.
Banks often send messages with links.
People enjoy typing in their passwords.
Spelling errors make messages look more official.
qs.why: She says the trick works “because people act quickly when they are scared.” Spelling errors were actually a sign of the fake.

title: Shorter Is Better
text: Ms. Adeyemi returned the history essays on Friday with one word written at the top of most pages: "Shorter." She wanted her students to learn that a good essay is concise, not padded. "Many of you said the same thing three times," she told the class. "If a sentence is redundant, cut it." She explained that she graded on one main criterion: does the argument hold together? An essay could be full of facts and still fail if it was not coherent, jumping from idea to idea with no clear thread. She held up a paper by Jonah, a quiet student who rarely spoke in class. In writing, he was very articulate, and his two pages said more than some students' six. "I want to emphasize," she said, "that length is not the same as quality."

qs.q: In the passage, what does “redundant” mean?
options: not needed because it repeats something already said
qs.why: Students “said the same thing three times,” so the extra sentences repeat earlier ones. “No longer having a job” is another meaning, used for workers.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “criterion” mean?
options: a rule about how long an essay must be
a prize for the best essay
a standard used to judge something
qs.why: Her one test for grading was whether the argument holds together. It was not about length, which she says does not equal quality.

qs.q: What is Ms. Adeyemi's main message?
options: Students should write at least six pages.
Essays should include as many facts as possible.
Quiet students always write better than talkative ones.
Repeating main points makes an essay clearer.
Spelling is the most important part of grading.
A clear, well-organized argument matters more than length.
qs.why: She says “length is not the same as quality” and grades on whether the argument holds together. Jonah is one example, not a rule about all quiet students.

title: The Vine at Lake Mirren
text: Twenty years ago, a few fast-growing vines escaped from a garden near Lake Mirren. Today the plant is an invasive pest that smothers native shrubs and blocks sunlight from young trees. Along some stretches of shore its growth is rampant, covering whole hillsides in a thick green blanket. Scientists say the vine is detrimental to local birds, which lose the berries and insects they depend on. Removing it entirely may be impossible, but volunteers are working to mitigate the damage. Each weekend they work systematically, clearing one marked section at a time and recording what they remove. The job does not end when the vines are pulled. Residual roots left in the soil can sprout again within weeks, so every cleared area is checked monthly for new shoots.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “rampant” mean?
qs.why: The vine covers whole hillsides, so it is spreading everywhere with nothing to stop it. “Growing in neat rows” would mean it was under control.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “Residual” mean?
options: belonging to people who live nearby
left over after most has been removed
qs.why: These are the roots still in the soil after the vines are pulled. The word is about what remains, not about age or health.

qs.q: Why do volunteers check cleared areas every month?
options: Roots left in the soil can grow new shoots.
Birds bring new seeds every week.
They need to count how many birds return.
New volunteers need training each month.
The vines grow back only in winter.
qs.why: Leftover roots “can sprout again within weeks,” so the areas must be watched. The passage does not mention birds spreading seeds.

title: The Curtains on Maple Street
text: Everyone on Maple Street agreed that Mr. Halvorsen was eccentric. He walked his tortoise on a leash, wore a bow tie to the grocery store, and played the violin on his roof at dawn. So when he disappeared for a week, the neighbors were curious more than worried. Nine-year-old Rosa found the situation intriguing. She noticed a peculiar detail: his curtains opened and closed at exactly the same times each day, as if someone were still at home. Rosa knocked, but no one answered. On the eighth day, she saw a note taped to the window, and the truth was startling. Mr. Halvorsen had been in the hospital the whole time. He had set his curtains on a timer to conceal the fact that his house was empty, and he had kept his whereabouts secret so the neighbors would not worry.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “eccentric” mean?
options: odd or unusual in a harmless way
qs.why: Walking a tortoise and playing violin on the roof are strange but harmless habits. Nothing suggests he was unfriendly or dangerous.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “conceal” mean?
qs.why: The timer made the house look lived-in so no one would know it was empty. He was hiding that fact, not showing it.

qs.q: Why did Mr. Halvorsen's curtains open and close at the same times each day?
options: A friend was staying in his house.
Rosa was opening them for him.
He was secretly at home all along.
He had set them on a timer so the house would look lived-in.
His tortoise kept pulling on them.
qs.why: The note revealed he was in the hospital and had set the curtains on a timer. Rosa only noticed them; she did not open them.

title: Fixing the Paperwork
text: When Farah Haddad became head of operations at a mid-sized shipping company, she found a mess. Each department used its own software, and many of the programs were incompatible, so files from one office could not be opened by another. Worse, the main tracking system was proprietary, owned by a small firm that charged high fees for every change. Approving a simple purchase required six forms and three signatures, a bureaucratic process that could take a month. Farah decided to overhaul the whole system. She asked staff from every department to collaborate on a list of what they truly needed. Then she replaced the old programs with one shared system and cut the purchase forms down to one. "My goal was to simplify," she said. "People should spend their time moving packages, not paperwork."

qs.q: In the passage, what does “proprietary” mean?
options: free for anyone to use or change
built by the shipping company's own staff
owned and controlled by one company
qs.why: It was owned by a small outside firm that charged fees for every change. It was not made by Farah's own company.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “incompatible” mean?
qs.why: Files from one office could not be opened by another, so the programs did not work together. “Easy to share” is the opposite.

qs.q: What did Farah do before replacing the old programs?
options: She paid the small firm to fix the old system.
She added more forms for approving purchases.
She asked staff from every department to list what they really needed.
She let each office choose its own software.
She bought the tracking system from its owner.
qs.why: First she had staff from every department work together on a list of needs, and then she brought in one shared system.

title: My Aunt's Kitchen
text: Growing up, Marco thought vegetables were bland, boiled until gray and served without salt. Everything changed the summer he worked in his aunt's restaurant in Naples. She roasted peppers until their skins blistered, dressed tomatoes with good oil and basil, and turned simple beans into a soup so rich that he found himself craving it on cold nights. Her cooking was wholesome, mostly vegetables, grains, and fish, yet nothing about it felt like a diet. On Sundays, she would indulge the staff with a lavish lunch: six dishes, fresh bread, and a tray of tiny lemon pastries. The pastries were exquisite, each one shaped by hand and dusted with sugar. Marco is now a chef himself, and his menu carries a line in his aunt's honor: "Simple food, cooked with care."

qs.q: In the passage, what does “bland” mean?
qs.why: Vegetables boiled until gray with no salt would have almost no taste. “Too spicy” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “indulge” mean?
options: to put them on a strict diet
to treat them to something enjoyable
qs.why: She gave the staff a big, generous lunch with pastries, which is a treat. It was not a punishment or a diet.

qs.q: What did Marco learn from his aunt's cooking?
options: Vegetables are always boring to eat.
Good food must be fancy and expensive.
Healthy, simple food can be delicious when it is cooked with care.
Dessert is the most important part of a meal.
Boiling is the best way to cook vegetables.
qs.why: Her food was healthy and simple yet so good he craved it, and his menu line is “Simple food, cooked with care.” The lavish Sunday lunch was a special treat, not the lesson.

title: Coffee and Sleep
text: Coffee can stimulate the brain, making us feel alert and focused. The effect is useful in the morning, but it can last much longer than people expect, because the body clears caffeine slowly over several hours. A cup at four in the afternoon may leave someone only mildly alert at bedtime, yet that small effect can still delay sleep. Sleep experts warn that the losses are cumulative. Twenty minutes lost each night adds up to more than two hours over a week, and the tiredness builds. One implication of a late cup that few people consider is a tired, foggy week ahead. For anyone who struggles to rest, timing matters as much as amount. Some people try sleeping pills to induce sleep, but doctors usually suggest simpler steps first, such as a regular bedtime and a cool, dark room. It also helps to check your habits periodically, since what worked at twenty may not work at fifty.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “cumulative” mean?
qs.why: Twenty minutes a night “adds up to more than two hours over a week,” so the loss grows. “Too small to matter” is the careless reading.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “induce” mean?
qs.why: Sleeping pills are taken to make sleep happen. Coffee is what delays sleep, not the pills.

qs.q: Which statement best sums up the passage?
options: Sleeping pills are the best way to fix poor sleep.
Caffeine leaves the body within an hour.
Losing twenty minutes of sleep has no real effect.
Only people over fifty have trouble sleeping.
When you drink coffee can affect your sleep, and small nightly losses add up.
qs.why: The passage says timing matters and that small losses build over a week. It says caffeine clears slowly, over several hours, not within an hour.

title: The Quiet Challenger
text: At the regional chess championship, nobody paid much attention to Aditi Rao. She was fourteen, had played in tournaments for less than a year, and was listed as a novice on the official sheet. Her first opponent, a retired engineer, seemed to underestimate her; he played quickly and chatted with friends between moves. He lost in thirty moves. By the fourth round, people had begun to watch her board. Her final opponent was Viktor Ilić, a formidable player who had won the title three times and rarely made mistakes. For two hours the game was even. Then Viktor moved his queen one square too far, and Aditi saw her chance. She was poised to win but checked every line twice before moving. In the end she did prevail, and overnight she went from unknown to a serious contender for the national title.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “underestimate” mean?
options: to think she was stronger than she really was
to be very polite to her
to think she was weaker than she really was
to help her learn the game
to play very slowly against her
qs.why: He played fast and chatted, as if she were no threat, and then lost. Thinking she was stronger would be the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “poised” mean?
options: ready and about to do something
qs.why: After Viktor's mistake, she was about to win. “Calm and graceful” is another meaning of poised, but here it is followed by “to win,” meaning about to.

qs.q: What do the details about Aditi's first game suggest?
options: Her opponent did not take her seriously and played carelessly.
Her opponent let her win to be kind.
Aditi was already famous before the tournament.
The game was long and very even.
Aditi made many mistakes but got lucky.
Her opponent was a former champion.
qs.why: He played quickly and chatted between moves, then lost. The long, even game and the former champion belong to the final round against Viktor.

title: The Lighthouse Keeper
text: For thirty-one years, Ingrid Solberg kept the lighthouse on a small island off the coast of Norway. She first arrived for what was meant to be a short stint, one winter while the regular keeper recovered from an injury. She never really left. Visitors often asked how she could stand the solitude, with no neighbors and the mainland an hour away by boat. Ingrid said she liked the quiet and the perpetual sound of the waves against the rocks. She chose to devote her days to small tasks: polishing the great lens, recording the weather, and painting the iron railings to protect them from salt. The tower itself was built of granite blocks, durable enough to stand through two centuries of storms. When asked about the secret of its longevity, Ingrid always gave the same answer: "Somebody takes care of it every day."

qs.q: In the passage, what does “stint” mean?
options: a career that lasts a lifetime
a period of time doing a job
qs.why: She came to keep the lighthouse for one winter while the regular keeper healed. It was meant to be short, though it turned into thirty-one years.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “perpetual” mean?
options: going on all the time without stopping
qs.why: The waves hit the rocks constantly, so the sound never stops. “Rare and special” is the opposite of something that is always there.

qs.q: What does Ingrid believe explains the lighthouse's long life?
options: It is far from the mainland.
Storms near the island are mild.
Few visitors come to the island.
Someone looks after it every day.
Its lens is made of granite.
qs.why: Her answer is “Somebody takes care of it every day.” The granite helps, but the tower, not the lens, is made of granite, and she points to daily care.

title: The Fence Comes Down
text: The feud between the Nakamura and Bello families began with a fence. In 1998, Mr. Bello built it a foot onto what Mrs. Nakamura believed was her land. Angry words were followed by letters from lawyers, and for twenty years the two households did not speak. The discord spread to the whole street; neighbors learned not to invite both families to the same barbecue. Old resentment ran deep on both sides. Things began to change when the grandchildren, who went to the same school, became best friends. Their parents agreed to a truce so the children could visit each other's homes. Over shared birthday cakes and school plays, small acts of goodwill followed: a borrowed ladder, a plate of cookies, a hand with snow shoveling. Last summer, the two grandmothers finally met to reconcile, and together they took down the fence.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “truce” mean?
options: a final ruling by a judge
a new fence between the homes
an agreement to stop fighting for a while
qs.why: The parents agreed to stop the conflict so the children could visit. It was a pause in the fight, and the real peace came later.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “discord” mean?
options: a musical sound that does not fit
qs.why: The families' quarrel spread so neighbors avoided inviting both. In music the word can mean sounds that clash, but here it is about people.

qs.q: What first began to change the relationship between the two families?
options: A judge decided where the fence belonged.
The neighbors forced them to meet.
The grandchildren became best friends at school.
Mrs. Nakamura took down the fence by herself.
qs.why: The change began when the grandchildren became friends, which led to the truce. The fence came down only at the end, taken down by both grandmothers.

title: Chasing the Comet
text: For amateur astronomer Chidi Eze, the comet had been elusive. For three weeks, clouds rolled in every evening it was supposed to be visible. Large observatories had already worked out its trajectory, a long curve that would carry it near the sun and then back into deep space for thousands of years, so Chidi knew time was running out. Finally, on a cold, clear night in March, he drove to a hill outside the city. Through his telescope, the view was astonishing: a glowing head with a pale tail that split into thin, intricate threads. He and a friend in another town took simultaneous photographs, timed to the same second, so they could compare the comet's position against the stars. Later, his niece asked what would happen if a comet like that hit Earth. Chidi smiled. "That's a hypothetical question," he said. "This one will stay far away."

qs.q: In the passage, what does “elusive” mean?
qs.why: Clouds hid it every night for three weeks, so he could not manage to see it. It was hard to catch, not dangerous.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “hypothetical” mean?
options: imagined for the sake of talking about it, not real
qs.why: Chidi means the crash is only imagined, since this comet will stay far away. “Very likely to happen” is the opposite.

qs.q: Why did Chidi feel that time was running out?
options: His telescope was about to break.
The comet was about to hit Earth.
The comet would soon head back into deep space for thousands of years.
His friend was moving to another town.
Clouds were expected to stay all year.
The observatories were closing for the season.
qs.why: The comet's path would carry it near the sun and then far away for thousands of years. Chidi says it will not hit Earth.

title: A Letter of Support
text: To the hiring committee: I am writing to recommend Sofia Petrovic for the position of laboratory manager. Sofia worked in my lab at a reputable university research center for four years, and I can say with confidence that she is one of the finest staff members I have known. Her diligence is the first thing people notice. She labels every sample, double-checks every order, and has never missed a safety inspection. Her technical competence is equally clear; new students go to her before they come to me. I will be candid about one weakness: she can be too modest and needs encouragement to share her own ideas in meetings. But her advice has been invaluable to my team, and several of our best results grew from her suggestions. You will rarely find a candidate of her caliber. Sincerely, Professor Ahmed Karim

qs.q: In the passage, what does “candid” mean?
qs.why: He openly names a real weakness instead of hiding it. A “candid photo” is a different use of the word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “caliber” mean?
options: the size of a gun barrel
qs.why: He means few candidates are as skilled and capable as she is. The gun-barrel meaning does not fit a person.

qs.q: What weakness does Professor Karim mention?
options: She is sometimes careless with labels.
She has missed some safety inspections.
She is not good at helping new students.
She talks too much in meetings.
She is too modest and needs encouragement to share her ideas.
qs.why: He says she “can be too modest and needs encouragement to share her own ideas.” The letter says she never missed an inspection.

title: Bringing a Hillside Back
text: Ten years ago, the hillside behind Esperanza Ruiz's farm in southern Spain was barren. Years of overgrazing had stripped it of grass, and rain simply ran off the hard ground, carrying soil away. Water was scarce, and the situation looked dire: some neighbors had already sold their land and moved to the city. Esperanza decided to try something different. She built low stone walls along the slope to slow the rain so it could soak in, planted shrubs that need little water, and kept her goats off the hill for five years. Slowly, fallen leaves and spreading roots began to revive the soil, and a dark, fertile layer formed where there had been only dust. Today, almond and olive trees flourish where almost nothing once grew, and her neighbors visit to ask how she did it.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “barren” mean?
options: so poor and dry that little could grow
qs.why: The grass was gone and the ground was hard, so almost nothing grew. Today trees grow there, which shows how much it changed.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “revive” mean?
qs.why: Leaves and roots brought the dead soil back to life, forming a rich layer. Rain washing soil away was the earlier problem.

qs.q: Why did Esperanza build low stone walls on the slope?
options: To slow the rain so it would soak in instead of washing soil away
To keep her neighbors off her land
To mark where the almond trees would go
To keep her goats on the hill
To store water in a pond for the city
To stop the wind from knocking trees down
qs.why: The walls slowed the rain “so it could soak in,” fixing the problem of rain running off with the soil. She kept the goats off the hill, not on it.

title: Finding a Voice
text: When Yusuf joined the debate club in ninth grade, he was hesitant to speak even in small groups. His voice shook, and he often let others answer first. His coach, Mrs. Laurent, noticed his reluctance but also saw that his written arguments were sharp. Instead of pushing him onto the stage, she gave him small roles: timing speeches, then asking one question, then giving a one-minute summary. Her aim was to empower students to find their own voices rather than copy anyone else's. She reminded the team that confidence is not something you are born with; it is something you cultivate through practice. Yusuf never became as outgoing as some of his teammates, who chatted easily with strangers. But he learned to be mindful of his breathing, to pause before speaking, and to trust his ideas. By his final year, he was the team captain.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “reluctance” mean?
qs.why: He held back from speaking and let others go first. It came from nerves, not laziness, since his writing was sharp.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “cultivate” mean?
options: to plant and grow in a field
to develop over time with effort
qs.why: Confidence is built “through practice.” Growing crops is another meaning, and the passage says it is the opposite of being born with it.

qs.q: How did Mrs. Laurent help Yusuf gain confidence?
options: She put him on stage right away.
She made him copy the best speaker.
She told him to stop writing and start talking.
She moved him to a different club.
She gave him small roles that slowly grew larger.
She let him skip speaking for four years.
qs.why: He went from timing speeches to one question to a short summary. She chose not to push him onto the stage and did not want students copying others.

title: Learning to Speak Cretan
text: Nikos Papadakis was born in Melbourne, Australia, a city with one of the largest Greek communities outside Greece. His parents spoke Greek at home, but Nikos answered them in English, and by his teens he understood far more than he could say. His upbringing was full of Greek food, music, and Sunday visits to relatives, yet the language itself felt distant. At thirty, he traveled to his grandparents' village on the island of Crete and found that even the Greek he knew sounded different there. The local dialect had its own words and a softer way of saying certain sounds. He felt an instant affinity for the place and stayed for six months, taking lessons and helping in a cousin's olive grove. Slowly his ear grew accustomed to the rhythm of local speech. Like many people in the diaspora, he says, he wanted to reclaim a part of himself that had nearly slipped away.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “dialect” mean?
options: the form of a language spoken in one area, with its own words and sounds
a polite way of speaking to elders
qs.why: The Greek in Crete had its own words and sounds but was still Greek. It is a local form of the language, not a separate language.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “diaspora” mean?
options: people who never leave their home village
people from one country who now live spread across other countries
people who have just moved back home
qs.why: Nikos is part of the Greek community living outside Greece, in Australia. That spread-out community is the diaspora.

qs.q: What was Nikos's Greek like before his trip?
options: He could not understand any Greek at all.
He already spoke the Cretan dialect.
He understood a lot but could not speak it well.
He only knew the words of Greek songs.
He could read Greek but had never heard it.
qs.why: The passage says he “understood far more than he could say.” He heard Greek at home every day, so he had heard it often.

title: When Tulips Cost a Fortune
text: In the Netherlands in the 1630s, tulips became more than flowers. Rare bulbs with striped petals were in high demand, and buyers began trading contracts for bulbs that were still in the ground. Much of this buying was speculative: people paid high prices not because they wanted tulips but because they expected to sell to someone else for more. The trading reached a frenzy in the winter of 1636 and 1637, with deals made in taverns. Some reports describe staggering prices, with a single bulb said to cost as much as a house. Then, in February 1637, buyers abruptly stopped showing up, and prices began to plunge. Historians now believe many of the wildest stories were exaggerated. Admittedly, the damage to the Dutch economy was probably small. Still, "tulip mania" remains a famous warning about prices that rise on hope alone.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “speculative” mean?
options: based on guessing that prices would rise
based on a love of flowers
qs.why: Buyers did not want tulips; they hoped to sell for more later. That is a guess about the future, not known facts.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “abruptly” mean?
qs.why: Buyers stopped coming all at once in February 1637, and prices fell. It was not a slow decline over years.

qs.q: What do historians now believe about tulip mania?
options: It ruined the Dutch economy for many years.
Tulip bulbs were never actually traded.
Many of the wildest stories were exaggerated, and the harm to the economy was probably small.
Prices rose slowly and never fell.
Every tulip bulb cost as much as a house.
qs.why: The passage says historians think the wildest stories were exaggerated and the damage was probably small. Only some reports claimed one bulb cost as much as a house.

title: The Low Screen
text: Lena Fischer, a graphic designer, never thought much about how she sat. Her work was mundane in one way: eight hours a day at the same desk, staring at the same screen. Over the years, though, her neck began to ache, and the pain grew progressively worse until it woke her at night. A physical therapist watched her work for ten minutes and spotted the problem at once. Lena's screen sat too low, so she inadvertently leaned her head forward all day, and her posture had slowly curved to match. The fixes were simple. She raised the monitor to eye level, set a timer to stand every half hour, and learned a few stretches. The therapist also told her to warm up beforehand if she planned a long day of drawing. Within two months, her neck felt better, and she could finally sleep adequately again.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “inadvertently” mean?
options: because a doctor told her to
qs.why: She did not plan to lean forward; the low screen made her do it without noticing. “On purpose” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “progressively” mean?
qs.why: The pain grew worse step by step over the years. “In a modern way” is a different use of “progressive.”

qs.q: What was the main cause of Lena's neck pain?
options: She drew for too long at night.
Her screen was too low, so she leaned her head forward.
qs.why: The therapist found that the low screen made her lean forward all day. Her work being dull is mentioned, but it did not cause the pain.

title: A Tribute in Three Notes
text: The inaugural Riverside Jazz Festival opened last Friday with a concert in homage to Josephine Akande, the late composer whose music shaped the city's jazz scene for fifty years. The evening was led by Marcus Bell, an eminent pianist who studied with Akande as a teenager. His band, which has kept dozens of her songs in its repertoire for years, played everything from her early dance tunes to the long, slow works she wrote in her final years. Listeners could hear a three-note motif that returns again and again in her music, sometimes bright and quick, sometimes slow and sad. Bell played it with real flair, adding playful runs and sudden pauses that made the crowd laugh and cheer. Near the end, he told the audience that Akande had always said a festival was what the city needed. "Tonight," he said, "she finally has one."

qs.q: In the passage, what does “motif” mean?
options: a short musical idea that is repeated
qs.why: The three notes “return again and again” in her music. “A reason for doing something” is a motive, a different word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “inaugural” mean?
qs.why: Bell says Akande wanted a festival and “finally has one,” so this is the first. It has not been running for decades.

qs.q: Why was the evening especially meaningful, according to Bell?
options: Akande had wanted the town to have a festival, and this was the first one.
It was Bell's first time playing in public.
The festival had been held for fifty years.
Akande played piano with the band.
It raised money to clean the river.
qs.why: Akande said a festival was what the town needed, and this was the first. The fifty years refers to how long her music shaped the scene, not the festival.

title: The Warehouse Fire
text: The fire at the Dunmore storage warehouse started late on a Sunday, and by morning half the building was gone. No one was hurt, but investigators spent weeks looking for the culprit. They found it in a back room: a cheap heater left running beside a stack of cardboard boxes. The report blamed negligence rather than bad luck. Safety rules at the warehouse had grown lax over the years; fire doors were propped open, and monthly checks were often skipped. One manager who was supposed to oversee the inspections admitted that he had stopped looking closely and had begun to overlook small problems because nothing had ever gone wrong. Workers had raised concerns about the heater twice, but no one chose to heed their warnings. The company has since hired a new safety officer and installed sprinklers in every room.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “lax” mean?
qs.why: Fire doors were propped open and checks were skipped, so the rules were not followed carefully. “Far too strict” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “heed” mean?
options: to pay attention to and act on
qs.why: The workers warned about the heater, but no one listened and did anything about it. Hearing by accident is a near miss; the point is acting on the warning.

qs.q: Why did the manager start overlooking small problems?
options: Workers asked him to ignore them.
He was too busy fixing the heater.
The company told him to skip the checks.
He did not know how to do inspections.
Nothing had ever gone wrong before, so he stopped worrying.
The fire doors were already broken.
qs.why: He admitted he began to overlook problems “because nothing had ever gone wrong.” Workers raised concerns; they did not ask him to ignore them.

title: The Corner Garden
text: In one of the most populous neighborhoods of the city, where apartment towers stand shoulder to shoulder, green space is hard to find. So when a corner lot sat vacant for three years, collecting trash and weeds, a group of neighbors decided to act. They asked the city for permission to turn it into a communal garden, with shared beds that anyone could plant and harvest. The idea began to garner support quickly; within a month, two hundred people had signed up. Volunteers hauled away the trash, built raised beds, and set up a rain barrel. Today the lot is vibrant, filled with tomatoes, sunflowers, children chasing butterflies, and older neighbors trading seeds and advice. For families without balconies, the garden has been a boon, offering fresh vegetables and a cool place to sit on hot evenings. "We came for the vegetables," one gardener said, "but we stayed for the people."

qs.q: In the passage, what does “communal” mean?
options: shared by everyone in the group
used to grow food for sale
qs.why: The beds are shared, and anyone can plant and harvest. That is the opposite of private.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “boon” mean?
qs.why: The garden gives families without balconies fresh food and a cool place to sit, which makes life better. It is not a problem.

qs.q: What does the gardener mean by “We came for the vegetables, but we stayed for the people”?
options: The vegetables did not grow well.
People stopped gardening and only talked.
Only a few people came to the garden.
Getting to know neighbors became the best part of the garden.
The garden is now used only for parties.
The vegetables are sold to other neighborhoods.
qs.why: People joined for food but came to value the friendships, like neighbors trading seeds and advice. The vegetables still grow; they are not called a failure.

title: The Piltdown Puzzle
text: In 1912, an amateur collector named Charles Dawson announced that he had found pieces of an ancient human skull near the village of Piltdown in England. Many experts were thrilled. The bones seemed to show a missing step in human history, and museums displayed casts and replica skulls based on the find. Some scientists had doubts, because the remains did not fit well with early human fossils found in Africa and Asia. Finally, in 1953, new chemical tests showed that the find was bogus: a human skull from a much later time combined with the jaw of an orangutan, stained to look old. The teeth had even been filed down by some sly hand to look more human. Since then, many different people have been named as the hoaxer, and each new allegation has started fresh debate; a 2016 study concluded that Dawson most likely acted alone. The Piltdown hoax remains a lesson: exciting discoveries still need careful tests to validate them.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “bogus” mean?
options: fake, though made to look real
qs.why: The bones were a later skull and an ape jaw stained to look ancient. They were faked, not just damaged.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “validate” mean?
options: to explain them to the public
to confirm that they are true
qs.why: The lesson is that exciting finds must be tested to prove they are real, as the 1953 tests finally showed this one was not.

qs.q: Why did some scientists doubt the Piltdown find before 1953?
options: Chemical tests had already shown it was fake.
The bones were found by children.
It did not fit well with early human fossils found in Africa and Asia.
The skull was clearly brand new.
qs.why: The passage says the remains did not fit well with fossils from Africa and Asia. The chemical tests came only in 1953.

title: Starting Over in Rotterdam
text: At thirty-four, Grace Mwangi reached a crossroads. She had a steady job at an insurance office in Nairobi, but she had long dreamed of studying architecture. For months she would contemplate the choice on her evening walks, listing reasons for and against. Leaving meant giving up a good salary; staying meant always wondering. In the end, she chose to embark on a two-year program in Rotterdam, a city she had seen only in photographs. The first weeks were hard. She had to navigate a new language, a confusing tram system, and gray, rainy winter days. Some nights she felt uneasy, wondering whether she had made a terrible mistake. But her classmates were welcoming, and her teachers praised her drawings. By spring, her optimism had returned, and she began sketching plans for the house she would one day build for her mother.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “crossroads” mean?
options: a point where she had to make an important choice
qs.why: She had to choose between her steady job and studying architecture. A street corner where roads meet is the literal meaning, not this one.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “navigate” mean?
qs.why: She had to work her way through a new language and a confusing tram system. She could not avoid them.

qs.q: How did Grace's feelings change during her first months?
options: She grew more and more unhappy.
She felt confident from the very first day.
She moved from doubt to renewed hope.
qs.why: Early on she felt uneasy and doubted her choice, but by spring her optimism had returned. The first weeks were hard, so she was not confident from day one.

title: The Rush Before Dawn
text: Every morning at four, the kitchen at Lin's Bakery turns hectic. Ovens bang open, timers ring, and six bakers move around one another like dancers who never practiced together. Last spring the shop fell behind on wedding-cake orders, and a backlog of forty cakes sat on the calendar with no one free to start them. The owner, Mei Lin, decided to streamline the work. She gave each baker one station, posted a clear checklist by every oven, and moved the flour bins closer to the mixers. Her head baker, Tomás, became indispensable during the change. He is meticulous: he weighs every ingredient twice and writes the time on each tray. By June the waiting list was gone. At the staff dinner, Mei stood up to commend Tomás for his calm leadership, and the whole team cheered.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “streamline” mean?
options: hand the work to another company
make the shop look more modern
make the work simpler and more efficient
qs.why: Mei gave each baker one station, added checklists and moved supplies closer: she made the process simpler and more efficient. Nothing in the passage says she cut workers or changed the ovens.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “indispensable” mean?
options: unable to do his job well
always free to help on short notice
qs.why: “Indispensable” means absolutely necessary; Tomás was too important to the change to do without. “Easy to replace” is the opposite.

qs.q: How did the bakery clear its waiting list of cakes?
options: By working through the night every day
By organizing the work better, with set stations, checklists and a better layout
By letting Tomás make all the cakes alone
qs.why: The passage describes stations, checklists and moving the flour bins, and then says the list was gone by June. No new staff, ovens or refused orders are mentioned.

title: Desert Lessons
text: When Amara and her cousin Joel planned a two-day hike across a dry valley, an old ranger gave them one warning: carry more water than you think you need. The land there is arid; it can go many weeks without a single drop of rain. Plants are sparse, mostly low bushes standing far apart, so there is almost no shade. The first climb was strenuous, and by noon both of them were breathing hard. Joel, who runs marathons, had more stamina, but even he slowed down. Late in the afternoon Amara pointed at a shining lake ahead. Joel laughed. It was a mirage, made by hot air bending the light. Without the ranger's advice, the trip could have been perilous. Instead, they finished tired, sunburned and proud, with one full bottle of water still in each pack.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “sparse” mean?
qs.why: The next words explain it: low bushes “standing far apart,” so there is little shade. “Tall and thick” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “mirage” mean?
options: something that looked like water but was not really there
a small lake fed by an underground spring
a real pond reflecting the sky
a dream Amara had while resting
a trick Joel played on Amara
a sign that rain was coming
qs.why: Joel laughs because the shining lake is a mirage, caused by hot air bending light; there was no real water. It was not a trick by Joel.

qs.q: What does the passage suggest made the trip end safely?
options: Joel's marathon training carried them both
They followed the ranger's advice and carried extra water
They found shade under tall trees
They drank from the lake they saw
qs.why: The passage says the trip could have been dangerous without the ranger's advice, and they still had a full bottle each at the end. The lake was a mirage, so they could not drink from it.

title: The Missing Grams
text: For three weeks, chemistry student Priya Raman could not explain a discrepancy in her results. Her notebook said each sample should weigh ten grams after drying, but the scale kept showing a little less. To understand the problem, she first tried to quantify it: on average, each sample was losing 0.3 grams. Her professor asked her to ascertain where the missing weight was going before she wrote anything up. One evening, while waiting for a bus in the rain, Priya had an epiphany. Water! Her method expected some water to stay locked inside the crystals, but the hot drying oven was driving it out. The next morning she tentatively shared the idea with her lab group, unsure whether it would hold up. Two more weeks of testing gave a conclusive answer: she was right, and the fix was simply a cooler oven.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “ascertain” mean?
options: find out for certain by checking
qs.why: The professor wanted Priya to find out for sure where the weight went before writing up her results. A guess would not be enough.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “tentatively” mean?
qs.why: The passage adds that she was “unsure whether it would hold up,” so she shared the idea hesitantly. “Loudly and proudly” is the opposite.

qs.q: Why did the samples weigh less than expected?
options: She weighed the samples on the wrong day
The hot oven drove out water that her method expected to stay in the crystals
Some samples were lost on the bus
qs.why: Her sudden realization, later confirmed, was that the oven was removing water. The rain only gave her the idea; it did not get into the lab.

title: Two Chairs on the Porch
text: For eleven years, Darius and Kofi Mensah did not speak. A quarrel over their late father's fishing boat had left the brothers estranged, and Kofi held a grudge that seemed to grow heavier every holiday. Their mother found solace in her garden, where, she joked, the tomatoes never argued. Last summer, Darius drove six hours to Kofi's house with the boat's old wooden steering wheel in the back seat. He said he had been wrong to sell the boat without asking, and he wanted to make amends. Kofi was quiet for a long time. Then he laughed and admitted he had always hated that boat. The two men sat on the porch until midnight, speaking fondly about the trips they took as boys. Their mother called it the most poignant evening of her life.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “estranged” mean?
options: no longer close or in contact after a fight
qs.why: The quarrel left the brothers not speaking for eleven years: they were no longer in contact. Nothing says they lived in different countries.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “amends” mean?
options: a legal change to an agreement
something done to make up for a wrong
a promise never to visit again
qs.why: Darius admitted he was wrong and came to make up for it. An excuse would defend the mistake instead of making up for it.

qs.q: What helped end the brothers' long silence?
options: Darius admitted he had been wrong and came to see Kofi in person
Their mother forced them to meet
A holiday party brought them together
Kofi apologized for selling the boat
qs.why: Darius drove to Kofi's house and said he had been wrong to sell the boat. It was Darius, not Kofi, who sold it.

title: The Final Board
text: At the city youth chess championship, fourteen-year-old Ana Sokolova faced her nemesis for the fifth time. Rafael Ortiz had beaten her in four straight tournaments, always in the last round. His prowess in endgames was well known; coaches said he could squeeze a win out of almost nothing. This time Ana had a small lead, but Rafael attacked relentlessly, move after move, for nearly two hours. Ana's hands shook under the table, yet she kept her composure, breathing slowly and checking each move twice. Her coach later said it was her tenacity that mattered most. She refused to trade away her last advantage, even when a draw would have been easier. On move seventy-one, Rafael finally offered his hand in defeat. Ana had managed to clinch the title, and the first person to congratulate her was Rafael.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “clinch” mean?
qs.why: Rafael offered his hand in defeat, so Ana finally won the title. Sharing it would have meant a draw, which she refused.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “composure” mean?
qs.why: Although her hands shook, she stayed calm and in control, breathing slowly. Nervousness is what she was fighting, not what she kept.

qs.q: Which best describes how Ana won?
options: She held on to a small lead under heavy pressure instead of settling for a draw
She attacked quickly and won in a few moves
Rafael made a careless early mistake
She accepted a draw and shared the title
Her coach told her what moves to make
She had beaten Rafael many times before
qs.why: Rafael attacked for two hours, and Ana refused an easier draw until he gave up. Rafael had beaten her four times before, not the other way round.

title: A Book in the Attic
text: When the venerable Hollis Library, open since 1790, cleaned out its attic, a volunteer named Grace Okafor found a small book wrapped in cloth. Inside was a handwritten treatise on beekeeping, page after page about hives, honey and the habits of queen bees. The spelling was archaic, full of words nobody has used for two hundred years, and the ink had faded to brown. It took Grace and two experts a month to decipher the hardest pages. Next came the question of provenance. Who had written it, and how had it reached the attic? A note in the back led them to a farming family that had given books to the library in the 1800s. The experts believe it is the only extant copy of the work, which makes it the most valuable book the library owns.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “provenance” mean?
options: where it came from and who had owned it
the main subject of the book
qs.why: The next questions explain it: who wrote it and how it reached the attic. Its value comes later and is a different idea.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “extant” mean?
qs.why: The experts think this is the only copy still in existence. “Lost long ago” is the opposite.

qs.q: Why is the book so valuable to the library?
options: It is the oldest book in the world
It was written by a famous scientist
It explains how to earn money from honey
It is believed to be the only copy of the work still in existence
qs.why: The last sentence links its value to being the only copy that still exists. Nothing says it is the oldest book in the world or by a famous author.

title: Saving Willow Creek
text: For years, Willow Creek Park was a mess of plastic bags and broken shopping carts, and most neighbors simply walked past. Some blamed the city; others blamed apathy, saying no one cared enough to act. Then a retired nurse named Rosa Delgado printed fifty flyers and knocked on doors. Within two weeks she had managed to mobilize more than a hundred volunteers, from teenagers to grandparents. The cleanup became a concerted effort: one team pulled trash from the water, another cut back thorny weeds, and local shops gave gloves and bags. Rosa knew one day would not eradicate litter forever, so the group now meets every month. The creek is not pristine yet, but herons have returned to the shallow water. The mayor, who supported the project wholeheartedly, plans to try the same idea in other parks.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “apathy” mean?
qs.why: The passage explains it right away: “no one cared enough to act.” Anger would push people to act, not walk past.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “pristine” mean?
options: perfectly clean, as if never harmed
qs.why: The creek has improved but is not yet perfectly clean. “Dirty and unsafe” describes how it was before, not what it has not become.

qs.q: Why does the group now meet every month?
options: The herons need to be fed
The shops wanted to sell more gloves
The creek was already perfectly clean
One cleanup day could not get rid of the litter for good
qs.why: Rosa knew one day would not remove litter forever, so the group keeps meeting. The first cleanup did work: herons came back.

title: Too Good to Be True
text: Dear members: This month we want to warn you about a common scam. It often begins with an unsolicited text message saying you have won a prize or qualified for a special low-interest loan. The message is designed to entice you with something pleasant, such as cash or a free vacation, so that you click a link. The website that opens may look exactly like ours, but the design is deceptive; the page exists only to steal your password. These schemes are predatory, often aimed at older people or anyone short on money. You do not have to be gullible to be fooled. Busy, tired people fall for these tricks every day. Please stay vigilant. We will never ask for your password by text or email. If in doubt, call the number printed on the back of your card. — Maple Hollow Savings

qs.q: In the passage, what does “unsolicited” mean?
qs.why: The text arrives out of nowhere, without the person asking for it. Being free or short has nothing to do with the word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “gullible” mean?
options: easily tricked because you believe what you are told
qs.why: The letter says you need not be the kind of person who believes everything to be fooled. “Careless with money” is close but is not the meaning.

qs.q: What is the main message of the letter?
options: Only foolish people fall for scams
The bank is offering special low-interest loans
Members should move their money to another bank
Anyone can be fooled, so members should be careful with unexpected messages
The bank's website has been shut down
Members should text their passwords to check them
qs.why: The letter says busy, tired people fall for these tricks and asks everyone to stay alert. It says directly that you do not have to be gullible to be fooled.

title: Lost on Purpose
text: Hiro had planned every hour of his trip to the hill town. His itinerary listed a castle at nine, a museum at eleven, and lunch at exactly twelve-thirty. But the old center was a labyrinth of narrow lanes, and within ten minutes he had no idea where the castle was. He wandered past quaint shops selling hand-painted plates and wooden toys. In one cramped café, with only four tables pressed against the walls, an old woman served him the best soup he had ever tasted. Later he stepped into a small church whose ceiling was ornate, covered in gold leaves, stars and painted birds. He decided to linger there for an hour, just looking up. He never reached the museum. That evening he wrote in his journal that getting lost had been the best part of the whole trip.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “labyrinth” mean?
options: a confusing set of paths where it is easy to get lost
qs.why: Within ten minutes in the narrow lanes, Hiro had no idea where he was. A wide main road would be easy to follow.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “linger” mean?
qs.why: He stayed an hour just looking up, which is why he never reached the museum. “Leave in a hurry” is the opposite.

qs.q: How does Hiro come to feel about his trip?
options: He is angry about the confusing streets
The unplanned moments were better than the schedule he made
He wishes he had hired a guide
The castle was the best part
The café was too small to enjoy
qs.why: His journal says getting lost was the best part. He found great soup and a beautiful ceiling only because he left his plan.

title: Mr. Haddad's Math Class
text: When Samir Haddad began teaching ninth-grade math, several students told him they were simply bad at numbers. He wanted to reassure them that this was not true. In his first week, he avoided anything that sounded condescending; he never called a problem easy or sighed at a wrong answer. Instead, he asked students how they had reached their answers, even the wrong ones. Slowly he built a strong rapport with the class. Students who had sat silently in the back started asking questions. One girl, Lucía, showed a real aptitude for geometry, solving puzzles faster than anyone. Samir gave her harder problems to nurture that talent. Not every idea worked; his weekly quizzes were unpopular. But the class was receptive when he suggested replacing them with group challenges, and test scores rose by spring.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “condescending” mean?
options: acting as if he were smarter or more important than the students
qs.why: Calling a problem easy or sighing at mistakes makes students feel looked down on. “Too strict” is about rules, not about looking down on people.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “receptive” mean?
options: willing to listen to and consider the idea
qs.why: The class welcomed his suggestion to replace the quizzes. “Firmly against it” is the opposite.

qs.q: Why did Samir ask students how they reached even their wrong answers?
options: To find out who was bad at numbers
To show he valued their thinking and make them less afraid of mistakes
To make the lessons last longer
To choose who got harder problems
qs.why: He wanted students to stop believing they were bad at numbers, and he avoided anything that made them feel small. Asking about their thinking fits that goal; nothing suggests he was checking for copying.

title: Back on Her Feet
text: After a serious lung infection last winter, Helen Park spent six weeks in the hospital. The illness was debilitating; at first she could not walk to the bathroom without help, and she felt frail, as if a strong wind could knock her over. Her doctor explained that recovery would be incremental. Day one: stand for two minutes. Day five: walk to the end of the hall. Before getting sick, Helen had a sedentary job, sitting at a computer for nine hours a day, and she admits she rarely exercised. Now walking became her main task. After Helen came home, her daughter visited every afternoon, giving Helen's husband a respite from caring for her. The nurses praised Helen's fortitude, since she rarely complained even on painful days. Today she walks three miles each morning and has asked her office for a standing desk.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “incremental” mean?
options: happening in small steps over time
qs.why: The doctor's plan goes from standing two minutes to walking down the hall: small steps, one after another. “Sudden and complete” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “respite” mean?
options: a short break from something hard
qs.why: The daughter's visits gave Helen's husband a short break from caring for her. It was not a long trip.

qs.q: What change suggests Helen has learned from her illness?
options: She asked for a standing desk so she will sit less at work
She moved closer to the hospital
She asked her daughter to visit every day
qs.why: Before, she sat nine hours a day and rarely exercised; now she walks daily and wants to stand at work. Her daughter's visits happened during recovery and do not show a new habit.

title: Dinner at the Blue Lantern
text: The Blue Lantern, a small restaurant on Fourth Street, has an eclectic menu. In one meal you might eat Korean fried chicken, Mexican street corn and Italian lemon cake, and somehow it all works. Owner Nadia Fern says her cooking comes from her travels and from her neighbors' kitchens. The portions are copious; my friend and I took home enough rice for two more lunches. Service was impeccable. Our water glasses never sat empty, and our server remembered, without writing anything down, that I could not eat nuts. Even on a busy Friday, the staff kept a relaxed, friendly demeanor, smiling as they slipped between crowded tables. Nadia herself came out to give us a cordial greeting. Fresh, bold flavors are the hallmark of her cooking. Book a table early; this place is no secret anymore.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “copious” mean?
qs.why: The writer took home enough rice for two more lunches, so the servings were more than enough. “Small but expensive” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “demeanor” mean?
options: the way they looked and behaved
qs.why: The staff came across as relaxed and friendly, smiling between tables. That is their outward manner, not their clothes.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the service was excellent?
options: The server remembered the writer could not eat nuts without writing it down
The menu mixed foods from many countries
The restaurant was busy on a Friday
qs.why: The note about nuts comes right after “Service was impeccable” as proof. Large portions and a varied menu are about the food, not the service.

title: The Dog Park Debate
text: Few issues in Maple Falls have been as contentious as the plan to turn half of Riverside Field into a dog park. At last Tuesday's town meeting, dog owners filled one side of the room and youth soccer parents filled the other. Each group had a grievance: dog owners said they had nowhere to let pets run, while parents said their children already had too little space to play. Town leaders asked a retired judge, Eleanor Voss, to mediate. Everyone agreed she would be impartial, since she owns no dog and has no children on a team. Voss let each side speak for ten minutes. Then she proposed using a fenced corner of the field on weekday mornings only, when no games are played. One by one, speakers stood to concur. Before closing, Voss chose to reiterate the agreement so no one could later claim to have misunderstood it.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “mediate” mean?
options: decide who was right and punish the other side
help the two sides reach an agreement
qs.why: Voss listened to both sides and suggested a plan they could accept. A judge in court might decide who is right, but here she helped them agree.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “reiterate” mean?
options: say again to make it clear
qs.why: She repeated the agreement so no one could later say they misunderstood it. She did not change it.

qs.q: Why was Eleanor Voss chosen to lead the discussion?
options: She had no personal stake in either side
She had written the dog park plan
qs.why: People trusted her to be fair because she owns no dog and has no child on a team. Nothing says she owned the field, led the town, coached soccer or wrote the plan.

title: The Keeper's Light
text: The lighthouse on Gull Point had been dark for twenty years when Maya Brooks bought it. On her first night, a thick fog rolled in, so dense and gray that the windows seemed opaque. Around midnight she heard a slow knocking from the stairs. The sound was eerie, soft and steady, like someone patiently waiting to be let in. Maya told herself that no one could lurk in a tower with one locked door. Still, she climbed the stairs with a flashlight. At the top, the old lamp, which had no bulb and no power, began to emit a faint green glow. It was inexplicable. Then she noticed an uncanny detail: the knocking matched the rhythm of the waves below. In the morning, a fisherman told her that the old keeper used to tap the railing to count the waves.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “lurk” mean?
options: stay hidden, waiting to do something bad
qs.why: Maya was reassuring herself that no one could be hiding in the tower. Making loud noises is the opposite of hiding.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “opaque” mean?
qs.why: The thick gray fog made the glass seem as if no light could pass through it. Fog can make windows wet, but that is not what the word means.

qs.q: What does the fisherman's remark suggest?
options: The fisherman was making the noise
The keeper was still living in the tower
The knocking may be connected to the old keeper's habit
qs.why: The keeper tapped the railing to count waves, and the knocking matched the waves. The story hints at a link without explaining it.

title: The App That Fell Flat
text: In 2019 two friends, Kwame and Leila, launched a meal-planning app that they were sure would change family dinners. Early reviews were warm, and downloads rose for months. Then they grew complacent. They stopped asking users what they wanted and spent their money on a flashy ad campaign instead. The app had one major drawback: it worked with only three grocery chains, so many users could not order food through it. When a rival offered the same features for every store, users left fast. The final three months were a debacle; the company lost most of its customers and nearly all its cash. In hindsight, Kwame says, ignoring users was the real folly. 'We thought our early success could not be lost,' he says. 'We didn't see that each lazy choice could jeopardize everything we'd built.' The pair now give free advice to new founders.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “complacent” mean?
options: too satisfied to notice danger or keep improving
qs.why: After early success, they stopped asking users what they wanted: they felt too safe. “Nervous about failing” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “hindsight” mean?
options: understanding after it has already happened
a quick look at the numbers
qs.why: Kwame sees the mistake now, looking back. Regret may come with it, but the word means understanding gained afterward.

qs.q: According to Kwame, what was the main mistake?
options: They launched the app too early
They partnered with too many grocery chains
They stopped listening to their users
They spent too little on ads
qs.why: He calls ignoring users “the real folly.” In fact they worked with too few chains, not too many, and spent a lot on ads.

title: Six Cookies Short
text: Six-year-old twins Ollie and Zara are known in their family as the most mischievous children on the block. Last Saturday they wanted the chocolate cookies cooling on the kitchen counter, so they came up with a ruse. Zara ran into the garden shouting that she had seen a deer. The commotion worked. Their father, Ben, rushed outside, and their grandmother followed with her phone, hoping for a photo. Ollie, meanwhile, climbed onto a chair and grabbed six cookies. He was so focused that he was oblivious to the family cat, which jumped onto the counter beside him and knocked the whole tray to the floor. Ben came back inside at the crash. He could barely restrain his laughter at the sight of Ollie, the cat and a floor covered in crumbs. He was angry only momentarily.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “ruse” mean?
options: a clever trick to fool someone
qs.why: Zara's fake deer was a trick to get the adults out of the kitchen. An honest request is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “oblivious” mean?
qs.why: Ollie was so focused on the cookies that he did not notice the cat. “Watching closely” is the opposite.

qs.q: Why did Zara shout that she had seen a deer?
options: So her grandmother would take her photo
To get the adults outside so Ollie could take cookies
To warn her father about danger
qs.why: The shout was part of the twins' trick to reach the cookies. The grandmother wanted a photo of the deer, not of Zara.

title: The Vine That Ate the Forest
text: On the small island of Kelsa, a quiet battle is going on in the forests. Decades ago, a gardener planted a pretty climbing vine from overseas. Today it is pervasive, wrapping trees on every hillside. The threat is insidious: the vine grows slowly at first, and by the time people notice, it has already blocked the sunlight that young trees need. This adversely affects the island's birds, which depend on fruit from native trees. Scientists have tried pulling the vines by hand, but the work is slow, and steep slopes hamper their efforts. To counteract the spread, they are now testing a tiny insect that eats only this vine. Meanwhile, there is burgeoning interest among islanders in planting native trees, and school groups alone have planted ten thousand seedlings this year.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “insidious” mean?
options: easy to see from far away
harmful in a slow, quiet way that is hard to notice
qs.why: The vine grows slowly and is noticed only after the damage is done. “Fast and violent” is the opposite; it did come from overseas, but that is not the meaning.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “counteract” mean?
options: act against it to reduce its effect
qs.why: The insect that eats only the vine is meant to work against its spread. “Speed up” is the opposite.

qs.q: Why has the vine been so hard to control?
options: Islanders protect it because it is pretty
It is noticed only after it spreads, and steep slopes slow down removal
Scientists are not allowed to remove it
qs.why: The passage gives both reasons: the slow, hidden growth and the steep slopes. Nothing mentions birds spreading seeds or rules against removal.

title: A Letter to Lily
text: Dear Lily, Congratulations on your first job! Your mother tells me you will be living alone in the city, so let me share a few thoughts. My years working on my uncle's farm were formative; they shaped how I think about money to this day. My uncle was frugal. He reused nails, patched his boots, and never bought a new tool if an old one could be fixed. His favorite maxim was 'Buy once, buy well.' Here is an anecdote I still laugh about: he once spent a full afternoon repairing a ten-cent shovel handle, then proudly told the neighbors he had saved a fortune. People in our village revered him, not for his money, but for his honesty. I think you have unknowingly picked up some of his habits. You turn off lights without being asked. Keep that. Love always, Grandpa Teo

qs.q: In the passage, what does “formative” mean?
options: having a strong influence on how he developed
qs.why: He says those years shaped how he thinks about money to this day. “Short and easy to forget” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “unknowingly” mean?
qs.why: Lily picked up the habits without noticing, such as turning off lights without being asked. “On purpose” is the opposite.

qs.q: What does the shovel story show about the uncle?
