options: He was bad at making repairs
He wanted to fool his neighbors
He disliked working on the farm
He liked fixing things instead of buying new ones, even when the savings were tiny
qs.why: Spending an afternoon to save ten cents is funny, but it fits his careful habits. He was joking with the neighbors, not fooling them.

title: Three Hundred Voices
text: The community choir of Brookhaven had never performed in the big concert hall until last December. Three hundred singers, ages eight to eighty-five, walked onto the stage in matching blue scarves. Because the hall is old and large, the sound crew placed small microphones to amplify the children's quieter voices. The first song, a slow lullaby, had an ethereal quality, the high notes floating up toward the ceiling like smoke. Many listeners said the music seemed to evoke memories of their own childhoods, and more than a few wiped their eyes. For the finale, all three hundred voices sang in unison, the same notes at the same moment, and the floor seemed to shake. When the last note ended, the crowd leaped up. Backstage, the singers hugged in pure euphoria. The next week, newspaper critics gave the concert wide acclaim.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “evoke” mean?
qs.why: Listeners remembered their own childhoods and some cried. “Erase” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “unison” mean?
options: at exactly the same time, together
qs.why: The passage explains it: “the same notes at the same moment.” “One after another” is the opposite.

qs.q: Why did the sound crew use microphones?
options: To make the children's quieter voices louder in the big old hall
To record the concert for sale
Because the choir was too loud
So the critics could hear better
qs.why: The passage says the microphones were placed to amplify the children's quieter voices. The floor shook because of the whole choir in the finale.

title: The Missing Painting
text: When a small painting vanished from the Hartwell Gallery, Detective Ines Moreau was handed one clue: a cryptic note left on the empty wall. It read only, 'The heron flies at six.' From the note she could infer that something would happen at six o'clock on the Heron, a ferry that left the harbor at that hour. But she suspected a ploy. Why would a thief leave directions? While other officers rushed to the ferry, Ines checked camera footage from a nearby parking garage and learned that a guard had been holding clandestine meetings there with an art dealer. She found the painting in the dealer's car at the airport. Prosecutors now allege that the guard switched off the cameras while the dealer, his accomplice, carried the painting out. Both men say they are innocent, and a trial is planned for the spring.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “infer” mean?
qs.why: Nobody told Ines about the ferry; she worked it out from the note. “Be told directly” is the opposite of inferring.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “allege” mean?
options: say they did wrong without having proved it yet
qs.why: The men say they are innocent and the trial has not happened, so the claim is not yet proved. “Prove” goes too far.

qs.q: Why did Ines doubt the note?
options: The writing was not in English
The ferry left at seven o'clock
A guard told her it was fake
It seemed strange that a thief would leave directions to where he would be
It was signed by the art dealer
She could not understand it at all
qs.why: She asked herself, “Why would a thief leave directions?” She did understand the note; she simply did not trust it.

title: Storm on the Ridge
text: The weather on Mount Kessel is known for abrupt changes, but the storm that hit last August surprised even experienced guides. Within twenty minutes, a clear afternoon turned to sleet and wind. Guide Aiko Tanaka was leading six climbers down a narrow ridge when the path became treacherous, covered in ice that was hard to see on dark rock. Aiko walked at the front, taking the brunt of the wind so the others could shelter behind her. When one climber slipped, Aiko made a valiant grab, catching her backpack strap just before she slid over the edge. Aiko was resolute that no one would be left behind, even when a younger guide suggested splitting the group. By roping everyone together, she managed to avert disaster. All seven reached the mountain hut by nightfall, cold but unhurt.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “brunt” mean?
qs.why: Aiko walked in front so she faced the strongest wind and the others could hide behind her. “A small amount” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “avert” mean?
qs.why: Roping everyone together kept a disaster from happening at all. “Avert your eyes” is a different use of the word.

qs.q: Why did Aiko refuse to split the group?
options: She wanted to reach the top first
The climbers asked her to keep going
She did not trust the mountain hut
She wanted to go back for a lost bag
She was determined that every climber would get down safely together
qs.why: She was firm that no one would be left behind, and she roped everyone together. Nothing suggests the younger guide was lost.

title: Mud on a Board
text: When the painter Odile Nkemelu first showed her work in 1962, critics were quick to ridicule it. Her methods were unorthodox: she painted with kitchen sponges, coffee and sand instead of brushes and oil. One newspaper called her pictures mud on a board. Odile kept working. By the 1980s, younger artists were copying her methods, and her painting River at Noon came to be seen as a seminal work that shaped a whole generation of painters. Today her renown reaches far beyond her home country, and her pictures hang in museums on four continents. Next month the city art museum, itself an illustrious institution with a two-hundred-year history, will open a large show of her work. The curator says Odile's gift was to transcend the materials she used; looking at her paintings, you forget the coffee and see only light.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “seminal” mean?
options: very important and shaping much of the later work
qs.why: The painting “shaped a whole generation of painters.” It came early in a movement, but the word means influential, not unfinished.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “transcend” mean?
options: go beyond the usual limits of
qs.why: Her paintings rise above their humble materials, so viewers forget the coffee. “Fall below” is the opposite.

qs.q: How did opinions of Odile's work change over time?
options: It was praised from the very beginning
It was admired at first and later forgotten
She stopped painting after the criticism
It became popular only in her home country
Museums still refuse to show it
Critics mocked it at first, but later it was widely admired and copied
qs.why: In 1962 critics made fun of her; by the 1980s others copied her, and now museums worldwide show her work. She kept working despite the early criticism.

title: The Mill Comes Back
text: For thirty years, the old textile mill in Carver's Bend stood empty. The company that built it was long defunct, and the brick building had become a relic of the town's busier past, its windows broken and its clock stopped at 3:15. News in the town was dismal; young people moved away, and shops on Main Street closed one by one. Then the architect Farah Siddiqui moved back home. She could envision the mill as something new: apartments upstairs, a food market downstairs and a walking path along the river. It took eight years of meetings, loans and building work for her plan to reach fruition. The market opened last spring, and the town is now seeing a small resurgence. Two cafés and a bike shop have opened nearby, and for the first time in decades, the school is adding a classroom.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “envision” mean?
options: picture as a possibility in the future
qs.why: Farah imagined what the empty mill could become. “Remember as it once was” looks to the past, not the future.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “defunct” mean?
qs.why: The company was long gone, which is why the mill had been empty for thirty years. “Newly started” is the opposite.

qs.q: What evidence shows the town is recovering?
options: Young people are still moving away
New businesses have opened, and the school is adding a classroom
More shops on Main Street are closing
qs.why: The last sentence lists new cafés, a bike shop and an extra classroom. The passage never says the clock was fixed.

title: The Twelve-Page Form
text: At Delmar Shipping, every employee knew the old expense form. It was cumbersome: twelve pages, three signatures and a printer that jammed at page nine. The software behind it was rudimentary, unable even to add up totals, so workers did the math by hand. Filing the form was obligatory for any purchase over five dollars, even a coffee for a client. Not surprisingly, some staff found a loophole. The rule covered single purchases over five dollars, so they split larger bills into several small receipts. Managers knew people would always try to circumvent a rule that wasted so much time. So last year the company built a simple phone app: take a photo of the receipt, and you are done. Managers also agreed to waive the form completely for purchases under fifty dollars. Complaints dropped almost overnight.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “loophole” mean?
options: a hole in the paper form
a gap in the rule that let people avoid obeying it
qs.why: Splitting bills into small receipts let staff avoid the form while seeming to follow the rule. It was a gap in the rule, not a hole in paper.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “waive” mean?
qs.why: For purchases under fifty dollars, managers no longer demand the form. “Make stricter” is the opposite; “wave” only sounds the same.

qs.q: What was the company's main solution?
options: It fired staff who split receipts
It lowered the limit to five dollars
It made the process simpler so people had less reason to avoid it
It hired more managers to check forms
It banned buying coffee for clients
qs.why: The company built an easy app and dropped the form for small purchases, and complaints fell. The five-dollar limit was the old rule, not the fix.

title: A Lesson on the Field
text: In the final minute of a youth soccer match in Glenwood, a player on the home team blatantly tripped an opponent who was running toward an open goal. Everyone in the stands saw it. The referee showed a red card, but the player's coach, Marcus Hale, ran onto the field, shouting that the call was unwarranted. When the referee asked him to leave, Hale stayed defiant, standing with his arms crossed. League rules say a team must forfeit the match if a coach refuses to obey an official. Some parents expected the league to be lenient, since it was Hale's first problem in twelve seasons. Instead, the league director chose to rebuke him in a public letter and suspended him for three games. Hale later apologized to the referee. 'I set a bad example for the kids,' he said.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “forfeit” mean?
options: lose as a penalty for breaking a rule
end early but keep the score
qs.why: Under league rules, a coach who will not obey an official makes his team lose the match. “Win without playing” is what the other team gets.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “lenient” mean?
qs.why: Parents thought his good record might earn him a lighter punishment. “Very harsh” is the opposite.

qs.q: Why did some parents expect a light punishment for Hale?
options: The trip was hard to see
He had had no problems in his twelve earlier seasons
The referee had made a wrong call
The other team asked for mercy
qs.why: The passage links the expectation to his clean record. Everyone saw the trip, and Hale apologized only later.

title: Delayed, Then Ignored
text: When her flight to Lima was canceled for the third time, Carmen Ruiz joined a long line of disgruntled passengers at the airport desk. The airline had offered no hotel and no meal coupons. The worker at the desk, clearly exhausted, gave a curt reply to every question: 'No seats. Check the app.' By midnight, the airline's social media page faced a barrage of angry posts, with hundreds arriving every hour. Carmen had paid a hefty price for a last-minute hotel room, nearly four hundred dollars. Instead of shouting online, she wrote a calm, detailed email asking the airline to rectify the situation. Two weeks later, a manager replied with an apology. As restitution, the airline paid back her hotel bill and gave her a free flight. 'Being calm and specific worked better than shouting,' Carmen says.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “curt” mean?
qs.why: “No seats. Check the app.” is as brief as possible and not friendly. “Long and detailed” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “restitution” mean?
options: a punishment for the desk worker
payment to make up for her loss
qs.why: The airline paid back the hotel bill and added a free flight. The apology came too, but restitution means the repayment.

qs.q: What lesson does Carmen take from her experience?
options: Never fly with that airline again
Angry posts force companies to pay
Always book a hotel before flying
A calm, specific complaint can get better results than anger
qs.why: Her own words say calm and specific worked better than shouting. The angry posts are not linked to any result.

title: Myth Check: Cracking Knuckles
text: Many of us grew up hearing a warning: crack your knuckles and you will get arthritis. It is a widespread misconception, and it is easy to see why people believe it. The popping sound is loud, and it seems as if something must be breaking. But the claim is erroneous. The sound comes from gas bubbles in the fluid inside the joint, not from bones grinding. Researchers have tried to refute the myth in several ways. One doctor cracked the knuckles of only one hand for about sixty years and found no arthritis in either hand. Larger studies comparing knuckle-crackers with non-crackers also found no link. Still, old beliefs are hard to change. When a reader sent us a long rebuttal to an earlier column, pointing to his aunt's sore fingers, we replied with a lucid explanation of the science. We hope this column helps dispel the fear for good.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “erroneous” mean?
options: wrong because it is based on a mistake
qs.why: The column says the claim is false and explains the real cause of the sound. “Partly true” is a near-miss; the column says there is no link at all.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “rebuttal” mean?
options: a letter agreeing with the column
an argument trying to show the column was wrong
qs.why: The reader used his aunt's sore fingers to argue against the column. Agreeing with it is the opposite.

qs.q: Why, according to the writer, do so many people believe the myth?
options: Doctors still recommend not cracking knuckles
The loud pop makes it seem as if damage is happening
Gas bubbles slowly wear down bones
qs.why: The writer says the loud sound makes it seem something is breaking. The studies mentioned found no link.

title: The Spring Gala
text: Every spring, the affluent families of Linden Heights hold a glittering gala, ostensibly to raise money for the town's food bank. Tickets cost five hundred dollars, and guests arrive in long cars and evening dresses. Last year, however, a local reporter, Jun Takeda, looked at the numbers. Most of the money raised paid for the band, the flowers and the catering, and the food bank received only a few thousand dollars. To many readers, the event's benevolent image was just a veneer over what was really an expensive party. Some called the organizers hypocritical for celebrating their kindness while giving so little. One organizer, Patricia Chu, responded differently. She admitted the problem and changed the format: this year there is a simple potluck dinner, and every dollar goes straight to the food bank. 'Real philanthropy,' she said, 'isn't about how good it looks.'

qs.q: In the passage, what does “ostensibly” mean?
options: as it is claimed, though maybe not truly
qs.why: The gala claimed to help the food bank, but most of the money went to the party itself. “Openly and honestly” misses the hint of doubt.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “veneer” mean?
options: a thin layer of fine wood
a pleasant surface that hid what it really was
qs.why: The kind image covered up an expensive party. Veneer can mean a thin wood layer on furniture, but that is not the meaning here.

qs.q: What made this year's event better, according to the passage?
options: All of the money now goes directly to the food bank
The reporter now runs the event
It is held in a fancier hall
qs.why: Patricia replaced the gala with a potluck so every dollar reaches the food bank. Nothing is said about the band or the hall.

title: New City, Familiar Bread
text: When Oleksandr Bondar moved from a small village in Ukraine to Toronto for university, he felt lost. In his first month, his inclination was to stay in his room and call his parents. Then a classmate took him to a Ukrainian bakery in a neighborhood that felt like a little enclave of home, where shop signs and conversations mixed Ukrainian and English. He felt an instant kinship with the older men playing chess outside. Still, his advisor warned him not to spend all his free time there. 'Use these years to broaden your circle,' she said. Oleksandr had a strong aversion to big parties, where he never knew what to say. So he joined the university cycling club instead, where talking came naturally on long rides. By spring he could mingle at club dinners with ease, joking with riders from Brazil, Kenya and Vietnam. He still buys his bread at the bakery every Sunday.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “aversion” mean?
options: a strong dislike that made him want to avoid them
qs.why: He never knew what to say at big parties, so he looked for another way to meet people. A talent for parties is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “enclave” mean?
options: a small area whose people differ in culture from the area around it
a village far from the city
qs.why: The neighborhood had signs and talk in Ukrainian inside a mostly English-speaking city. It was part of the city, not a faraway village.

qs.q: Why did Oleksandr join the cycling club?
options: It let him meet people without the pressure of big parties
To get to the bakery faster
qs.why: He disliked big parties, and on long rides talking came naturally. His advisor only told him to broaden his circle; she did not name the club.

title: The Bread-Loaf Satellite
text: For the engineering students at Halden Technical College, last Thursday was a momentous day. After four years of work, they were ready to unveil the satellite they had built. It is small, about the size of a loaf of bread, but building it was a colossal task. The team faced one major constraint: their budget was a tiny fraction of what space companies spend. That forced ingenuity. Instead of buying costly parts, they built the frame from recycled aluminum, used a modified phone camera, and wrote all the control software themselves. Before any launch, a satellite must pass a shaking test that copies the strong vibrations of a rocket ride. Passing it is a prerequisite for a place on the rocket. The students' satellite passed on the first try. If all goes well, it will launch next spring and take photographs of forests to track changes in tree cover.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “constraint” mean?
options: something that limited what they could do
qs.why: Their small budget limited what they could buy. It was not their goal.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “prerequisite” mean?
options: something that must happen before something else can
qs.why: The satellite must pass the shaking test before it can get a place on the rocket. It is required, not optional.

qs.q: What forced the students to be so creative?
qs.why: The passage says the small budget “forced ingenuity,” so they reused materials and built parts themselves. The shaking test is a later step, which they passed on the first try.

title: The First Day of Bread
text: When Amara Okafor opened her tiny bakery on Elm Street, the first morning was auspicious: a line of neighbors stretched past the bus stop before sunrise. Her savings were meager, so she had bought a used oven and borrowed tables from her church. Friends called her resourceful, and she proved them right again and again. When the flour ran low at noon, she walked to the grocery store across the road and came back with ten bags to replenish her shelves. By evening, every loaf was gone. Amara sat on the back step with the last cinnamon roll, which she had saved for herself, and decided to savor it slowly. She felt buoyant, even though her feet ached. A good first day, she knew, did not promise a good first year. Still, she let herself enjoy the moment before she began planning for tomorrow.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “auspicious” mean?
options: showing signs that success is likely
qs.why: A long line of customers on the first morning was a good sign for the future, so “auspicious” means showing signs of likely success. “Very crowded” describes the scene but not the word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “replenish” mean?
qs.why: The flour had run low, so she bought more to fill her shelves again. “Give away” or “sell cheaply” would empty the shelves, not refill them.

qs.q: What does the end of the passage suggest about Amara?
options: She expected the bakery to fail soon.
She was too tired to enjoy anything.
She planned to close the bakery after one year.
She was sure the first year would be easy.
She was happy with the day but knew future success was not certain.
She was upset that all the bread sold out.
qs.why: She lets herself enjoy the moment while knowing “a good first day did not promise a good first year.” She is not sure of failure or of easy success.

title: The Strange Water Sample
text: Dr. Lena Kowalski noticed the anomalous number on a Tuesday. One of the forty water samples from the lake showed a salt level ten times higher than the rest. Her first thought was that a machine had failed. But she had tested every sample meticulously, cleaning each glass tube twice, so a careless mistake seemed unlikely. Her colleague Tomás, a born skeptic, refused to get excited. “One strange result proves nothing,” he said. “Test it again, and test it somewhere else.” Lena sent half of the sample to a lab in another city. A week later, their report arrived, and it seemed to corroborate her finding. From the place where the sample was taken, she was able to deduce that a nearby road was the source: workers had spread salt on it all winter, and melting snow had carried the salt downhill. Now the town's officials finally gave her warning some credence.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “anomalous” mean?
options: different from normal and hard to explain
qs.why: The number was ten times higher than all the others, so it was unusual and hard to explain. “Very dangerous” is a careless guess; the passage is about the number being strange.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “credence” mean?
qs.why: After the second lab's report, officials finally believed her warning. “Doubt” is the opposite of what changed.

qs.q: Why did Lena send half of the sample to another lab?
options: Because her own machine was broken
Because Tomás wanted to take the credit
To find out which road had been salted
To see whether a separate lab would get the same result
Because town officials ordered her to
To have the sample cleaned again
qs.why: Tomás told her to “test it somewhere else,” so she sent it away to check that another lab got the same result. Her machine was not shown to be broken.

title: From Last Place to Champions
text: Halfway through the season, the Riverside Hawks reached their nadir: six losses in a row and a crowd so small that you could count the fans. Their play had been lackluster for weeks, with slow passes and tired legs. Then a new coach, Rosa Medina, arrived. She did not shout. Instead, she had the players eat lunch together, run together, and stay late to help one another practice. Slowly, a real camaraderie grew among them. The team's captain, a tenacious defender named Kwame, told reporters, “We just stopped giving up on each other.” The Hawks won eight of their last ten games and made it to the final. They won it 4–0, a resounding victory that no one had predicted. Afterward, the exuberant players danced on the field, sprayed water on Coach Medina, and sang until the stadium lights went off.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “nadir” mean?
qs.why: Six losses in a row and almost no fans was the worst point of their season. It happened “halfway through,” but the word itself means the lowest point, not the middle.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “resounding” mean?
options: great and complete, leaving no doubt
qs.why: A 4–0 win in the final is a clear, complete victory. “Loud and echoing” is another sense of the word, but here it describes how decisive the win was.

qs.q: What mainly turned the team's season around?
options: The new coach shouted at them more.
The team signed new star players.
The players learned to trust and support one another.
More fans came to cheer them on.
They practiced less and rested more.
The other teams in the league got weaker.
qs.why: The coach built friendship and support among the players, and the captain says they “stopped giving up on each other.” She “did not shout.”

title: Grandma Hana's Wooden Box
text: When my grandmother Hana turned ninety, she called me into her bedroom and opened a wooden box I had never seen. Inside lay the family's greatest heirloom: a silver hair comb that had belonged to her own grandmother in Osaka. Next to it was a small memento from her wedding: a dried flower from her bouquet, pressed flat and wrapped in thin paper. Everyone in our family seems to revere Grandma Hana, but she has always been quiet about her past. That afternoon, though, she decided to divulge something she had kept to herself for seventy years: as a young woman, she had run away from home to study painting, against her father's wishes. Her story was so evocative that I could almost smell the paint and hear the trains. “Write it down,” she told me. “Not for me. For posterity.” So I did, and I keep the notebook beside the comb.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “revere” mean?
qs.why: The family treats her with deep respect and admiration. “Feel a little afraid of” is a near miss that a careless reader might choose.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “divulge” mean?
qs.why: She shared something she had kept to herself for seventy years, so she revealed a secret. “Hide even more carefully” is the opposite.

qs.q: Why did Hana want her story written down?
options: So that she could remember it herself
So that future generations would know it
So that it could be sold as a book
So that her father could finally read it
Because the narrator might lose the comb
To prove that she became a famous painter
qs.why: She says “Not for me. For posterity,” meaning future generations. That rules out writing it for herself, the most tempting wrong answer.

title: The Bridge Over the Gap
text: The trail to Eagle Lake is only twelve kilometers long, but the guidebook warns that it is grueling, with steep climbs over loose rock. Priya and her brother Dev started at dawn. Halfway up, they reached a narrow chasm, perhaps two meters wide and so deep that they could not see the bottom. A wooden bridge crossed it. Dev, usually the intrepid one, stopped and stared. Priya took his hand, and they walked across together without looking down. By the time they reached the lake, both of them looked haggard, with sunburned faces and heavy eyes. Dev knelt at a cold stream, filtered a bottle of water, and drank deeply to quench his thirst. Coming down took four more hours. They arrived at the car tired and sore but unscathed, and already arguing about which mountain to climb next.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “intrepid” mean?
options: brave and willing to face danger
qs.why: Dev is “usually the intrepid one,” which is why it is surprising that he stops. “Easily scared” describes his moment at the bridge, not his usual nature.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “unscathed” mean?
qs.why: They were tired and sore but had no injuries. “Badly injured” is the opposite.

qs.q: What happened at the bridge?
options: Dev was afraid, and Priya helped him cross.
They turned back and took another trail.
qs.why: Dev stopped and stared, and Priya took his hand so they could walk across together.

title: A Vote on Linden Park
text: The Maple Grove town council planned to convene on Monday night to decide the future of Linden Park. A company wanted to build apartments on part of the land, and dozens of residents came to speak. At first, the meeting could not begin, because only three of the seven members had arrived, and the town's rules require a quorum of four. When the fourth member rushed in from the rain, Mayor Ines Duarte began to preside over the discussion. Parents spoke about the playground; builders spoke about the town's need for homes. After two hours of careful deliberation, the council voted for a one-year moratorium on any building in the park, giving both sides time to study the plan. The mood was surprisingly amicable. As people left, a builder and a mother who had argued at the microphone were seen sharing an umbrella on the way to the parking lot.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “quorum” mean?
options: all seven members of the council
the smallest number of members needed to make official decisions
a vote that everyone agrees on
the room where meetings are held
a list of people who want to speak
qs.why: The meeting could not start until four members were present, the minimum needed to decide things. It is not all seven members.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “moratorium” mean?
qs.why: The ban on building lasts one year, so it is temporary. “Permanent law” and “final decision to build” miss that point.

qs.q: What did the council's vote do?
options: It allowed the apartments to be built right away.
It banned new homes in the whole town forever.
It removed the mayor from the council.
It canceled the meeting because of the rain.
It paused building in the park for a year while both sides studied the plan.
qs.why: The council chose a one-year ban on building in the park to give everyone time to study the plan. Nothing was approved or banned forever.

title: Dinner at the Golden Lantern
text: I rarely splurge on dinner, but my sister's birthday seemed like a good excuse, so we booked a table at the new Golden Lantern downtown. The room is sumptuous, with deep red chairs, gold lamps, and silk on the walls. The food was mostly a pleasure. The fish soup arrived with a pungent smell of garlic and ginger that filled the whole table, and it tasted even better than it smelled. My sister, a real tea connoisseur, praised the jasmine tea, which she said was the finest she had ever had in a restaurant. Not everything worked. The dessert came with gold leaf, a cloud of smoke, and a sparkler, all of which felt superfluous; the simple rice pudding underneath needed none of it. I have read some scathing reviews of the service online, but our waiter was friendly and quick. I would go back.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “pungent” mean?
qs.why: The garlic and ginger smell “filled the whole table,” so it was strong and sharp. The writer liked it, so “burnt and unpleasant” does not fit.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “superfluous” mean?
qs.why: The writer says the pudding “needed none of it,” so the extras were unnecessary.

qs.q: What is the writer's overall opinion of the restaurant?
options: They agreed with the bad reviews of the service.
They thought the room looked plain and cheap.
They thought the dessert decorations were the best part.
They will not return because it cost too much.
They were disappointed by the tea.
They liked it and would return, despite small complaints.
qs.why: The writer enjoyed most of the meal, found the waiter friendly, and ends with “I would go back.” The service was better than the online reviews said.

title: Why Refunds Took So Long
text: At Brightline Shipping, customer refunds took an average of three weeks, and nobody could say why. The new operations manager, Hiroshi Tanaka, decided to follow a single refund from start to finish. He found that the process was convoluted: forms passed through five departments, and two of them asked for the same information. The real bottleneck was one office where every refund, even a five-dollar one, needed a signature from a single supervisor who was often away. Hiroshi did not dream of a perfect new computer system. With typical pragmatism, he asked a simpler question: what is the smallest change that would help most? He let staff approve small refunds themselves, which removed an onerous task from the supervisor's desk and helped expedite the whole process. Within a month, the team had made real headway. Most refunds now took four days, and customer complaints fell by half.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “bottleneck” mean?
options: a point where a process slows down or gets stuck
the busiest department in the company
qs.why: The one office that needed a single, often absent supervisor's signature was where refunds got stuck and held everything up.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “pragmatism” mean?
options: a practical approach based on what works
qs.why: Instead of dreaming of a perfect system, he looked for the smallest change that would help most, which is a practical approach. “Big dreams of perfection” is the opposite.

qs.q: What is the main lesson of the passage?
options: A new computer system solved the problem.
Several departments had to be closed.
A small, practical change can fix a slow process.
Customers complained more after the change.
qs.why: Letting staff approve small refunds cut the time from three weeks to four days. No new computer system was used.

title: The Youngest Violinist
text: Mei Lin was only eight when she played her first concert in the city hall, and the newspaper called her precocious. Her teacher, an old virtuoso who had played in orchestras across Europe, said he had never taught a child who learned so fast. Before the concert, Mei Lin admitted to her mother that she felt apprehensive. What if she forgot the notes? What if her bow slipped? But when she walked onto the stage, she showed remarkable poise, bowing calmly to the crowd as if she had done it a hundred times. Her fingers moved up and down the strings with a dexterity that made adults in the front row lean forward. The performance was riveting; no one coughed, and no one checked a phone. When the last note faded, the hall was silent for a moment, then filled with applause.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “precocious” mean?
options: showing adult skills much earlier than usual
qs.why: An eight-year-old playing a full concert and learning faster than any child her teacher knew shows skills far beyond her age.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “apprehensive” mean?
options: worried that something bad might happen
qs.why: She worried she might forget the notes or that her bow might slip. “Excited and confident” describes how she later looked on stage, not how she felt before.

qs.q: What does the moment of silence after the last note suggest?
options: The audience did not like the performance.
People were waiting for her to make a mistake.
Mei Lin had forgotten the final notes.
The audience was deeply moved by the music.
The hall's sound system had failed.
qs.why: The crowd had been completely focused, and the silence came just before loud applause, which shows they were moved, not displeased.

title: Saving the Hartley House
text: When Carlos and Femi bought the old Hartley house, their friends thought they were crazy. The place was dilapidated: the roof leaked, half the windows were broken, and a tree was growing through the back porch. The wiring was so antiquated that the inspector laughed when he saw it. But Carlos, a carpenter, could see the quality hidden under the dirt. The stairs were made of solid oak, and the workmanship of the carved railings was finer than anything built today. For two years, the couple painstakingly repaired the house, room by room, scraping old paint with small tools so they would not damage the wood. The hardest job was the foyer, where a hundred-year-old tile floor had to be cleaned piece by piece. Today, when guests step through the front door, they stop and stare. The house has its old splendor back.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “dilapidated” mean?
options: old and falling apart from lack of care
qs.why: A leaking roof, broken windows, and a tree growing through the porch show a house falling apart. Nothing in the passage suggests it was haunted.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “foyer” mean?
options: the entrance hall just inside the front door
qs.why: Guests see the tiled foyer when they “step through the front door,” so it is the entrance hall.

qs.q: Why did Carlos believe the house was worth saving?
options: The inspector said it was in good condition.
He saw high-quality building work under the damage.
Their friends told them to buy it.
He wanted to keep the tree on the porch.
qs.why: As a carpenter, he noticed the solid oak stairs and the fine carved railings. The inspector laughed at the wiring, and the friends thought they were crazy.

title: The Keeper of Gull Island
text: For thirty years, Agnes Byrne kept the lighthouse on Gull Island, and people on the mainland called her a recluse. She came to town only twice a year, bought supplies, and left without small talk. Visitors who sailed out on summer days thought her life looked idyllic: white cliffs, wildflowers, seals on the rocks, and a placid sea that shone like glass. They did not see the island in November, when the sky stayed dreary and gray for weeks and rain hit the windows day and night. Her work could be monotonous, too. Every evening she climbed the same ninety-two steps, cleaned the same lamp, and wrote the same notes in the same book. When a reporter once asked whether she was lonely, Agnes smiled. “I chose this seclusion,” she said. “It gives me room to think. Loneliness is something else.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “placid” mean?
qs.why: A sea that “shone like glass” is calm and still. “Stormy” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “monotonous” mean?
qs.why: She did the same steps, the same lamp, and the same notes every evening, so the work was dull because it never changed.

qs.q: What does Agnes mean by her last words?
options: She is very lonely but hides it.
Being alone by choice is different from feeling lonely.
She wants to move back to the mainland.
She thinks everyone should live on an island.
Her work leaves her no time to think.
qs.why: She chose to be apart from people and says it gives her room to think, while “loneliness is something else.” She does not say she is lonely.

title: A Trial in a Novel
text: In a new courtroom novel, the trouble for accountant Martin Hale begins when a grand jury votes to indict him for stealing money from a children's charity. The main witness is his former assistant, who says she saw him move the funds. Hale's lawyer attacks the veracity of her story, pointing out that her dates do not match the bank records. Another witness admits that what he knows is only hearsay: a friend of a friend told him about the theft. The tension rises when the lawyer suggests that the assistant may have tried to fabricate emails to protect herself. In the end, the jury finds Hale culpable, but for a smaller crime than the one first charged. At sentencing, he asks the judge for clemency, and the judge agrees to a shorter sentence because Hale has paid back every dollar.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “veracity” mean?
options: how true or accurate it is
qs.why: The lawyer questions whether her story is true by showing that her dates do not match the bank records.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “clemency” mean?
options: mercy that makes a punishment less harsh
qs.why: He asks the judge to be merciful, and the judge gives a shorter sentence. He was already found guilty, so it is not proof of innocence.

qs.q: Why did the judge give Hale a shorter sentence?
options: Because he had paid back all the money
Because the assistant's story was false
Because the jury found him innocent
Because the evidence was only hearsay
Because the charity asked for it
qs.why: The passage says the judge agreed “because Hale has paid back every dollar.” The jury did find him guilty of a smaller crime.

title: A Virus at Oakdale
text: Last winter, a stomach virus swept through Oakdale Middle School, and the school nurse, Fatima Rahman, found herself at the center of the story. The virus was unusually virulent: within two days, almost a third of the students were home sick. Parents called the office nonstop, and their apprehension grew with every new case. Fatima knew that fear would spread faster than any germ, so she worked to quell it with facts. She sent a letter home explaining that the illness was unpleasant but rarely serious in healthy children. She also explained how contagion happens: the virus passes on hands, door handles, and shared snacks. In the ensuing week, the school cleaned every classroom, put soap at every door, and asked sick children to stay home for two days after they felt better. Slowly, the number of cases began to subside, and by the end of the month the hallways were full again.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “virulent” mean?
qs.why: A third of the students got sick in two days, so the virus was strong and spread quickly. “Mild and harmless” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “quell” mean?
options: calm or put an end to
qs.why: She used facts to calm the parents' fear. “Make stronger” is the opposite of what she wanted.

qs.q: Why did Fatima send a letter home?
options: To calm worried parents with clear facts
To announce that the school would close
To blame students for spreading the virus
To ask parents to keep every child home for a month
To ask families for money to buy soap
qs.why: She wanted to calm the parents' fear “with facts,” so she explained the illness and how it spreads.

title: The Shipping Magnate
text: Vera Lindqvist started with one rusty boat in a small Swedish port. Forty years later, she is a shipping magnate with sixty vessels and offices on three continents. People who work with her point to her acumen as the secret of her success: she makes quick decisions, and they are rarely wrong. Her boldest move came when two struggling family firms asked her for help. Instead of buying just one, she arranged an amalgamation of both, creating a single company strong enough to compete with the industry's behemoth, a giant firm that controlled half the market. A year later, a court ruled that the giant had broken competition laws and must pay its rivals for lost business. Vera's company received a windfall of two hundred million dollars that no one had planned for. She used part of it to buy new ships, and she decided to divest the company's hotels, which had never made much money, so she could focus on the sea.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “acumen” mean?
options: skill at making good judgments and quick decisions
qs.why: The passage explains her acumen right away: she makes quick decisions that are rarely wrong. “Great wealth” is what she has, not what this word means.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “divest” mean?
options: sell off or get rid of
qs.why: The hotels made little money, and she wanted to focus on ships, so she got rid of them.

qs.q: Why did Vera combine the two family firms?
options: Because she wanted to own more hotels
Because the families were her relatives
To make one company strong enough to compete with the giant firm
qs.why: The combined company was “strong enough to compete with the industry's behemoth.” The court money came later and was not planned.

title: The Library Debate
text: Every spring, the Westbrook High debate team holds a contest open to the whole town. This year's final paired two very different speakers. Samuel Osei is a natural orator who fills the room with his deep voice and his stories. He spoke eloquently about why the town should build a new library, and several people in the audience wiped their eyes. His opponent, Grace Kim, took the other side. Her style was succinct: three points, each explained in a single clear sentence. When Samuel claimed that without a new library “our children will forget how to read,” Grace smiled and called it hyperbole; children were reading at the old library every day. “Then imagine how much they'd read in a better one,” Samuel retorted, and the crowd laughed. Through it all, both speakers showed civility, shaking hands warmly at the end. The judges called it a tie.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “succinct” mean?
qs.why: Three points, each in a single clear sentence, is a short and clear style. “Long and detailed” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “hyperbole” mean?
qs.why: Saying children “will forget how to read” makes the problem sound much bigger than it is, so Grace calls it an exaggeration.

qs.q: How were the two speakers' styles different?
options: Grace told long stories, while Samuel was brief.
Samuel was rude, while Grace was polite.
Samuel spoke quietly, while Grace shouted.
Grace made people cry, while Samuel bored them.
Samuel used stories and emotion, while Grace used short, clear points.
Both speakers used exactly the same style.
qs.why: Samuel moved people with his voice and stories; Grace gave three points in single sentences. Both were polite.

title: The Petrov Brothers
text: For years, the enmity between the Petrov brothers was the worst-kept secret in our neighborhood. It started with a small thing. When they were teenagers, Ivan would belittle his younger brother's drawings, calling them “baby scribbles” in front of friends. Years later, Nikolai did something spiteful in return: he told Ivan's boss about a mistake Ivan had made, just to see him embarrassed. After that, they did not speak for a decade. Their mother finally invited both of them to her seventieth birthday and seated them side by side. When the first argument began, their aunt Olga stepped in to defuse it, using great tact. She did not take a side. She simply asked each of them to tell one happy memory about the other. By dessert, Nikolai was apologizing, and Ivan offered to atone for the old insults by framing one of his brother's new paintings for the family room.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “belittle” mean?
options: make something seem unimportant or worthless
qs.why: Calling the drawings “baby scribbles” in front of friends makes them seem worthless. “Draw smaller” is a trap based on the word “little.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “defuse” mean?
qs.why: Olga stepped in to calm the argument, and she “did not take a side,” so she did not decide who was right.

qs.q: How did aunt Olga help the brothers?
options: She told them which of them was right.
She seated them side by side.
She asked each brother to share a happy memory about the other.
She bought a frame for the painting.
She scolded them in front of the guests.
qs.why: Olga asked each one to share a happy memory. It was their mother, not Olga, who seated them side by side.

title: When the Desert Blooms
text: For most of the year, the desert near our town looks empty. But after a rare spring rain, it changes almost overnight. Seeds that have waited in the dry ground for years suddenly sprout, and within a few weeks the hills are covered in yellow and purple flowers. The bloom is ephemeral; in a month, the heat returns and the plants begin to wither. While it lasts, though, the desert is teeming with life. Bees move from flower to flower, and birds arrive to eat the seeds and insects. For many animals, this short season provides the sustenance they need to survive the long dry months ahead. Even the lizards seem happier: on cool mornings, they bask on warm rocks, waiting for the sun to give them energy. By midday, the morning clouds dissipate, and the sky turns a hard, bright blue.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “ephemeral” mean?
qs.why: The flowers last only about a month before the heat returns. “Very colorful” is true of the flowers, but it is not what this word means.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “bask” mean?
qs.why: The lizards rest on warm rocks in the sun to gain energy, which is enjoying warmth.

qs.q: Why is the short blooming season important for many animals?
options: It is when they move to cooler places.
It is the only time they can drink water.
It gives them food that helps them survive the dry months.
It is when lizards lay their eggs.
It gives them shade from the sun.
qs.why: The passage says the season provides the sustenance, or food, they need “to survive the long dry months ahead.”

title: Letters in the Basement
text: When the old city library cleared out its basement, volunteer Ana Ribeiro found a trove of letters, notebooks, and photographs in a forgotten cabinet. They had belonged to Dr. Lucia Ferreira, a local doctor who died in 1962. Ana spent months helping to sift through the papers, sorting thousands of pages by date. Some notebooks were hard to read, full of arcane symbols that only an old-fashioned pharmacist could understand. Slowly, a remarkable story appeared. For forty years, Dr. Ferreira had treated poor families for free, often paying for their medicine herself. She had never asked for thanks, and she had remained an unsung hero of the city. Now the library has published a compendium of her letters and notes, with photographs and a short history of her clinic. Last spring, the city honored her posthumously, naming a new health center after her.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “arcane” mean?
options: understood by only a few people
qs.why: The symbols could be understood only by “an old-fashioned pharmacist,” so few people know them. “Simple and common” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “unsung” mean?
options: not praised or recognized, though deserving it
qs.why: She did great good but “never asked for thanks” and was not honored until after her death. “Unable to sing” is a trap based on the word's parts.

qs.q: What did the papers reveal about Dr. Ferreira?
options: She was famous during her lifetime.
She quietly helped poor families for free for many years.
She was a pharmacist, not a doctor.
She asked the city to name a building after her.
She wrote a book about her clinic.
She once worked in the library basement.
qs.why: The papers showed she treated poor families for free for forty years without asking for thanks. The city named the building after her death.

title: Ending the Bus Dispute
text: For three months, talks between the bus drivers and the city transit company were stuck in a stalemate. The drivers wanted longer breaks; the company said it could not afford more staff. Each side insisted the onus was on the other to make the first offer. Then a new negotiator, Esther Mwangi, suggested a different approach based on reciprocity: for every request one side made, it had to offer something in return. The drivers agreed to cover some weekend routes, and the company agreed to add ten minutes to every break. At first, both sides were cautious. The drivers' leader asked for a few days to mull over the deal with her members. In the end, most drivers were amenable to it, and they voted to ratify the agreement by a wide margin. The buses kept running, and riders barely noticed that anything had happened.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “onus” mean?
qs.why: Each side said it was the other side's duty to make the first offer. “The blame” is close but misses the idea of a duty to act.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “ratify” mean?
qs.why: The drivers voted for the agreement “by a wide margin,” making it official. “Reject” is the opposite.

qs.q: How did Esther's approach end the stalemate?
options: The company gave the drivers everything they asked for.
Each side gave something in exchange for what it got.
The drivers dropped all of their requests.
The city hired many new drivers.
Bus riders voted on the deal.
Esther made the final decision herself.
qs.why: Under her rule, every request had to come with an offer in return: weekend routes for longer breaks.

title: Too Fast, Too Big
text: When Jake Brennan launched his food-delivery app, he was young, brash, and sure of himself. In his first interview, he announced grandiose plans: within two years, he said, his company would be in every city on Earth. Investors liked his confidence, and money poured in. Jake spent it fast, opening offices in twelve countries before the app worked well in even one. Then customers began to complain about late orders and cold food. Within months, the number of users began to plummet, and the company's value fell by ninety percent. Looking back, Jake calls his mistake hubris. “I believed I couldn't fail,” he says, “so I never asked whether I might.” The experience was sobering. He has started over with a tiny team in one city, and he hopes to slowly recoup some of the money his early investors lost.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “grandiose” mean?
qs.why: Promising to be “in every city on Earth” within two years is a showy plan that was not realistic. “Careful and modest” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “recoup” mean?
options: get back money that was lost
qs.why: He hopes to win back some of the money his investors lost.

qs.q: What does Jake now think caused his failure?
options: His extreme confidence kept him from seeing the risks.
Investors did not give him enough money.
His customers were unfair to him.
qs.why: He says, “I believed I couldn't fail, so I never asked whether I might.” He had plenty of money and opened too many offices, not too few.

title: The Class That Took Things Apart
text: On her first day at Lakeview Elementary, Ms. Divya Rao met a class that earlier teachers had called unruly. Children climbed on desks, threw paper, and ignored the bell. By lunch, Divya was exasperated, and she wondered if she had chosen the wrong job. That night, she changed her plan. The next morning, she brought in a box of old radios and clocks and asked the children to take them apart. The room was still boisterous, but now the noise was about gears and wires. One quiet boy, Marco, turned out to be deeply inquisitive, asking question after question about how speakers make sound. Divya used his curiosity to coax him into reading a library book about electricity. Over the year, she tried to instill one simple habit in her students: when you are curious, find out. By June, other teachers were asking what had changed.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “exasperated” mean?
qs.why: After a morning of children climbing on desks and ignoring her, she was so frustrated she doubted her job choice.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “coax” mean?
qs.why: She used Marco's own curiosity to lead him patiently toward the book. “Force” is the opposite of gentle persuasion.

qs.q: Why did Divya bring old radios and clocks to class?
options: To make the room completely quiet
To punish the class for misbehaving
To sell them to the students
To have the children repair them for the school
To turn the children's energy toward learning
qs.why: The room stayed noisy, but the noise was now “about gears and wires,” so she had turned their energy toward learning, not silenced it.

title: Between Two Worlds
text: Bat-Erdene grew up as a nomad in the Mongolian hinterland, far from the capital and from any paved road. Each season, his family packed their round felt tent, called a ger, and moved their sheep and horses to fresh grass. Life was austere. There was no running water, little furniture, and only a small stove against the bitter winter cold. At eighteen, he left to study engineering in the capital, Ulaanbaatar. He worked hard to assimilate into city life, learning to ride crowded buses, eat at noisy cafés, and dress like his classmates. Still, on hot summer nights in his apartment, he would yearn for the wide, quiet land and the smell of horses. Now thirty, he has a good job, but he spends his whole vacation each summer helping his parents. To do it, he must forgo trips abroad with his friends. “It's worth it,” he says.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “austere” mean?
qs.why: No running water, little furniture, and only a small stove describe a plain life without comfort. “Full of luxury” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “forgo” mean?
qs.why: Because he spends his vacation with his parents, he gives up trips abroad with friends.

qs.q: What can you infer about Bat-Erdene?
options: He dislikes the city and plans to quit his job.
His parents moved to the city with him.
He travels abroad with friends every summer.
He has adapted to city life but still feels close to his family's way of life.
He never learned how to live in the city.
qs.why: He learned city ways and has a good job, yet he longs for the land and spends every summer helping his parents.

title: Rumors on the Third Floor
text: For weeks, rumors had been moving around the third floor of the Carver Insurance office. The company was purportedly planning to close the branch, though no one had seen any proof. Most of the talk was innuendo: someone would mention “big changes coming” and then raise their eyebrows. Leila, who had worked there for twelve years, had only a vague inkling that something was going on, mostly because her manager had become evasive whenever anyone asked about next year's budget. Finally, she asked him directly, and he closed his office door. “I'll confide in you,” he said quietly, “but please keep the details to yourself.” The branch was not closing; it was moving in with another office across town, and everyone would keep their jobs. Leila discreetly told her team only that they had nothing to fear, and the rumors died within a week.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “evasive” mean?
qs.why: Whenever people asked about the budget, the manager avoided answering clearly. “Honest and open” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “inkling” mean?
options: a slight suspicion or vague idea
a fear of losing her job
qs.why: The passage calls it “only a vague inkling,” so she had a weak sense that something was happening, not proof.

qs.q: What was really happening to the branch?
options: Half of the staff would be let go.
The manager was leaving the company.
It was moving in with another office, and no one would lose their job.
The budget was being cut in half.
qs.why: The manager explained that the branch was joining another office across town and everyone would keep their jobs, so the rumor about closing was wrong.

title: From Caterpillar to Wings
text: In our classroom, the monarch caterpillars arrive in a plastic box, each one diminutive, hardly longer than a grain of rice. For about two weeks they do little but eat milkweed leaves and grow, until they are nearly as long as a finger. Then the most amazing part begins. Each caterpillar hangs upside down and forms a green shell called a chrysalis. For about ten days, it hangs there, inert, as if nothing were happening. Inside, however, a complete metamorphosis is taking place: the caterpillar's body breaks down and rebuilds itself as a butterfly. Near the end, the shell turns clear, and the orange and black wings become discernible through it. When the butterfly finally comes out, it rests for a few hours while its wings dry. Then, nimble and light, it climbs onto a child's finger and lifts itself aloft, out through the open window.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “inert” mean?
qs.why: The chrysalis hangs still “as if nothing were happening,” but the caterpillar inside is alive and changing, so “dead” is wrong.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “discernible” mean?
options: able to be seen, though only just
qs.why: Once the shell turns clear, the wings can be seen through it. “Impossible to see” is the opposite.

qs.q: What is happening while the chrysalis seems still?
options: The caterpillar's body is completely changing into a butterfly.
The caterpillar is waiting for warmer weather.
qs.why: The passage says that inside, “the caterpillar's body breaks down and rebuilds itself as a butterfly.”

title: Keeping the Library Open
text: Last fall, the Harbor Point library faced bad news. The town budget had been cut, and officials said the library would have to curtail its hours, closing on weekends and two evenings a week. For many families, this was a serious problem. There is a dearth of quiet places to study in the neighborhood, and many students have no internet at home. Head librarian Kofi Asante did not want money to be an impediment to learning. He and a group of teenagers began to solicit donations, setting up a table at the farmers market and writing letters to local businesses. Then, in December, a retired teacher named Ruth Engel came forward as a benefactor, giving enough money to keep the library open at its usual hours for two more years. The library had won a reprieve, and on the first Saturday after the news, it was busier than ever.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “dearth” mean?
qs.why: Families needed the library because the neighborhood has too few quiet places to study. “A large number” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “reprieve” mean?
options: a delay or cancellation of something unpleasant
qs.why: Thanks to the gift, the cut in hours was put off for two years. “A final closing” is what was avoided.

qs.q: What did Ruth Engel's gift do?
options: It paid for internet in students' homes.
It kept the library at its usual hours for two more years.
It closed the library on weekends.
It paid the teenagers for their work.
It kept the library open forever.
qs.why: Her money kept the library open “at its usual hours for two more years,” not forever.

title: Goodbye to Mr. Ortiz
text: The hall was somber on Friday as the town said goodbye to Rafael Ortiz, who taught science at Central High for thirty-five years. His former student, Dr. Naomi Fischer, gave the eulogy. She described a man who worked tirelessly, arriving at six each morning to set up experiments and staying late to help anyone who was struggling. “He was a paragon of patience,” she said. “I never once heard him raise his voice.” She also spoke of his altruistic side. For decades, he quietly paid for lab coats and calculators for students who could not afford them, and he never told anyone. Naomi only found out years later, from the school secretary. At the end of the service, the principal announced that the school would bestow a new yearly award in his name, to be given to the student who most helps others.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “paragon” mean?
options: someone who has too little of a quality
a person who teaches a quality
a person who pretends to have a quality
a perfect example of a quality
a person who rarely shows a quality
a person who demands a quality from others
qs.why: Naomi never heard him raise his voice, so he was a perfect example of patience. He was a teacher, but the word itself means a perfect example.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “bestow” mean?
qs.why: The school will give a new award in his name each year.

qs.q: How did Naomi learn that Mr. Ortiz paid for students' supplies?
options: The school secretary told her years later.
She read about it in the newspaper.
The principal announced it at the service.
His family told her after he died.
She found receipts in his desk.
qs.why: The passage says she “only found out years later, from the school secretary.” He never told anyone himself.

title: The Nephew in the Corner Office
text: At Silverline Foods, everyone knew how hard it was to reach the company's top echelon. Managers usually spent fifteen years proving themselves. So when the owner's nephew, Trevor, became vice president at twenty-four, with no experience, the staff called it nepotism. It was a flagrant case: Trevor had never worked in the food business, and two well-qualified managers had applied for the same job. His behavior made things worse. He hired an old college friend who acted like his lackey, agreeing with every idea Trevor had and reporting any criticism straight back to him. The staff's indignation grew until two hundred employees signed a letter to the company's board. After a long meeting, the board voted to oust Trevor and give the job to Lucía Moreno, a manager who had worked her way up from the warehouse floor.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “echelon” mean?
qs.why: Reaching the “top echelon” took fifteen years of proving yourself, so it means the highest level or rank. “Office floor” is a trap based on the warehouse floor mentioned later.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “lackey” mean?
options: a rival who competes for the same job
a cook in the company kitchen
someone who obeys a powerful person without question
qs.why: The friend agreed with every idea Trevor had and reported criticism back to him, like a servant obeying a master.

qs.q: Why were the staff upset?
options: A relative with no experience got a job over qualified managers.
Trevor was too old for the job.
The board wanted to sell the company.
Trevor worked on the warehouse floor.
qs.why: The owner's nephew became vice president with no experience, even though two well-qualified managers had applied.

title: The Night of the Storm
text: For the people of Port Ellis, a sudden flock of seabirds flying inland is often seen as a harbinger of a big storm. When the birds came on Thursday, fishermen pulled their boats onto the beach, and families began to fortify their homes, nailing boards over windows and piling sandbags by the doors. Forecasters warned that the winds could wreak serious damage along the coast. They were right. The night was tumultuous, with roaring wind, crashing waves, and rain so heavy that the streetlights disappeared from view. By morning, the wind had toppled dozens of trees, including the old oak in front of the school. The town came to a standstill: roads were blocked, shops were closed, and the power was out for two days. Yet no one was hurt, and by the weekend, neighbors were working side by side to clear the streets.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “harbinger” mean?
options: a sign that something is coming
qs.why: People see the birds as a sign that a storm is on its way. The birds do not cause the storm.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “standstill” mean?
options: a complete stop of all activity
qs.why: Blocked roads, closed shops, and no power mean everything in town had stopped.

qs.q: What happened after the storm?
options: The fishermen lost all their boats.
Most families left town for good.
Neighbors worked together to clear the streets.
qs.why: The passage ends: “no one was hurt, and by the weekend, neighbors were working side by side to clear the streets.” The tree in front of the school fell, not the building.

title: How Adaeze Saved
text: When Adaeze Nwosu retired from nursing, her friends asked how she had saved so much on a modest salary. Her answer was simple: be prudent, and be patient. She never bought a new car, and she paid every bill on time, so she never fell into arrears or paid late fees. She also avoided store credit cards, whose exorbitant interest rates, often above twenty-five percent, can turn a small debt into a large one. Instead, she put a little money every month into a simple fund that followed the whole stock market. Its value would fluctuate, sometimes dropping sharply in a bad year, but she never panicked and sold. Over thirty years, gains continued to accrue, and her savings grew to far more than she had put in. Her son calls her canny. “She never looked like an investor,” he says, “but she made smarter choices than most experts.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “arrears” mean?
options: owing money that is already overdue
qs.why: Because she paid every bill on time, she never owed overdue money or paid late fees.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “fluctuate” mean?
qs.why: The fund's value sometimes dropped sharply and then rose again. “Grow steadily” ignores the drops.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: She became rich by earning a very high salary.
She made money by using store credit cards.
She sold her investments whenever the market dropped.
Her son managed all of her money.
Careful, patient habits helped her build large savings on a modest income.
She saved by buying a new car every few years.
qs.why: She avoided debt and late fees, invested a little each month, and stayed calm in bad years for thirty years. Her salary was modest.

title: Two Streets
text: The new painting in the city museum, Two Streets, has become the most talked-about work of the year. At first glance, it shows two streets side by side. On the left, a flamboyant parade fills the road with feathers, gold costumes, and bright balloons. On the right, a drab line of workers in gray coats waits for a bus in the rain. The artist, Yusuf Demir, says the painting is an allegory: the parade stands for the life we show online, and the bus stop stands for everyday life. The juxtaposition of the two scenes is what makes viewers stop and think. Look closer, and you will find a nuance that many people miss: one worker at the bus stop is smiling, while a dancer in the parade looks close to tears. Even the title has a connotation of choice, as if each of us must decide which street to walk down.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “drab” mean?
qs.why: The workers wear gray coats and stand in the rain, in contrast to the bright parade. “Colorful and lively” describes the parade, the opposite side.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “juxtaposition” mean?
options: placing two very different things side by side
painting on a very large canvas
qs.why: The two very different streets are shown next to each other, and that contrast makes people think. They are side by side, not mixed into one.

qs.q: What small detail does the passage say many viewers miss?
options: It is raining at the bus stop.
A worker is smiling while a dancer looks sad.
The artist painted himself into the scene.
qs.why: The “nuance that many people miss” is that a worker is smiling while a parade dancer looks close to tears. The other details are easy to see.

title: The New Kitchen Hand
text: When Tomás took his first job at a busy café, his manager handed him the most menial tasks: scraping plates, mopping floors and carrying bags of trash to the alley. The pay was a pittance, barely enough to cover his bus fare and lunch. Still, he was industrious. He arrived early every morning, always punctual, and kept busy even when the room was quiet. The older cooks, who had seen many young workers come and go, grudgingly admitted that he was different. One evening, a regular customer left a large gratuity on the table with a note: 'For the young man who never stops.' Tomás used the money to buy his first chef's knife. Two years later, he was running the grill, and he still mopped the floor at closing time, because, as he told the new hires, no job in a kitchen is beneath anyone.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “menial” mean?
options: dull, low in status and needing little skill
done only after the café closed
qs.why: Scraping plates and mopping floors are simple, low-status jobs. Nothing suggests they were dangerous or needed training.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “grudgingly” mean?
options: proudly, as if they had trained him
unwillingly, as if they did not want to
qs.why: The older cooks had seen many workers fail, so they admitted his worth reluctantly. 'Proudly' is tempting, but nothing says they trained him.

qs.q: What lesson does Tomás pass on to new workers?
options: Even simple jobs deserve respect from everyone, however senior.
New workers should refuse low-paid tasks.
Tips matter more than wages in a kitchen.
Customers notice only the grill cooks.
Arriving early is the only way to get promoted.
Older cooks rarely accept young workers.
qs.why: He still mops the floor as head of the grill and tells new hires no kitchen job is beneath anyone.

title: Grandma Ifeoma's Table
text: Every December, the Okafor family gathers at the home of Grandma Ifeoma, the matriarch who has guided four generations through weddings, moves and hard times. By noon the house is raucous: cousins shouting over card games, toddlers banging pots, uncles arguing happily about football. Uncle Chidi, jovial as always, tells the same jokes and laughs loudest at them himself. After dinner, the noise fades, and the older relatives begin to reminisce about the village where they grew up, the mango tree behind the school and the long walk to the river. Grandma listens with a wistful smile, thinking of her husband, who loved these evenings and is no longer here to share them. For her, the family's story and the house itself are inextricably joined; every scratch on the kitchen table holds a memory she would never sand away.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “raucous” mean?
qs.why: Shouting, banging pots and arguing make the house loud and rowdy.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “wistful” mean?
options: quietly sad, missing something she cannot have
qs.why: She is thinking of her late husband, so her smile is gently sad, not proud or annoyed.

qs.q: Why would Grandma never sand away the scratches on the kitchen table?
options: She cannot afford to fix the table.
The scratches make the table worth more money.
Her husband told her never to change it.
She plans to give the table to Uncle Chidi.
The marks are tied to family memories she treasures.
She has not noticed the scratches.
qs.why: The passage says every scratch holds a memory, because the family story and the house are joined for her.

title: The Miracle Tea
text: Last spring, a video spread online claiming that a bitter herbal tea could cure colds, back pain, poor sleep and even bad grades. Its seller called it a panacea. Priya Raman, a high school chemistry teacher, decided to turn the claim into a class project. Her students began by asking what evidence would substantiate such a promise. They found none: the seller's 'proof' was a handful of happy customer comments. Next they had to scrutinize the reasoning itself. One student pointed out that people often feel better from a cold after a few days anyway, so giving the tea the credit was fallacious. The class wrote a short, cogent report explaining each problem in plain language and posted it on the school website. They did not set out to embarrass anyone, Ms. Raman said. They wanted to learn how to debunk a claim politely, with facts instead of insults.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “panacea” mean?
options: something said to cure every problem
a rare plant found only in mountains
a drink that tastes very bitter
a product that costs too much
qs.why: The tea was claimed to fix colds, pain, sleep and grades, so it was presented as a cure for everything. 'Bitter' describes the tea, not the word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “fallacious” mean?
qs.why: Colds get better on their own, so crediting the tea is a mistake in reasoning, not a health danger.

qs.q: Why did a student say it was wrong to give the tea credit for curing colds?
options: The tea was too bitter for anyone to drink.
The seller refused to share the recipe.
Colds usually get better on their own after a few days.
The customers who wrote comments were paid.
The video was made by a student.
qs.why: The student noted people feel better after a few days anyway, so the tea may have done nothing.

title: Fog on the Ridge
text: Amara and her brother Kofi had planned the ridge hike for months, but the morning brought inclement weather: cold rain, gusts of wind and a thick fog that hid the trail markers. At the first lookout, the path ran within a few steps of a precipice, and the valley below disappeared into gray cloud. Kofi admitted his trepidation; his boots were slipping, and he could not see more than ten meters ahead. Amara was undaunted, but she was not careless. She suggested they wait under a rock ledge, eat lunch and check the weather on the radio. Within an hour the fog began to recede, sliding down into the valley like a slow tide. They finished the hike in sunshine. Later, Kofi said the day had tested their mettle, but the bravest choice had been to stop and wait, not to push on blindly.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “inclement” mean?
options: cold and unpleasant, with rain or wind
qs.why: The weather brought cold rain, wind and fog, which is what inclement means.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “recede” mean?
options: move back and slowly become smaller
qs.why: The fog slid away down into the valley, so it was pulling back, not coming closer.

qs.q: According to Kofi, what was the bravest decision of the day?
options: Walking close to the edge to see the valley.
Stopping to wait instead of pushing on in the fog.
Starting the hike despite the rain.
Finishing the hike as fast as possible.
Going on alone while his sister rested.
qs.why: Kofi says the bravest choice was to stop and wait, not to push on blindly.

title: Saving the Corner House
text: For twenty years, the house on the corner of Elm Street was the neighborhood eyesore. Its paint had peeled away, two windows were covered with plywood, and the porch steps were so rickety that the mail carrier refused to climb them. When Marisol and Ben Hartley bought it, their friends laughed. 'You've bought a decrepit old box,' one said. The couple saw something else. Under the layers of grime were oak floors, tall windows and a staircase carved by hand. They spent two years working painstakingly, one room at a time, saving every piece of original wood they could. The house had fallen into disrepair simply because no one had cared for it, they explained, not because it was badly built. Their work seemed to rejuvenate the whole street; soon, neighbors were repainting fences and planting flowers of their own.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “rickety” mean?
qs.why: The mail carrier would not climb them because they looked ready to break.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “rejuvenate” mean?
options: make fresh and full of energy again
make more expensive to live in
make look older and more historic
qs.why: After their work, neighbors began repainting and planting, so the street felt fresh and lively again.

qs.q: Why, according to the Hartleys, had the house become so run-down?
options: It had been built with cheap wood.
A storm had damaged the porch.
The mail carrier had reported it.
Nobody had looked after it for years.
The neighbors had tried to tear it down.
qs.why: They said it fell apart because no one cared for it, not because it was badly built.

title: The Parking Lot Debate
text: The town council expected a quiet evening, but forty residents arrived, many of them irate about a plan to turn part of Riverside Park into a parking lot. One retired nurse gave a vehement speech, waving photos of the old oak trees that would be cut down. Councilwoman Lena Duarte tried to placate the crowd by promising that new trees would be planted elsewhere, but that only drew groans. Then a young father named Hamid stood up. His tone was conciliatory: he said he understood the shops needed parking, and asked whether the empty lot behind the post office might work instead. No one had dared to broach that idea before, because the land belonged to the state and earlier talks with state officials had ended badly.
