The council agreed to adjourn the meeting for two weeks so staff could find out whether the state would sell it.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “placate” mean?
qs.why: She offered new trees to make the angry crowd less upset; it did not work, but that was her aim.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “broach” mean?
qs.why: No one had brought up the post office lot before; to broach an idea is to begin discussing it.

qs.q: Why was the meeting stopped for two weeks?
options: The crowd was too angry to continue.
The trees had already been cut down.
Hamid asked for time to prepare a speech.
The shops refused to share their parking.
Staff needed to learn whether the state would sell its lot.
qs.why: The council paused so staff could find out if the state-owned lot could be bought.

title: The Upstart from Millbrook
text: No one expected much from the Millbrook Otters, a small-town basketball team that had joined the regional league only two years earlier. The established clubs called the team an upstart and joked about their faded uniforms. But the Otters' rise was meteoric: they won twelve games in a row, and in the final they beat the three-time champions handily, 81 to 59. Their fans were jubilant, dancing in the aisles and hugging strangers. On the other bench, the champions sat dejected, towels over their heads. Coach Rosa Lindqvist gathered her players before they could celebrate too loudly. 'You can be proud,' she told them, 'but don't gloat. Next year we'll be the team everyone wants to beat, and those players will remember how we treated them tonight.' Then she walked across the court and shook every opponent's hand.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “handily” mean?
options: just barely, in the last second
easily and by a big margin
qs.why: An 81 to 59 score is a large, easy win. 'Using their hands' is a careless reading of the word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “dejected” mean?
qs.why: Sitting with towels over their heads after losing shows sadness and disappointment.

qs.q: Why does the coach tell her players not to gloat?
options: She thinks they won only by luck.
She wants them to save energy for practice.
Their rivals will remember how the Otters behaved when they meet again.
The league has a rule against celebrating.
Their fans are already too loud.
She is unhappy with how they played.
qs.why: She warns that next year everyone will want to beat them and the losers will remember tonight.

title: The Seaside Market
text: On her first trip abroad, Hana wandered into a seaside market where hundreds of sellers peddle everything from spices to sandals. Her guide, a cheerful woman named Dalia, gave her one rule: never pay the first price. 'Here, everyone expects you to haggle,' she said. 'It is part of the conversation.' Hana stopped at a stall full of gaudy souvenirs: glittering plastic camels, mugs covered in pink seashells and snow globes that played music. Dalia laughed. 'That is pure kitsch. Some people buy it as a joke.' A wily seller noticed Hana's interest and swore that a dull brass lamp was two hundred years old. Dalia turned it over, showed Hana the factory stamp on the bottom and smiled at the man, who smiled back. 'He was not really trying to swindle you,' she explained. 'He was testing whether you were paying attention.'

qs.q: In the passage, what does “haggle” mean?
options: argue back and forth about a price
qs.why: Dalia's rule is never to pay the first price, so buyers bargain over prices.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “gaudy” mean?
options: too bright and showy in a cheap way
qs.why: Glittering plastic camels and pink seashell mugs are bright and tasteless.

qs.q: How does Dalia see the seller's claim about the lamp?
options: As a test of whether Hana was careful, not a serious attempt to cheat.
As proof that he was a dangerous criminal.
As a true story about a rare lamp.
As a reason to call the police.
As a fair price for an antique.
As an insult to her as a guide.
qs.why: She says he was not really trying to cheat Hana, only testing whether she was paying attention.

title: The Brother Who Took the Crown
text: In an old legend from the imaginary kingdom of Varelia, King Oskar began his reign as a fair ruler but slowly became a despot, jailing anyone who questioned his taxes. His brother, Duke Anselm, decided the king had to be stopped. Anselm traveled through the provinces with a small retinue of knights and advisers, asking each lord to break his oath of fealty to the king. Many agreed, tired of Oskar's cruelty. Within a year, their armies surrounded the capital, and the nobles voted to depose Oskar. Yet the story does not end happily. After the king's ouster, Anselm refused to give the crown to Oskar's young daughter, its rightful heir, and took it for himself. Storytellers still argue about him. Some call him a hero who saved the people; others say he simply waited for the right moment to usurp the throne.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “fealty” mean?
qs.why: The lords had sworn an oath of loyalty to the king, which Anselm asked them to break.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “retinue” mean?
options: a group of followers traveling with an important person
qs.why: The knights and advisers traveling with Anselm were his retinue. It was small, so 'an army of thousands' is wrong.

qs.q: Why do storytellers disagree about Duke Anselm?
options: They cannot agree whether Oskar was cruel.
Some think the daughter was the cruel ruler.
He removed a cruel king but then took a crown that was not his.
He refused to fight in the war.
He gave the crown away too quickly.
qs.why: He freed people from a cruel king, yet kept the crown from its rightful heir, so he can be seen as hero or thief.

title: A Seminar for Beginners
text: When Lucy signed up for Professor Adebayo's poetry seminar, she was nervous. She had read almost no poetry, and the professor was famously erudite; his office walls were lined with books in five languages. She feared he would be pedantic, stopping students to correct every comma, or patronizing, explaining things slowly as if they were children. Instead, he began the first class with a confession: as a teenager, he had hated poems. 'For the uninitiated,' he said, 'poetry can feel like a locked door. My job is to hand you keys.' He rarely lectured. When a student wrote a didactic poem that told readers exactly how to live, he did not mock it; he simply asked her what would happen if she trusted the reader more. By the end of the term, under his tutelage, Lucy had filled a notebook with poems of her own.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “pedantic” mean?
options: too focused on small details and rules
qs.why: Correcting every comma is the kind of fussing over small rules that pedantic describes.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “uninitiated” mean?
options: people without knowledge or experience of something
people who have not paid for the class
qs.why: He is speaking to beginners like Lucy who have little experience of poetry.

qs.q: How did the professor respond to the student's preachy poem?
options: He laughed at it in front of the class.
He told her to stop writing poems.
He gave it the highest grade.
He gently suggested she trust her readers more.
qs.why: He did not mock it; he asked what would happen if she trusted the reader more.

title: Where the River Bends
text: From the plane window, the river looked like a ribbon dropped carelessly on the land. It seemed to meander for hundreds of kilometers, looping back on itself through verdant forest so thick that no road could cross it. Our guide, a biologist named Teodoro, told us that parts of this forest were primeval, never cut down by people. On the second day we hiked to a monolith, a single tower of gray stone rising above the trees like a lighthouse. From its top we could see a wide swath of farmland to the south, where the forest had been cleared for cattle. Teodoro was quiet for a while. Then he explained that in the rainy season the river could rise and engulf the lowest villages for weeks, and that cutting trees upstream made the floods worse.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “meander” mean?
options: follow a winding path with many turns
qs.why: The river is 'looping back on itself,' which is a winding path.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “swath” mean?
qs.why: From the tower they saw a wide area of cleared farmland.

qs.q: What connection does Teodoro point out?
options: The stone tower protects villages from floods.
Clearing forest upstream makes floods worse.
Cattle farmers are moving into the villages.
The river is getting smaller each year.
qs.why: He says that cutting trees upstream made the floods worse.

title: Uncle Victor's Money
text: When Uncle Victor died, his will held a surprise. He left a large bequest to his niece, Noor, a librarian who had visited him every Sunday. Some relatives expected her to squander it, just as Victor had spent freely all his life. He had lived in opulence, with gold taps, a heated pool and three cars he rarely drove. His home was so ostentatious that neighbors called it 'the palace.' But Noor had noticed something on those Sunday visits: her uncle seemed lonely. His affluence had bought him beautiful things and few real friends. Near the end, he told her his greatest extravagance had been a forty-foot boat he took out only twice. Noor kept a modest amount for herself and used the rest to fund a reading room at the community center, where retired people could meet for coffee and books. She named it after Victor.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “ostentatious” mean?
options: showy, meant to impress others with wealth
qs.why: Gold taps and a home called 'the palace' show a house built to impress.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “squander” mean?
qs.why: The relatives expected her to waste the money, but she used it well.

qs.q: What did Noor learn about her uncle that shaped how she used the money?
options: That his wealth had not given him many real friends.
That he wanted her to buy a boat.
That he disliked the community center.
That he had lost most of his money.
That the neighbors had cheated him.
That he planned to sell his house.
qs.why: She saw he was lonely, so she funded a place where people could meet and connect.

title: The Missing Payroll
text: When twenty thousand dollars vanished from the Harbor Shipping office, suspicion fell on Rafael, the newest clerk. A coworker's statement seemed to implicate him: she said she had seen him near the safe after closing. Rafael insisted he had only gone back for his phone. His lawyer, Grace Chen, asked for the building's security video. It showed Rafael leaving after two minutes, empty-handed, and a manager entering an hour later with a key. The video was irrefutable, and within a week the charge was dropped and Rafael was exonerated. The manager later admitted his culpability. At his hearing, he asked the judge for leniency, saying he had planned to return the money once his debts were paid. The judge noted that he had confessed, but said that good intentions could not absolve him of stealing from his own workers.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “implicate” mean?
options: suggest he was involved in wrongdoing
qs.why: Saying she saw him near the safe made him look involved in the theft.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “leniency” mean?
options: a chance to speak to reporters
qs.why: He hoped his plan to repay the money would earn a softer punishment.

qs.q: Why did the judge refuse to treat the manager as blameless?
options: He had stolen from a bank.
The video showed him with a weapon.
Rafael asked the judge to be harsh.
Planning to repay the money did not undo the theft.
qs.why: The judge said good intentions could not clear him of stealing. He had confessed, so the first option is wrong.

title: Back on His Feet
text: After a bad case of pneumonia last winter, my grandfather Hiroshi spent three weeks in the hospital, and he came home shocked by his own frailty. He needed both hands on the railing to climb four steps. The doctor told him to recuperate slowly: rest, short walks and plenty of food. The first week was the hardest. A heavy lethargy kept him in his armchair most afternoons, and he complained of a vague malaise, not pain exactly, just a sense that nothing felt right. Then one morning he woke up ravenous and ate two bowls of rice porridge and a whole plate of eggs. From then on, the change was appreciable. Each day, his walk around the block got a little faster. By spring he was back in his garden, telling everyone that hunger was the best sign a body is healing.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “malaise” mean?
options: a general feeling of discomfort with no clear cause
a sharp pain in the chest
a strong wish to go outside
qs.why: He described it as not pain but a sense that nothing felt right, a vague unease.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “appreciable” mean?
options: large enough to be clearly noticed
qs.why: His walks got faster every day, so the improvement could be seen. 'Thanked' confuses it with 'appreciate'.

qs.q: What marked the turning point in Hiroshi's recovery?
options: Waking up very hungry one morning.
A new medicine from his doctor.
A long walk around the block.
qs.why: After he woke up hungry and ate a big breakfast, the improvement became clear.

title: Night of the Festival
text: The music festival opened at sunset, and by eight o'clock a throng of nearly ten thousand people filled the field. While bands tuned up on three stages at once, the air was a cacophony of drums, guitars and squealing speakers. Six-year-old Mateo clutched his mother's hand, overwhelmed. Then the lights dimmed on the main stage, and a lone violinist began to play a slow, simple tune. Mateo was mesmerized; he stood perfectly still, mouth open, for the whole song. The next act was the opposite: a frenetic dance group that leapt and spun so fast their costumes blurred. Their exuberance spread through the crowd, and soon even the security guards were clapping along. Near midnight, a sudden storm sent everyone running for the exits, and for ten minutes there was pandemonium. Mateo, safe on his father's shoulders, thought it was the best part.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “cacophony” mean?
options: a harsh mix of unpleasant sounds
qs.why: Many bands tuning at once with squealing speakers makes a harsh mix of noise.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “mesmerized” mean?
options: so held by what he saw and heard that he could not look away
qs.why: He stood perfectly still with his mouth open for the whole song, completely absorbed.

qs.q: How did Mateo's feelings change during the evening?
options: He was calm at first and became frightened by the end.
He was bored until the dancers came.
He wanted to leave after the violinist.
He was scared by the storm and cried.
He went from feeling overwhelmed to enjoying even the chaos of the storm.
qs.why: He began overwhelmed, then was captivated, and thought the storm rush was the best part.

title: Goodbye, Old Machine
text: For fifteen years, the accounts department at Kessler Tools ran on a single gray computer in a back closet. By last year it had become unwieldy: reports took hours, and only one employee, Bongani, knew all its secret commands. Management decided a cloud system would supersede it. Bongani surprised everyone by supporting the change. 'Every machine reaches obsolescence eventually,' he said. 'This one got there years ago.' The new system was approved provisionally, for a six-month trial. Early results were counterintuitive. Staff actually got slower in the first month, even though the software was faster. A consultant explained that people need time to unlearn old habits. Looking at the second and third months, when speeds doubled, she was willing to extrapolate: by the end of the year, the team would probably save a full day of work every week.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “unwieldy” mean?
options: hard to manage because of its size or complexity
qs.why: Slow reports and secret commands only one person knew made the system hard to manage. It still worked, so it was not broken.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “extrapolate” mean?
options: make a general guess from the facts she already had
qs.why: She used two months of results to predict the rest of the year.

qs.q: Why did staff work more slowly in the first month?
options: They needed time to drop old habits.
The new software was slower than the old machine.
They were not allowed to use it every day.
qs.why: The consultant said people need time to unlearn old habits; the software itself was faster.

title: Notes from a Writing Workshop
text: Every Thursday, the library hosts a writing workshop led by Ana Sousa, a retired newspaper editor. Her advice is famously pithy. 'Cut the first paragraph,' she says. 'It's usually throat-clearing.' Last week, a student read a story that began, 'It was a dark and stormy night.' Ana smiled kindly and called the line trite; it has been copied and joked about so often that readers no longer feel anything. She also warned against plots that are too formulaic, where the hero always wins and the villain always explains his plan. Then she asked each writer to describe their story succinctly, in one sentence. Several people found this harder than writing the whole thing. One man began to digress, talking about his cat, his old job and a trip to Portugal, until Ana gently pointed out that those details were tangential at best.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “trite” mean?
options: so overused it has lost its effect
qs.why: The line has been copied and joked about so often that readers feel nothing, which is what trite means.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “digress” mean?
options: wander away from the main topic
qs.why: Instead of describing his story, he talked about his cat, job and trip.

qs.q: What did several writers discover about the one-sentence task?
options: It was harder for them than writing the whole story.
It was the easiest part of the workshop.
Ana did not allow anyone to finish.
It only worked for stories about villains.
It required them to cut the first paragraph.
qs.why: The passage says several people found it harder than writing the whole thing.

title: The Fence Between Them
text: For eleven years, Mr. Novak and Mrs. Afolabi did not speak. The trouble began with a fence built six inches over the property line, and their antipathy grew with every leaf blown into the wrong yard. Neighbors stopped inviting them to the same parties. Then, last July, a storm dropped a huge branch through Mrs. Afolabi's roof while she was visiting her sister. Mr. Novak saw it first. He climbed up with a tarp in the pouring rain and covered the hole before her furniture was ruined. When she returned, she found a note on her door: 'Roof covered. No charge.' It was a magnanimous act, and she knew it. She decided to reciprocate with a lemon cake and a long-overdue apology. The rapprochement surprised the whole street. The two settled the fence question amicably over coffee, and whatever animus remained seemed to melt away.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “magnanimous” mean?
options: generous toward someone who had been a rival
qs.why: He helped a neighbor he had feuded with for years and asked nothing. 'Very large' is a careless guess.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “rapprochement” mean?
options: a court case over the fence
qs.why: After years of silence, the two neighbors became friendly again.

qs.q: What first broke the long silence between the neighbors?
options: Mr. Novak protecting her house during a storm.
A judge's ruling about the fence.
qs.why: His covering of her roof came first; the cake and apology were her response to it.

title: The Shadow in the Concert Hall
text: Detective Inés Moreau had a puzzle. For three weeks, someone had been entering the concert hall at night, and the cameras showed only a shadow. The guards were sure the visitor was a staff member, but the guilty person always seemed to elude them. Inés spent days talking to cleaners, ushers and musicians, trying to glean small clues from each. A cleaner remembered a stranger in a borrowed uniform. An usher mentioned that the second violinist had seemed strangely nervous. The answer turned out to be a clever subterfuge. A man had studied the violinist's habits and learned to impersonate him, from his limp to his gray scarf. The impostor had been surreptitiously photographing a rare old violin each night, planning to sell an exact copy as the real thing. The real violinist, it turned out, had been on vacation all month.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “glean” mean?
qs.why: She collected small clues from many people one at a time. 'Clean' only sounds similar.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “surreptitiously” mean?
options: openly, in front of the guards
secretly, so as not to be noticed
qs.why: He photographed the violin at night while avoiding the guards, so he acted secretly.

qs.q: Who was the 'nervous' violinist the usher noticed?
options: The real violinist, afraid of the detective.
The impostor, pretending to be the violinist.
A cleaner in a borrowed uniform.
A buyer for the copied violin.
qs.why: The real violinist was on vacation all month, so the person seen must have been the impostor.

title: Meet Our New Principal
text: Parents at Westfield Elementary were not sure what to expect from their new principal, Dr. Kwame Asante. His record was impressive, yet in person he was unassuming: he rode an old bicycle to school, wore the same brown sweater most days and introduced himself simply as 'Kwame.' He was also gregarious, the kind of man who learns the names of every lunch worker in his first week and stays late to chat with families at pickup. At his first parents' meeting, someone asked about the school's falling reading scores. Instead of giving a long, careful speech, he was forthright. 'The scores are bad, and some of that is our fault,' he said. His candor was disarming. People who had come ready to argue found themselves nodding. By the end of the evening, the affable principal had a list of thirty volunteers for a new reading program.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “unassuming” mean?
qs.why: An old bicycle, the same sweater and using his first name show modesty. He chats easily with families, so he is not shy.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “disarming” mean?
options: so honest and friendly that it made people stop feeling angry
so harsh that people became upset
qs.why: Parents ready to argue ended up nodding, because his honesty calmed them.

qs.q: Why did parents who came ready to argue end up nodding?
options: The principal promised higher test scores.
The meeting was too short for arguments.
He admitted the problem openly instead of making excuses.
He refused to answer any questions.
He blamed the parents for the scores.
qs.why: He said plainly that the scores were bad and partly the school's fault.

title: A Letter About Leo
text: Dear Mei, I need your advice about Leo. Since he turned thirteen, his moods have become mercurial: cheerful at breakfast, slamming doors by lunch, laughing with friends on the phone by dinner. When I ask him to clear the table, he turns petulant, complaining that his sister never has to do anything. Yesterday he was openly insolent to his football coach, rolling his eyes and talking back in front of the team. Then he spent the evening sullen in his room, refusing to say a word. I try to stay calm, but I have to admit my exasperation is growing. His older cousins don't help; they goad him by teasing him about his cracking voice until he explodes. You raised three boys. Is this normal, and how did you keep your patience? With love, your sister, Lan.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “mercurial” mean?
qs.why: His mood swings from cheerful to door-slamming to laughing in one day.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “goad” mean?
options: push into a reaction by teasing again and again
qs.why: The cousins keep teasing him until he explodes, which is goading.

qs.q: What is Lan's main purpose in writing the letter?
options: To complain about Leo's football coach.
To ask her sister for advice on handling Leo's behavior.
To tell her sister that Leo is ill.
To invite her sister to visit.
To blame the cousins for everything.
To share good news about Leo.
qs.why: She opens by asking for advice and ends by asking how Mei kept her patience with three boys.

title: After the Flood
text: When the dam above the fictional town of Corrin failed one spring, the water reached the streets in less than an hour. For the families who lived there, it was a cataclysm. Hundreds of homes were swept away, and thousands of people were uprooted in a single afternoon, forced to start over somewhere else with only the clothes they wore. Two older residents lost their lives, and the mayor's first public words were a message of condolence to their families. In the weeks that followed, the streets were filled with detritus: broken furniture, tangled fencing, soaked mattresses and children's toys. Yet the response was an outpouring of help from across the country. Trucks arrived with blankets and food, and strangers offered spare rooms. One woman, bereft of her home and her family's photographs, told a reporter that the kindness of strangers was the only thing keeping her going.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “uprooted” mean?
options: moved to a hotel for a holiday
asked to help clean up the streets
forced to leave their homes and settle somewhere new
pulled out of the ground like trees
qs.why: The families lost their homes and had to start over elsewhere, in spare rooms offered by strangers. 'Pulled out of the ground' is the word's literal sense for plants, not people.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “detritus” mean?
options: broken pieces and rubbish left behind
qs.why: The list that follows, broken furniture and soaked mattresses, is waste left by the flood.

qs.q: According to the passage, what helped the woman who lost her home keep going?
options: A new house from the mayor.
Help from her old neighbors in town.
qs.why: She told a reporter that the kindness of strangers was the only thing keeping her going.

title: The Food-Sharing App
text: The FreshShare app began as the brainchild of Imani Ortiz, a sixteen-year-old who hated seeing her school cafeteria throw away trays of untouched food. Her idea was simple: let nearby shelters see, in real time, what extra food was available and pick it up before it spoiled. She convinced two friends who knew how to code to help, and she agreed to spearhead the project herself, phoning shelter managers and cafeteria staff every day after class. Her dynamism was hard to resist; one manager said he agreed just to stop her from calling. Within a year, forty schools in the city were using the app. This spring, Imani received the city's top youth service accolade, and most people at the ceremony agreed that it was deservedly hers. Other teenagers now call her a trailblazer, and several have started similar projects in their own towns.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “spearhead” mean?
qs.why: She led the project, making the calls every day to drive it forward.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “accolade” mean?
qs.why: She received the city's top youth service honor at a ceremony.

qs.q: What problem did the app set out to solve?
options: Good food being thrown away while shelters could use it.
Teenagers having nothing to do after class.
qs.why: Imani hated seeing untouched food thrown away and wanted shelters to collect it.

title: Judging the Soup Contest
text: Every October, our town holds a soup contest, and this year I volunteered as a judge. The head judge, Chef Bernard, was famously fastidious; he wiped each spoon with a fresh napkin and wrote notes in tiny, perfect handwriting. The first entry, a pale chicken broth, was insipid. Even after two spoonfuls, I could barely taste anything. The second was a strange concoction of pumpkin, coconut, ginger and chili that I expected to hate but secretly loved. Bernard tasted it slowly and nodded. 'Real discernment,' he told me, 'means noticing why something works, not just whether you like it.' The crowd's response to the winner, a classic tomato soup, was tepid; people had hoped for something bolder. Still, the smell drifting from the tents was enough to whet everyone's appetite, and by noon every pot was empty.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “insipid” mean?
qs.why: After two spoonfuls the narrator could barely taste anything.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “tepid” mean?
qs.why: Here it describes the crowd's reaction: people had hoped for something bolder, so they were unexcited. 'Slightly warm' is the word's other meaning, about temperature.

qs.q: Why was the crowd unexcited about the winning soup?
options: They had hoped for something more daring.
It was a strange mixture of flavors.
qs.why: The passage says people had hoped for something bolder than a classic tomato soup.

title: The Chess Club Split
text: The Lakeside Chess Club had been calm for decades. Its president, ninety-year-old Walter Grigg, was mostly a figurehead; he cut the cake at the annual dinner while a committee made the real decisions. Trouble started when the committee voted to replace the club's wooden boards with electronic ones that recorded every move. Younger members loved the idea. Many older members felt ignored and became disaffected, skipping meetings and grumbling in the parking lot. The flashpoint came at the spring tournament, when a sensor failed in the middle of a close game. Shouting broke out, and the antagonism between the two groups was suddenly out in the open. A dozen older players announced they would secede and form their own club in a church basement. The upshot, oddly, was good for chess: the town now has two clubs, a friendly rivalry and twice as many tournaments.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “figurehead” mean?
options: the best player in the club
a leader in title only, without real power
qs.why: He cut the cake while the committee made the real decisions, so his role was in name only.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “secede” mean?
options: formally leave a group to become independent
qs.why: They left the club to start their own separate one.

qs.q: What made the hidden conflict burst into the open?
options: The church refused to host the club.
An argument at the annual dinner.
An electronic board failing during a close game.
qs.why: The flashpoint was the sensor failure at the tournament, when shouting broke out.

title: Stuck on Route 9
text: Ten years ago, the drive from the town of Bayview to the city took twenty minutes. Today, at rush hour, Route 9 often sits in gridlock, with cars not moving at all for minutes at a time, and commuters can spend an hour covering eight miles. The reasons are not mysterious. As new housing developments began to proliferate along the highway, the town approved each one separately, without asking where all the new cars would go. Meanwhile, the bus service was allowed to dwindle; there used to be twelve routes, and there are three today. Town engineer Farida Haddad calls the old approach myopic. 'We thought about the tax money each project would bring this year,' she said, 'not about the next twenty.' Her models show that, if nothing changes, travel times will keep rising inexorably as more families move in. Air quality near the highway, she added, is already alarmingly poor on summer afternoons.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “proliferate” mean?
qs.why: More and more developments appeared along the highway.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “myopic” mean?
options: unable to see far with the eyes
focused only on the present, not the future
qs.why: She says they thought about this year, not the next twenty. 'Unable to see far' is the word's literal eye meaning, not the one used here.

qs.q: According to Farida Haddad, what was the town's main mistake?
options: Judging projects by short-term money instead of long-term effects.
Moving the bus station to the city.
qs.why: She says they thought about this year's tax money, not the next twenty years.

title: Postcards from Everywhere
text: My grandmother Rosa never left the small town where she was born, but she had a powerful wanderlust. She satisfied it vicariously, through the postcards her younger brother Emilio sent home. Emilio was an itinerant carpenter who followed work from port to port, building docks and boat sheds for forty years. Every month a card arrived: a lighthouse, a desert market, a snowy mountain pass. Rosa pinned them above the sink and read them aloud while she washed dishes. My mother says it was a kind of escapism for her, a few minutes each day away from bills and chores. The best part of the story is pure serendipity. Last year, while clearing out Rosa's house, I found a box of cards she had written back but never mailed. By a fortuitous coincidence, Emilio, now eighty-four, was visiting that week, and he finally read every one.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “itinerant” mean?
options: traveling from place to place for work
qs.why: He followed work from port to port for forty years.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “vicariously” mean?
options: through someone else's experiences rather than her own
by saving money for a trip
qs.why: She never traveled herself; she enjoyed travel through her brother's postcards.

qs.q: Why was finding Rosa's unmailed cards so lucky?
options: They were worth a lot of money.
They showed Rosa had traveled secretly.
They were addressed to the narrator.
They explained why Emilio left town.
Emilio happened to be visiting and could finally read them.
qs.why: By chance Emilio was there that week, so the cards reached him at last.

title: The Tablets of Tarvos
text: When a farmer near the imaginary village of Tarvos plowed up a clay tablet, the regional museum sent a team to unearth whatever else lay beneath the field. They found the remains of a small trading town and dozens more tablets. Most were fragmentary, broken into pieces the size of a thumbnail, so reading them was slow. The villagers hoped the tablets would confirm their favorite legend: that Tarvos had been founded by a giant named Oro, the progenitor of every family in the valley. Dr. Selin Kaya, who led the dig, gently suggested that the giant story was probably apocryphal. The tablets were contemporaneous with the town's early years, she explained, and they mention farmers, potters and a busy salt trade, but no giant. One find did puzzle the team: a modern coin in the deepest layer. It looked anachronistic until they learned a worker had dropped it on the first day.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “apocryphal” mean?
options: widely told but probably not true
qs.why: Dr. Kaya doubts the giant story because the tablets never mention him.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “contemporaneous” mean?
options: modern and up to date with
temporary, lasting a short time in
made of the same clay as
from the same period of time as
qs.why: The tablets date from the town's early years, so they are from the same time.

qs.q: Why did the modern coin turn out not to be a real mystery?
options: It was a fake made by the villagers.
A worker had dropped it during the dig.
It belonged to the giant Oro.
It was found in the top layer of soil.
The farmer had buried it on purpose.
qs.why: The team learned a worker had dropped it on the first day.

title: Words on Stone
text: After my grandfather died, my family had to choose the words for his gravestone. Everyone had ideas. My aunt wanted a long poem about angels and eternal love, but my father worried it would drip with sentimentality; Grandpa had been a plain-speaking fisherman who laughed at greeting cards. In the end, we chose an epitaph he had once said himself, while mending nets: 'The sea was good to me.' Those six words carry a quiet pathos that a longer poem never could. Last week, I visited the grave alone. I sat on the bench beside it, pensive, watching the boats on the water, and slipped into a reverie: I was eight years old again, sitting in his boat at dawn while he taught me to tie a knot. That morning left an indelible mark on me. I still tie that knot every day.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “sentimentality” mean?
qs.why: A poem about angels and eternal love risked feeling too sweet for a man who laughed at greeting cards.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “reverie” mean?
options: a careful plan for the future
qs.why: Sitting by the grave, the narrator drifted into a warm memory of the boat at dawn while fully awake.

qs.q: Why did the father object to the long poem?
options: It was too expensive to carve.
It mentioned the sea too often.
The aunt had copied it from a card.
It did not suit a plain-speaking man who laughed at greeting-card feelings.
Grandpa had asked for no words at all.
qs.why: He worried it would be too sweet for a plain-speaking fisherman who laughed at greeting cards.

title: Open Mic Night
text: Comedy nights at the Copper Kettle are usually gentle, but the new host, Samira Patel, likes an irreverent style. She jokes about the town's beloved statue of its founder, saying he looks 'like a man who just smelled the cheese aisle.' Her delivery is deadpan; she never smiles, which makes the audience laugh even harder. Last Friday, the first performer, a nervous teenager, made a gaffe in his opening line, mixing up the mayor's name with the name of a local dog groomer. A few people in the back responded with derision, hooting and calling him a loser. Samira walked onstage, took the microphone and said, without a trace of a smile, 'Honestly, the groomer would do a better job.' The room filled with mirth. Her bit of levity rescued the boy, who finished his set to warm applause.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “deadpan” mean?
options: with a serious face, showing no feeling
qs.why: She never smiles while telling jokes, which is deadpan delivery.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “derision” mean?
qs.why: Hooting and calling him a loser is mocking him, not cheering.

qs.q: How did Samira help the nervous teenager?
options: She asked the audience to leave.
She told him to start his set again.
She turned his mistake into a shared joke, which eased the tension.
She scolded the people at the back.
She gave him her microphone for the night.
She explained the mayor's real name.
qs.why: Her joke built on his mix-up, the room laughed with him, and he finished to applause. She never scolded anyone.

title: The Night Market Stall
text: By the time Priya reached the night market, she was famished; she had skipped lunch to finish a report. The long rows of stalls offered a cornucopia of choices: grilled corn, steamed buns, spicy noodles, mango sticky rice and a dozen kinds of soup. Her friend Tomás, a finicky eater who picks the onions out of everything, walked past six stalls before he found one he trusted. Priya was far less fussy. She bought a skewer of grilled chicken and ate every morsel before Tomás had even ordered. The mood around the shared tables was convivial. Strangers passed sauces to one another, a family let the two friends squeeze onto their bench, and an old man explained which dumplings were worth the wait. An hour later, Priya leaned back with a happy sigh. Nothing, she said, could sate a hunger quite like food eaten outdoors with good company.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “finicky” mean?
options: very hard to please, especially about food
happy to try any new food
unable to eat certain foods for health reasons
slow and polite at the table
qs.why: Tomás picks onions out of everything and passes six stalls before choosing, so he is hard to please. Nothing in the passage says he has a health problem.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “convivial” mean?
qs.why: Strangers share sauces, make room on a bench and give advice, which shows a friendly, cheerful mood. The tables were shared, but they are not described as uncomfortable.

qs.q: Why did Priya finish eating before Tomás had ordered?
options: She was very hungry and chose quickly, while he took a long time to pick a stall.
Tomás had already eaten lunch and was not hungry.
The stall Tomás wanted was closed.
Priya wanted to leave the market early.
Tomás was waiting for a family to join them.
Priya's food was ready before anyone else's because it was cheaper.
qs.why: Priya had skipped lunch and was 'less careful,' while Tomás walked past six stalls before ordering.

title: A Hard Monday at the Front Desk
text: Every Monday, the front desk at Greenfield Dental fills with patients, phone calls and paperwork. Last week, the office manager, Dana Okafor, looked harried by nine o'clock: two staff members were sick, the printer was jammed, and a line was forming at the door. Much of her job is drudgery, such as copying insurance cards and typing the same details into three different computer systems. The new hire, Kwame, surprised her. He took on the dullest tasks with alacrity, offering to scan forms before anyone asked. He was laconic with coworkers, often answering with a nod or a single word, but patients liked him. He never gave a perfunctory greeting; he looked people in the eye and remembered their names. By late afternoon, the morning that had felt interminable was finally behind them, and Dana told Kwame he had saved her day.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “alacrity” mean?
qs.why: Kwame offered to scan forms before anyone asked, which shows eager, quick readiness. 'Slow unwillingness' is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “perfunctory” mean?
options: done quickly and without real care, just because it is expected
qs.why: The passage contrasts a perfunctory greeting with looking people in the eye and remembering names, so it means a careless, automatic greeting. 'Warm and personal' describes what Kwame actually did.

qs.q: What is true about Kwame?
options: He talked so much that he slowed down the line.
He spoke little with coworkers but gave patients real attention.
He avoided the boring tasks whenever he could.
He was the reason the printer jammed.
He was rude to patients but kind to coworkers.
He replaced Dana as office manager.
qs.why: Kwame answered coworkers with a nod or a word, yet he looked patients in the eye and remembered their names.

title: Bringing Back the Old Farmhouse
text: When Lena and Marco Rossi bought the farmhouse, their friends thought they were joking. The ramshackle building had a sagging porch, broken windows and a roof that let in the rain. It had fallen into disuse after the last owner moved away twenty years earlier. Inside, threadbare curtains still hung in the kitchen, so thin that light shone straight through them. The couple spent two years working to refurbish the house room by room. They replaced the wiring, fixed the floors and rebuilt the porch steps. Some days they walked gingerly across the upstairs boards, never sure which ones would hold their weight. They kept one vestige of the old place on purpose: a faded pencil chart on the pantry door showing the heights of children who had grown up there long ago. 'It reminds us the house had a life before us,' Lena said.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “gingerly” mean?
options: very carefully, to avoid danger or damage
qs.why: They were not sure which boards would hold their weight, so they stepped very carefully.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “vestige” mean?
options: a small remaining trace of something from the past
a rule for living in the house
qs.why: The pencil chart is a small trace left from the children who lived there long ago. It was old, not something new they added.

qs.q: Why did the Rossis keep the pencil chart?
options: It was too hard to remove from the door.
Their own children had drawn it.
It reminded them of the people who had lived in the house before.
It was worth a lot of money.
The law required them to keep it.
It covered a hole in the pantry door.
qs.why: Lena says the chart 'reminds us the house had a life before us.' The heights belong to children from long ago, not the Rossis' own children.

title: Testing the Miracle Bracelet
text: A company once claimed that its copper bracelet could cure back pain, improve sleep and sharpen memory. The ads used phrases like 'energy fields' but offered no real tests. Dr. Aiko Tanaka, a researcher who studies treatments for pain, decided to look closer. She is no alarmist; she does not believe every new product is dangerous. But she knows that pseudoscience often hides behind scientific-sounding language. The company's main argument was specious: thousands of customers felt better, so the bracelet must work. Tanaka pointed out that many people with back pain improve over time anyway. Her team gave some volunteers the real bracelet and others a look-alike made of a different metal, without telling them which was which. Tanaka judged the results in a dispassionate way, looking at numbers, not stories. Both groups reported the same small gains. That was not incontrovertible proof that the bracelet could never help anyone, Tanaka said, but it gave no sign that it was efficacious.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “specious” mean?
options: sounding reasonable at first but actually misleading
qs.why: The argument sounds sensible, but Tanaka shows it is misleading because people with back pain often get better anyway.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “alarmist” mean?
options: a person who installs alarm systems
a person who sells health products
a person who never trusts science
a person who makes dangers seem much worse than they are
a person who enjoys taking risks
qs.why: The next words explain it: she does not believe every new product is dangerous, so she does not exaggerate danger.

qs.q: What did Tanaka's test show?
options: The bracelet cured back pain for most volunteers.
The look-alike bracelet caused more pain.
The bracelet was proven to be dangerous.
People wearing the real bracelet did no better than those wearing a look-alike.
Customers had lied about feeling better.
The bracelet helped with sleep but not pain.
qs.why: Both groups reported the same small gains, so the copper bracelet showed no extra effect. Tanaka did not say it was dangerous.

title: An Upset at the Regional Final
text: For four straight years, Hana Kim had won the regional 10,000-meter race, and few people believed anyone could dethrone her. Then came Amara Diallo, a nineteen-year-old who had finished ninth the year before. Undeterred by that result, Amara had trained doggedly all winter, running hills in the snow and lifting weights before her college classes. On race day, Hana set a breakneck pace from the start, hoping to tire out the other runners early. Several of them fell behind after the first few laps. Amara stayed on her shoulder, her face calm and unflinching even as the pace began to hurt. With two hundred meters left, she moved wide and pulled ahead. When she crossed the line first, her teammates rushed onto the track in jubilation, hugging her and shouting her name. Hana, still breathing hard, was the first rival to shake her hand.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “dethrone” mean?
options: beat her in a practice run
qs.why: Hana had won four years in a row, so dethroning her means taking away her place as champion, not just beating her once in practice.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “Undeterred” mean?
qs.why: After finishing ninth, Amara trained hard all winter, so the poor result did not discourage her.

qs.q: Why did Hana run so fast at the start of the race?
options: She was injured and wanted to finish quickly.
She did not know how long the race was.
Her coach told her to save energy.
She hoped to tire out the other runners early.
She was trying to set a world record.
qs.why: The passage says Hana set a fast pace 'hoping to tire out the other runners early.'

title: Two Brothers, One Table
text: For eleven years, Samuel and David Mensah did not speak. Their estrangement began with an acrimonious argument over the family bakery after their father retired. Each brother believed the other had treated him unfairly, and the rancor lasted long after the bakery was sold. Last spring, David's daughter invited them both to her graduation. At first Samuel refused to go, but his wife kept asking, and finally he decided to relent. At the party, the brothers stood awkwardly at opposite ends of the room. Then David walked over, looking contrite. 'I said things I should never have said,' he told his brother quietly. Samuel did not answer right away. He looked wistfully at an old photo on the wall that showed the two of them as boys covered in flour. Then he pulled out a chair and asked David to sit down.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “relent” mean?
options: finally give in after refusing at first
qs.why: Samuel first refused, but after his wife kept asking he gave in and went.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “contrite” mean?
options: truly sorry for something wrong he had done
qs.why: David's words, 'I said things I should never have said,' show he was sorry.

qs.q: What does the ending of the story suggest?
options: Samuel wanted David to leave the party.
The brothers planned to buy back the bakery.
Samuel was still too angry to speak to David.
David's daughter forced them to sit together.
The old photo made Samuel angry again.
Samuel was ready to begin repairing the relationship.
qs.why: After looking at the photo with longing, Samuel invites David to sit with him, a first step toward making peace.

title: Opening Night at the Riverside
text: Rosa Delgado, the impresario behind the Riverside Theater, had spent her savings on this production, so opening night mattered. The play follows a lighthouse keeper who discovers that his brother has been lying to him. Its best moment comes in the second act, when the keeper, alone on stage, delivers a soliloquy about trust and fear. The lead actor, Ji-ho Park, had asked the cast not to upstage him during the big scenes, but he was generous in the comic ones and let the younger actors shine. There was one rough moment: a man in the back row began to heckle the actors, shouting jokes during a quiet scene. Ji-ho simply paused, smiled toward the dark, and went on, a bit of showmanship that drew warm applause. By the denouement, when the brothers finally learn the truth about their father, many people in the audience were in tears.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “heckle” mean?
options: interrupt them with rude or mocking shouts
ask them questions after the show
qs.why: The man was 'shouting jokes during a quiet scene,' which is rude interrupting, not cheering.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “denouement” mean?
options: the final part of the story, where its problems are explained or solved
the saddest song in the play
the moment the lights go out
qs.why: The denouement is when the brothers 'finally learn the truth,' the ending where the mystery is solved.

qs.q: How did Ji-ho deal with the man in the back row?
options: He calmly paused, then continued, and the audience liked how he handled it.
He stopped the play and had the man removed.
He shouted back at the man.
He let a younger actor take over the scene.
He left the stage in anger.
He ignored the man by speeding through his lines.
qs.why: Ji-ho 'simply paused, smiled toward the dark, and went on,' and the audience applauded.

title: Inside the Courtroom
text: Most trials look nothing like the ones on television, says retired judge Miriam Abebe. In thirty years on the bench, she was asked to adjudicate everything from neighbor disputes to serious crimes. Her first rule was simple: judge each case impartially. When a case involved someone she knew, even slightly, she would recuse herself and let another judge take over. In one widely reported case, news coverage was so heavy that she decided to sequester the jury in a hotel, without phones or newspapers, until the trial ended. The defendant, a young man accused of stealing a car, admitted he had driven it. His lawyer argued there were extenuating circumstances: he had taken the car, its keys left inside, to rush his badly injured sister to the hospital. After two days of debate, the jury voted to acquit him. 'Facts matter,' Abebe says, 'but so do the reasons behind them.'

qs.q: In the passage, what does “recuse” mean?
options: ask the lawyers for more evidence
step away from the case because a personal connection could make her unfair
qs.why: She stepped aside 'and let another judge take over' when she knew someone in the case, to avoid seeming unfair.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “sequester” mean?
options: dismiss the jurors from the trial
keep the jurors apart from other people
question the jurors one by one
let the jurors go home each night
replace the jurors with new ones
qs.why: The jury stayed in a hotel without phones or newspapers, kept away from outside news and people.

qs.q: Why did the jury find the young man not guilty?
options: They believed he had never driven the car.
They accepted that he took the car for an urgent and good reason.
News reports told them he was innocent.
qs.why: He admitted driving the car, but his lawyer showed he took it to save his injured sister, and the jury found him not guilty.

title: When the Hills Caught Fire
text: The fire started small, with a spark from a farm machine in a dry field outside the town of Pine Hollow. Within hours, strong winds had turned it into a conflagration that stretched across three hills. Smoke began to envelop the town, and the acrid smell burned people's throats even indoors. Firefighters worked through the night while helicopters dropped water to douse the flames near homes. For a while, the fire's advance seemed inexorable; each time crews cleared a line, sparks jumped across it. Then, on the third day, the wind shifted and a light rain fell. The town itself was saved, but the fire did decimate the forest to the north, burning about two-thirds of its trees. Today, young pines are growing back among the black stumps, and local schoolchildren help plant new ones each spring.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “envelop” mean?
qs.why: The smoke covered the whole town, so people smelled it even indoors.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “inexorable” mean?
qs.why: Each time crews cleared a line, sparks jumped across it, so the fire seemed impossible to stop.

qs.q: What finally helped stop the fire?
options: Helicopters dropping water on the forest
A change in the wind and some light rain
Crews clearing a single fire line
The fire running out of houses to burn
qs.why: The fire kept advancing until 'the wind shifted and a light rain fell' on the third day.

title: The Lantern Festival Returns
text: After a five-year break, the Lantern Festival returned to Harbor Street last weekend. City leaders had hoped the event would enliven a downtown that has grown quiet since several shops closed. It did. By sunset, the street was filled with a cheerful hubbub of voices, music and sizzling food. The parade offered plenty of pageantry: drummers in red silk, dancers carrying paper dragons, and children holding glowing lanterns shaped like fish and stars. Older residents said the gaiety reminded them of the festivals of their youth. Later in the evening, the revelry moved to the waterfront, where a band played until midnight. One moment turned riotous in the best way, when a sudden rain shower sent hundreds of dancers splashing and laughing through puddles instead of running for cover. Shop owners reported their busiest night in years.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “hubbub” mean?
options: a loud, confused noise of many people talking
qs.why: The street was full of voices, music and cooking sounds all at once.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “enliven” mean?
qs.why: The downtown had 'grown quiet,' so leaders hoped the festival would bring it energy and life.

qs.q: What did city leaders hope the festival would do?
options: Raise money to reopen the closed shops
Replace the band on the waterfront
Teach children to make paper lanterns
Bring life and visitors back to a quiet downtown
Keep people indoors during the rain
End a tradition that had grown old
qs.why: Leaders hoped the festival would enliven a downtown that had grown quiet, and shops had their busiest night in years.

title: Paying for College
text: When Diego Alvarez was accepted to an engineering program, his family did not have the wherewithal to pay the full cost. A local foundation offered him a scholarship paid in parts: the first tranche arrived in September, and the next would come only if he kept his grades up. A part-time job at the campus library helped defray the cost of books and bus fares. His grandmother, who had raised five children on a small income, gave him advice about money. 'Don't be a miser,' she said. 'Spend on what helps you grow, like a good laptop or a class trip.' But she also warned him not to be profligate, like the classmates who ran up credit card bills on fancy dinners. Diego still remembers her words. Pecuniary worries never fully went away, but he finished his degree without any debt.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “defray” mean?
options: pay part of the cost of
qs.why: His library job brought in money that covered some of the cost of books and bus fares.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “profligate” mean?
qs.why: The example is classmates running up credit card bills on fancy dinners, which is wasteful spending. 'Too careful' describes a miser, the opposite warning.

qs.q: What was the main idea of the grandmother's advice?
options: Use credit cards for special dinners.
Quit the library job to study more.
Ask the foundation for more money.
Spend on things that help you grow, but do not waste money.
Always buy the most expensive laptop.
qs.why: She warned against being a miser and against being wasteful: spend on what helps you grow.

title: The Long Way to Eagle Ridge
text: The guidebook promised a four-hour hike, but the trail to Eagle Ridge turned out to be far more circuitous than the map suggested, winding around two lakes and through a valley before it ever began to climb. By noon a storm had passed over, and Noor's socks were sodden. Wet socks chafe, and soon both her heels were red and sore. Her hiking partner, Felix, a small, wiry man who ran marathons, gave her a dry pair from his pack. Even so, for the last hour they had to trudge up a muddy slope, neither of them saying much. Then the clouds broke apart. From the top, they could see the whole valley shining below them, the lakes like two silver coins. Noor forgot her blisters. The exhilaration of that view, she said later, made every wet, aching step worth it.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “circuitous” mean?
options: taking a long, winding route instead of a direct one
qs.why: The trail wound around two lakes and through a valley before climbing, so it took a long, indirect way.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “wiry” mean?
qs.why: Felix is small and runs marathons, which suggests a thin, strong body. Nothing in the passage is about his hair.

qs.q: Why did Noor forget about her blisters?
options: Felix gave her medicine for the pain.
Her socks dried in the sun.
The cold rain made her feet numb.
The beautiful view from the top filled her with joy.
qs.why: The passage says the exhilaration of the view made every aching step worth it.

title: The Woman With Nine Languages
text: Leila Haddad works as an interpreter at international conferences, and her colleagues call her a true polyglot. She speaks nine languages, though she says she is fully conversant in only six. Her method is simple. She learns the rudiments first: common verbs, numbers and greetings. Then she finds a patient interlocutor, often a taxi driver or a shop owner, and talks for as long as they will let her. She jokes that her memory for words is encyclopedic, but her memory for where she left her keys is terrible. Her erudition goes beyond languages; she reads widely in history and poetry, which helps her understand the jokes and old sayings that speakers use. 'A language is not a list of words,' she says. 'It is a way of seeing the world.'

qs.q: In the passage, what does “rudiments” mean?
options: the most basic facts and skills
qs.why: The examples, common verbs, numbers and greetings, are the basic things learned first.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “interlocutor” mean?
options: a person to have a conversation with
a person who corrects written mistakes
a stranger who refuses to talk
qs.why: A taxi driver or shop owner who 'talks for as long as they will let her' is a conversation partner, not a teacher.

qs.q: Why does Leila read history and poetry?
options: It helps her understand the jokes and sayings people use.
She needs it to pass interpreter exams.
She wants to stop learning new languages.
It improves her memory for her keys.
She plans to become a poet.
qs.why: The passage says her reading in history and poetry 'helps her understand the jokes and old sayings that speakers use.'

title: Anatomy of a Phone Scam
text: The call came on a Tuesday. A polite voice told Lucía Ortega that her grandson had been in an accident and needed money for a lawyer. The caller was a swindler, and a skilled one. Scammers like him concoct detailed stories, using names and facts found online to sound believable. Every part of the call was artifice: the background noise of a police station, the second 'officer' who came on the line, the urgent request for secrecy. Experts say such criminals often falsify caller ID so the number looks local. The talk of legal papers was a smokescreen meant to keep her from thinking clearly. Luckily, Mrs. Ortega hung up and called her grandson, who was safe at work. 'The duplicity shocked me,' she said. 'He sounded so kind.' Police advise anyone who gets such a call to check with family directly before sending money.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “smokescreen” mean?
options: a sign that there was a fire
something meant to distract her and hide the real plan
a special kind of phone call
a way to protect her savings
qs.why: The legal talk was 'meant to keep her from thinking clearly,' hiding that it was a trick.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “concoct” mean?
qs.why: Scammers make up false stories to sound believable. 'Cook or mix' is another meaning of concoct, but not the one used here.

qs.q: How did Mrs. Ortega find out the call was a trick?
options: The caller ID showed a strange foreign number.
She hung up and called her grandson, who was fine.
The police called to warn her.
She noticed there was no background noise.
qs.why: Mrs. Ortega checked directly with her grandson and learned he was safe at work.

title: Grandpa Teo's Workshop
text: At eighty-six, Teodoro Reyes is still sprightly enough to climb the ladder in his garage workshop, much to his daughter's worry. The workshop is unpretentious: a wooden bench, a radio, and rows of old coffee cans full of nails and screws. Here, with gnarled hands that have worked wood for seventy years, he builds birdhouses for the neighborhood. His grandchildren visit every Sunday, and he is a doting grandfather, slipping them candy and praising every crooked birdhouse they make. Each visit includes at least one reminiscence, such as the time he built a boat with his own father and it sank in five minutes. Teodoro has already decided to bequeath his tools to his granddaughter Mia, the only one who sweeps up the sawdust without being asked. 'She respects the work,' he says.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “unpretentious” mean?
options: simple and modest, not trying to impress
qs.why: A wooden bench, a radio and old coffee cans describe a plain, modest space. Nothing says it is dirty.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “bequeath” mean?
options: leave to someone after he dies
qs.why: Deciding now who will get his tools later is leaving them to someone after his death.

qs.q: Why did Teodoro choose Mia to receive his tools?
options: She shows respect for the work, like cleaning up without being told.
She asked him for the tools.
She visits more often than the others.
She plans to sell the tools.
qs.why: He chose Mia because she 'sweeps up the sawdust without being asked' and 'respects the work.'

title: The Science Fair Prank
text: Farah Nasser has taught middle school science for twenty years, and she has seen every prank. This year, two boys hid a rubber snake inside a volcano model at the science fair. When a parent screamed, the boys laughed so hard they nearly fell off their chairs. It was asinine, but Ms. Nasser did not chastise them in front of the crowd. Instead, she took them aside after the event. She told them she knew they were callow, not cruel, but that the parent had been truly frightened. Her admonition was short and firm: 'Fun is fine. Scaring people is not.' The boys apologized sheepishly to the parent, staring at their shoes. One of them, Jake, is known as incorrigible; he has pulled a prank every month since September. But even he offered to help clean up the gym afterward.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “chastise” mean?
qs.why: She chose not to scold them harshly in public and instead spoke to them privately.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “incorrigible” mean?
options: having bad habits that seem impossible to change
qs.why: Jake has pulled a prank every month, so his habit seems impossible to correct.

qs.q: How did Ms. Nasser handle the prank?
options: She punished them in front of everyone.
She called their parents to the gym.
She spoke to the boys privately and firmly instead of scolding them in public.
She laughed and joined the joke.
She cancelled the rest of the science fair.
qs.why: She 'did not chastise them in front of the crowd' but took them aside and gave a short, firm warning.

title: Learning to Dance at Forty
text: For most of his life, Rahul Mehta was a wallflower at weddings, standing near the snack table while everyone else danced. He was bashful around strangers and felt gauche whenever he tried to move to music, as if his arms and legs belonged to someone else. At forty, he signed up for a salsa class at the community center. The teacher, an effervescent woman named Carmen who laughed at her own mistakes, made the room feel congenial from the first night. Nobody watched anyone else too closely; everyone was busy counting steps. By the sixth week, Rahul noticed something strange: he was smiling. At his cousin's wedding that summer, he danced for two hours straight, uninhibited and sweaty, while his family stared in amazement. 'I didn't get much better at dancing,' he says. 'I just stopped worrying about how I looked.'

qs.q: In the passage, what does “gauche” mean?
qs.why: He felt as if his arms and legs 'belonged to someone else,' which describes clumsy, awkward movement.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “effervescent” mean?
options: lively, cheerful and full of energy
qs.why: Carmen laughs at her own mistakes and makes the room friendly, so she is cheerful and lively. 'Giving off bubbles' is the word's literal meaning for drinks, not for a person.

qs.q: According to Rahul, what really changed?
options: He became a highly skilled dancer.
His family taught him to dance at home.
He stopped worrying about how he looked.
qs.why: Rahul says, 'I didn't get much better at dancing... I just stopped worrying about how I looked.'

title: Visitors in the Pantry
text: It began with a tiny hole in a bag of rice. Then Mei Lin found crumbs on the counter and heard something scurry behind the fridge at night. Mice had found their way into her apartment. A pest expert explained that mice scavenge for almost any food people leave behind, from crumbs and spilled cereal to scraps in the trash, and that two or three can quickly become dozens. Left alone, they can infest an entire building. They also gnaw on wires and wood, which can cause real damage. Mei Lin spent a Saturday sealing gaps with steel wool and putting food in glass jars. That night she crept stealthily into the kitchen with a flashlight to check her work. Nothing moved. A week later, she rummaged through the back of every cupboard, pushing boxes and cans aside to be sure, but she found no new signs. The visitors were gone.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “scavenge” mean?
options: search for food that others have left or thrown away
qs.why: Mice search for food that people leave behind or throw away, such as crumbs, spilled cereal and scraps in the trash.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “rummage” mean?
options: search by moving things around quickly and carelessly
qs.why: She pushed boxes and cans aside in the backs of cupboards to look for signs of mice.

qs.q: Why does the expert say mice should be dealt with quickly?
options: Mice are dangerous to adults who touch them.
Mice eat only rice and grain.
Steel wool makes mice more aggressive.
Mice usually leave on their own after a week.
A few mice can soon become many and damage a building.
qs.why: The expert says two or three mice can become dozens, can infest a building and gnaw wires and wood.

title: How Bayline Video Lost Its Grip
text: For twenty years, the Bayline Video chain had a stranglehold on movie rentals in its region; in many towns, it was the only place to rent a film. Its leaders saw no reason to change. Promotions went to the owner's old golf friends rather than the best managers, and workers complained of cronyism. When streaming services appeared, Bayline's executives called them a passing fad. They kept investing in store shelves and late fees, a business model that was quickly becoming outmoded. Customers left in huge numbers. Within three years the company saw a precipitous drop in sales, losing more than half its income. By the end, the once-busy stores were moribund, with a few bored clerks and empty aisles. Business students now study Bayline as a warning: no company is so strong that a better idea cannot supplant it.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “stranglehold” mean?
options: a small share of the market
complete control that kept others from competing
qs.why: Bayline was often 'the only place to rent a film,' so it had tight control of the market.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “moribund” mean?
options: declining and close to coming to an end
qs.why: With bored clerks and empty aisles after sales collapsed, the stores were dying out. 'Gloomy' fits the mood but misses the idea of coming to an end.

qs.q: What lesson do business students take from Bayline?
options: Even a powerful company can be replaced if it refuses to change.
Late fees are the key to business success.
Streaming services are a passing trend.
Small shops always beat large chains.
Golf is a good way to find managers.
qs.why: Bayline ignored streaming and lost its business; the lesson is that 'a better idea' can replace any company.

title: Notes From an Editor's Desk
text: As an editor, Grace Achebe reads hundreds of articles a year, and she sees the same problems again and again. Many writers are verbose, using five sentences where one would do. Some bury a strong idea under so much verbiage that readers give up before they find it. Others fall in love with florid language, describing a sunset as 'a magnificent, glorious tapestry of golden fire.' Grace also cuts hackneyed phrases like 'at the end of the day' and 'think outside the box,' which readers have heard a thousand times. Her advice is simple. Before you write, try to distill your main point into one sentence. If you cannot, you are not ready to start. Then write as concisely as you can, and read every line aloud. 'Good writing,' she says, 'respects the reader's time.'

qs.q: In the passage, what does “florid” mean?
options: using too many fancy words and decorations
qs.why: The sunset example piles up grand words, which is overly fancy writing. 'Having a red face' is another meaning of florid, but not this one.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “distill” mean?
options: heat a liquid to make it purer
express the most important part in a short, clear form
qs.why: She asks writers to put their main point 'into one sentence,' which means boiling it down to its core.

qs.q: What does Grace suggest writers do before they start writing?
options: Read every line of the article aloud.
Make sure they can state their main point in one sentence.
Write five sentences for each idea.
Ask an editor to choose a topic.
qs.why: Before writing, she says to put the main point into one sentence. Reading aloud comes after writing.

title: The Ferry Captain
text: Captain Olsen has run the ferry to Gull Island for thirty-one years. He is taciturn by nature; most passengers hear only 'Morning' and 'Mind the step.' His face is inscrutable, weathered and still, so newcomers often cannot tell whether he is pleased or annoyed. He can be testy when tourists stand in the way of the ropes. Yet the island children adore him, and over time he manages to endear himself to nearly everyone. The secret is his droll sense of humor. When the engine broke down halfway across one stormy day, he looked at the worried passengers and said, 'Good news. You'll all be very early for tomorrow.' Last year, when the island gave him an award, he studied the plaque and smiled wryly. 'Thirty-one years,' he said, 'and they finally noticed I was here.'

qs.q: In the passage, what does “inscrutable” mean?
qs.why: Newcomers 'cannot tell whether he is pleased or annoyed,' so his face is hard to read. 'Weathered' describes wrinkles, but that is a separate word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “testy” mean?
options: easily annoyed and sharp in reply
qs.why: He gets short-tempered when tourists block the ropes.

qs.q: What did the captain mean by his joke about the broken engine?
options: They would reach the island earlier than planned today.
They would be stuck so long that they would arrive the next day.
He was angry at the passengers.
They would have to swim the rest of the way.
The island was closed until tomorrow.
qs.why: 'Very early for tomorrow' is a dry way of saying they would be very late today. It does not mean the engine was fixed.

title: The Dog Park Vote
text: The Maplewood Neighbors Club needed every member to agree before it could turn an empty lot into a dog park, because the club's rules required unanimity on land decisions. Eleven of the twelve members said yes on the first night. The lone holdout was Bernard Haas, whose house faced the lot. His intransigence surprised people; he would not even discuss changes to the plan. The dissension dragged on for months, and some members began talking about changing the rules. Finally, a younger member, Yasmin Saleh, visited Mr. Haas at home and simply asked what worried him. It was the noise early in the morning. The club agreed to keep the park closed before eight. Mr. Haas did not exactly capitulate; he said he would acquiesce 'as long as the gate is locked on time.' The park opened in May.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “holdout” mean?
options: the owner of the empty lot
a member who owned a dog
the one person who refused to agree when others did
qs.why: Eleven members said yes, and Mr. Haas alone refused.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “intransigence” mean?
options: stubborn refusal to change his opinion
qs.why: He 'would not even discuss changes to the plan,' which shows a stubborn refusal to move.

qs.q: What finally settled the disagreement?
options: The club changed its voting rules.
Mr. Haas moved to another street.
Someone asked Mr. Haas what bothered him, and the club changed the hours.
Mr. Haas got a dog of his own.
The park was built on a different lot.
qs.why: Yasmin learned that early noise worried him, and the club agreed to close the park before eight. Members only talked about changing the rules.

title: The Castle on the Hill
text: Above the village of Tormont stands a ruined castle that local people have called 'the Old Keep' since time immemorial. According to the village story, a usurper seized the castle from its rightful lord in the Middle Ages and held it for seven years, until the lord's nephew returned with an army to besiege it. Historians say parts of the tale may be true, but the stones tell a more complicated story. The lower walls predate the tower by about two hundred years, which suggests the castle was built in stages. A narrow stone stair now leads nowhere; it is a vestigial piece of an upper floor that collapsed long ago. Visitors often smile at one anachronism in the village museum: a painting of the famous siege shows a soldier wearing a wristwatch, added by a joking painter in the 1950s.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “predate” mean?
qs.why: The lower walls came about two hundred years before the tower, which is why the castle seems built in stages. 'Newer than' is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “usurper” mean?
options: the lord who rightfully owned the castle
a person who took power that was not rightfully his
qs.why: He 'seized the castle from its rightful lord,' so he took what was not his.

qs.q: Why is the wristwatch in the painting funny?
options: The soldier in the painting was the usurper.
The painting is older than the castle.
The watch shows the wrong time of day.
The painter was once a soldier in the castle.
Wristwatches did not exist in the Middle Ages, so it is out of place.
Watches were banned inside the castle.
qs.why: The siege happened in the Middle Ages, long before wristwatches, so the painter put something from the wrong time period into the scene.

title: Songs for the Harbor
text: Every November, the fishing town of Port Ellery holds a concert to remember sailors lost at sea. It begins with the knell of the old church bell, one slow stroke for each name read aloud. Then the town band plays a dirge, so slow and heavy that even small children stand still. The middle of the program is elegiac but gentle, as a local choir sings old songs about boats that never came home. Thomas Breen, a folk-music aficionado who has recorded the town's songs for forty years, says the final piece is his favorite. It is a paean to the sea itself, praising its beauty and power, sung by the whole crowd. Its tune is so melodious that visitors often hum it for days. 'We are sad,' he explains, 'but we are also grateful.'

qs.q: In the passage, what does “paean” mean?
options: a prayer for safety at sea
a song about pain and loss
qs.why: The passage explains that the song is 'praising its beauty and power.' The slow funeral song is the dirge, a different piece.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “aficionado” mean?
options: a person who knows a lot about something and loves it
a critic who dislikes folk music
the leader of the town band
a beginner who is just learning
qs.why: Thomas has recorded the town's songs for forty years, showing deep knowledge and enthusiasm.

qs.q: How does the mood of the concert change from beginning to end?
options: It moves from joy to anger.
It stays cheerful from start to finish.
It moves from quiet calm to fear.
It begins with praise and ends with a funeral song.
It moves from deep sorrow toward praise and gratitude.
qs.why: It opens with a bell and a dirge, and ends with a song of praise; Thomas says, 'We are sad, but we are also grateful.'

title: When Critics Go Too Far
text: Restaurant critic Elena Petrova believes in honest reviews, but she draws a line. A trenchant review, she says, points clearly to what failed: the soup was cold, the fish was dry, the service was slow. A vitriolic one is different; it attacks people, not food, and its goal is to hurt. Early in her career, Elena wrote a long diatribe about a small café, mocking the owner's taste in furniture and even his accent. Readers loved it, but she felt ashamed when she met the owner months later. Now she refuses to disparage chefs as people.
