She also avoids the backhanded compliment, such as 'the dessert was surprisingly good for a place like this.' And she has no patience for derisive comments from readers. 'You can say a meal was bad,' she says, 'without saying the cook is worthless.'

qs.q: In the passage, what does “trenchant” mean?
options: sharp, clear and forceful in criticism
qs.why: A trenchant review 'points clearly to what failed.' Cruel, personal attacks are what Elena calls vitriolic.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “backhanded” mean?
options: seeming like praise but really hiding an insult
qs.why: 'Surprisingly good for a place like this' sounds kind but insults the restaurant.

qs.q: Why did Elena change the way she writes about chefs?
options: Readers complained about her early reviews.
Her editor told her to be kinder.
She felt ashamed after meeting the owner of a café she had mocked.
She stopped eating at small cafés.
A chef took her to court.
She decided that honest reviews are unfair.
qs.why: After mocking a café owner in an early diatribe, she felt ashamed when she met him, and now she refuses to disparage chefs as people. Readers did not complain; they loved the review.

title: Stranded at Gate 14
text: The snowstorm arrived at the most inopportune moment possible: the night before the holiday, when the airport was packed with families. By midnight, every flight had been cancelled. Travelers wandered through the terminal looking befuddled, staring at screens that kept changing. The long lines at the help desk were exasperating, and several people began shouting at the staff. In the middle of it all sat an older woman named Mrs. Adeyemi, knitting a scarf. She looked completely unperturbed. When a nervous teenager asked how she could stay so calm, she shrugged nonchalantly. 'I've been stuck in airports in four countries,' she said. 'The plane leaves when it leaves.' Her equanimity seemed to spread. Soon a small group had gathered around her, sharing snacks and phone chargers, and the long night felt a little shorter.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “befuddled” mean?
options: confused and unable to think clearly
qs.why: Travelers were staring at screens that kept changing, unsure what was happening.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “inopportune” mean?
qs.why: The storm came the night before the holiday, when the airport was most crowded, which was the worst possible time.

qs.q: What effect did Mrs. Adeyemi have on the people around her?
options: She convinced the airline to restart the flights.
Her calm helped others relax and start helping one another.
She made the other travelers angrier.
She taught everyone how to knit.
She found hotel rooms for the group.
She left on the first flight out.
qs.why: 'Her equanimity seemed to spread,' and people gathered to share snacks and chargers.

title: The Garden Between Towers
text: In the middle of a busy city block, between two apartment towers, lies a small community garden that feels almost bucolic. Chickens peck near a wooden shed, and in summer there is a profusion of tomatoes, beans and sunflowers, far more than the gardeners can eat. The garden's rules are homespun, written in marker on a board by the gate: 'Share your extras. Close the hose. Be kind.' Most days the mood is collegial, with neighbors trading seeds and advice. That does not mean there are no problems. Gardeners still squabble over small things, like whose pumpkin vine has crept into whose bed. But the garden's founder, a retired nurse named Ruth Coleman, keeps things peaceable. Her method is to hand each side a basket and ask them to pick the pumpkins together.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “bucolic” mean?
options: like peaceful country or farm life
qs.why: With chickens and a wooden shed, the garden feels like the countryside, even in the city.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “squabble” mean?
qs.why: They argue over 'small things,' like a pumpkin vine. Nothing suggests a serious fight.

qs.q: How does Ruth handle disagreements in the garden?
options: She writes a new rule on the board.
She takes the pumpkins for herself.
She gets the two sides to solve the problem together.
She reports them to the city.
She lets them argue until they get tired.
qs.why: Ruth hands each side a basket and asks them to pick the pumpkins together.

title: A Slow Recovery
text: When Kenji Watanabe came home from a hiking trip with a fever, he thought it was just a cold. Instead, the malady lasted for weeks. The virus that afflicted him left him so weak that even climbing the stairs was hard. For a month, tiredness would incapacitate him by mid-afternoon, and he had to leave work early or stay home. His face looked pallid, and friends who visited noticed how listless he seemed, staring at the television without really watching it. His doctor explained that recovery would take time, but that some steps could ameliorate his symptoms: plenty of water, short walks, regular sleep and a slow return to normal activity. Kenji followed the plan. By the third month he was walking a mile each morning, and the color had come back to his cheeks.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “pallid” mean?
qs.why: Later 'the color had come back to his cheeks,' which shows his face had been pale.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “ameliorate” mean?
options: make better or easier to bear
qs.why: The steps could make his symptoms easier to live with. The doctor said recovery would take time, so they were not a complete cure.

qs.q: What best describes Kenji's recovery?
options: It happened overnight after he took medicine.
Going back to hiking cured him at once.
It was slow and gradual, helped by steady daily habits.
Staying in bed all day made him recover fastest.
qs.why: Recovery took months and came through water, short walks, sleep and a slow return to activity.

title: The Watcher on the Bench
text: Detective Nadia Brooks had been watching the jewelry shop for three nights. Each evening, the same man would loiter near the bus stop across the street, never catching a bus. His glances toward the shop's back door were quick and furtive, as if he feared being seen. On the fourth night, Nadia sat on a bench close enough to eavesdrop on his phone call. 'Not yet,' he said quietly. 'The alarm is still on.' The next morning, she brought him in for questioning. He was cagey, giving short answers and claiming he simply liked the quiet street. Nadia watched him warily; she knew one wrong move could warn his partners. Then she placed a small object on the table: a key to the shop, found in his coat. His face went white. The key alone did not prove he had planned a crime, but together with the phone call, it was beginning to incriminate him.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “furtive” mean?
options: secret and nervous, trying not to be noticed
qs.why: His glances were quick, 'as if he feared being seen,' which is secret, nervous behavior.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “cagey” mean?
qs.why: He gave short answers and a weak excuse, avoiding saying what he really knew. 'Trapped' is a careless link to the word 'cage.'

qs.q: What can we conclude about the case at the end?
options: The man confessed to planning a robbery.
The key proved the man was innocent.
The shop was robbed that night.
Nadia let the man go for good.
Nadia had a useful clue but still needed more proof.
His partners had already been arrested.
qs.why: The key 'alone did not prove he had planned a crime,' though with the phone call it was beginning to make him look guilty, so more proof was needed.

title: From Office Job to Taco Truck
text: When Isabel Cruz quit her office job to open a taco truck, her parents called the plan foolhardy. She had no cooking degree and only a small amount of savings. But Isabel had gumption. She spent six months working at other food trucks for free, learning how they handled permits, suppliers and long lines. She was circumspect about money, buying a used truck and testing her menu at farmers' markets before signing any long contract. Her resourcefulness showed when her generator failed on the busiest day of the summer; she borrowed power from a friendly ice cream truck parked next door and kept serving. The biggest pitfall, she says, was one she never expected: the paperwork. 'It takes moxie to stand in a hot truck for twelve hours,' she laughs, 'but it takes even more to fill out tax forms.'

qs.q: In the passage, what does “circumspect” mean?
options: careful to think about risks before acting
qs.why: She bought a used truck and tested her menu before signing contracts, which shows careful thought about risk.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “pitfall” mean?
qs.why: She calls paperwork the problem 'she never expected.' A hole in the ground is the literal meaning, not the one used here.

qs.q: Why did Isabel work at other food trucks for free?
options: Because she could not find paid work
To save money for a cooking degree
To learn how the business worked before starting her own
qs.why: She worked for free to learn 'how they handled permits, suppliers and long lines.'

title: The Critic's Verdict
text: Every Friday, the food writer Amara Osei visits a new restaurant and tells her readers the truth. Amara is a proud gourmand who will happily eat six courses, but she is not easy to please. Last week she tried a small place near the river run by a young cook named Tomás. The kitchen was redolent of garlic and roasted peppers, and the first dish, a fish soup with a piquant lime sauce, made her sit up. She asked for a second bowl. Dessert was another story. The cake was so cloying that she left most of it on the plate, and she noted that even a smidgen of salt would have helped. Her review was fair but famously acerbic: “The soup deserves a parade. The cake deserves an apology.” Tomás laughed when he read it, and changed the recipe the next day.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “redolent” mean?
qs.why: The kitchen smelled strongly of garlic and peppers. It was not empty of them or cleaned of them; the smell filled the room.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “acerbic” mean?
options: sharp and harshly critical, with biting humor
full of lies meant to hurt
qs.why: Her joke that the cake “deserves an apology” is sharp and biting. The review was fair, so it was not full of lies.

qs.q: What can we infer about Tomás from the end of the passage?
options: He was hurt and stopped reading reviews.
He believed the cake was already perfect.
He closed the restaurant after the review.
He asked Amara to change her review.
He accepted the criticism and used it to improve his cooking.
He decided the soup needed more work.
qs.why: He laughed and changed the cake recipe the next day, so he took the criticism well. The soup was praised, so it did not need work.

title: Alone Around the World
text: When Ingrid Halvorsen set out to circumnavigate the globe in a small sailboat, her friends worried about everything that could go wrong. They had reason to. In the Southern Ocean, the wind was unremitting for eleven days, and huge waves crashed over the deck day and night. Twice she feared the boat would capsize, and once it nearly did, tipping so far that the mast touched the water. Ingrid simply tied herself to the boat and kept steering. After months alone she had become inured to cold meals, wet clothes and broken sleep; they no longer bothered her. She bore a cracked rib stoically, mentioning it in her log only as “a small problem.” Now home, she has become a fine raconteur, and crowds at the harbor café laugh and gasp as she tells the story of the night a whale swam beside her for an hour.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “inured” mean?
options: so used to them that they no longer upset her
qs.why: The passage explains that these hardships “no longer bothered her” after months at sea. “Insured” looks similar but means something different.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “raconteur” mean?
options: a person who runs a café
a person who tells stories in an entertaining way
a person who avoids talking about the past
qs.why: Crowds laugh and gasp as she tells her stories, so she is a skilled storyteller. She tells them aloud at the café; she does not run it.

qs.q: What does the detail about the cracked rib show about Ingrid?
options: She was not really injured at all.
She dealt with pain calmly and without fuss.
She ended the trip early because of it.
She filled her log with complaints.
She was more afraid of the whale than the storm.
Her friends had been wrong to worry.
qs.why: She called a cracked rib “a small problem,” which shows calm endurance. The passage says her friends had good reason to worry.

title: The Parking Lot Debate
text: The meeting at the Linden Street library was supposed to last an hour. It lasted three. The topic was whether to turn a small parking lot into a community garden, and it caused quite a kerfuffle. Mr. Novak, who runs the hardware store, argued vociferously that his customers needed every space, waving his arms as he spoke. The garden group was just as intransigent; they would not discuss sharing the lot or putting the garden somewhere else. When one speaker began talking about the price of gasoline, the chair, Mrs. Adeyemi, said curtly, “Not germane. Next.” Later someone offered the platitude that “we all want what’s best for the neighborhood,” and several people rolled their eyes. In the end, a teenager suggested a garden on the library roof. The room went quiet, and then, for the first time all night, people agreed.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “germane” mean?
options: related to the topic being discussed
allowed by the rules of law
qs.why: Gas prices had nothing to do with the garden question, so the chair said the remark was not relevant. She was not judging whether it was true or polite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “curtly” mean?
options: after a long pause to think
in a short, rude way, with very few words
qs.why: “Not germane. Next.” is a very short, abrupt reply. “Loudly and with great feeling” describes Mr. Novak’s style instead.

qs.q: Why did people roll their eyes at the remark about wanting “what’s best for the neighborhood”?
options: It was a tired, empty saying that did nothing to solve the problem.
Everyone knew it was a lie.
It was spoken by the teenager.
It went on for far too long.
They did not care about the neighborhood.
qs.why: The remark is called a platitude: a dull, overused line with no real content. The teenager is the one who later gave a useful idea.

title: The Missing Pages
text: Dr. Leila Haddad is often called a polymath. She has degrees in chemistry and history, speaks five languages, and has written about medieval music. Her latest project is a fourteenth-century book of herbal medicine kept in a small library in Portugal. The book is fascinating but also abstruse, full of old terms that even experts find hard to follow. There is also a lacuna in the middle: eight pages were torn out long ago, and no other copy survives. Through assiduous work, checking every remaining page against other books of the time, Dr. Haddad has made careful guesses about what the missing pages contained. She is now writing a short guide for the layperson. “My goal is to demystify this book,” she says. “You shouldn’t need three degrees to enjoy it.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “lacuna” mean?
options: a gap where part is missing
qs.why: The passage explains the lacuna right away: eight pages were torn out. It is a missing part, not a damaged or hidden one.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “layperson” mean?
options: a person who works in a library
someone who is not an expert in the subject
qs.why: Her guide is for people without special training, so they will not “need three degrees.” The word is not about religion or laziness here.

qs.q: How has Dr. Haddad dealt with the missing pages?
options: She found the pages in another library.
She discovered a complete second copy.
She made careful guesses by comparing the book with others from the same period.
She decided to leave them out and ignore them.
She invented new pages from her imagination alone.
She asked other experts to rewrite the whole book.
qs.why: She checked the remaining pages against other books of the time to guess what was missing. No other copy survives, so she could not find the pages.

title: My Grandfather Sol
text: My grandfather Sol is an octogenarian who still walks two miles every morning. To strangers he can seem like a curmudgeon: he grumbles about loud music, new phones and the price of bread. His face is wizened from decades of working outdoors on his farm, lined like an old map. But anyone who stays longer than five minutes discovers his jocular side. He tells silly jokes at dinner and pretends to be shocked when we groan. He also has an impish streak. Last spring he hid a plastic frog in my aunt’s handbag and waited, perfectly calm, for her to find it at the bank. When I asked whether he regretted the scene she made, he smiled ruefully. “A little,” he said. “She’s still not speaking to me. But you should have heard her scream.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “wizened” mean?
options: thin, dried and lined with age
qs.why: His face is “lined like an old map” after years outdoors. The word looks like “wise,” but it describes how his face looks.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “ruefully” mean?
options: proudly, with no regret at all
with some regret mixed with humor
qs.why: He admits he regrets it “a little” but still enjoys the memory, which is regret with a touch of humor. He is not proud with no regret.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Sol is weak and in poor health.
Sol dislikes most of his family.
Sol regrets nothing he has ever done.
Sol’s farm is failing because of his age.
Sol stopped telling jokes after last spring.
Sol may seem grumpy at first, but he is playful and funny once you know him.
qs.why: The passage moves from his grumpy surface to his jokes and pranks. He does admit some regret, so “regrets nothing” is wrong.

title: The Comeback Season
text: After a 7–0 drubbing in their first match of the season, the girls of the Riverside soccer team sat in the locker room, crestfallen. Several were crying. Coach Mbeki did not shout. Instead, she showed them a video of their own best moments from the year before, and she exhorted them to remember how much fun the game used to be. The talk seemed to galvanize the players. The very next morning, half the team showed up an hour early to practice, and the captain, Priya, asked for extra running drills. They redoubled their efforts all autumn. The turnabout was remarkable: the team that had been laughed at in September finished second in the league in November. When reporters asked Coach Mbeki for her secret, she shrugged. “They always had it,” she said. “They just needed to remember.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “galvanize” mean?
options: coat with metal to stop rust
qs.why: After the talk, players came early and asked for extra drills, so it pushed them into action. Coating metal is a different, technical use of the word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “turnabout” mean?
options: a sharp turn in a road
a complete change in their situation
a short break during a game
qs.why: The team went from being laughed at to finishing second, a complete reversal. Nothing in the passage suggests a new coach.

qs.q: How did Coach Mbeki respond to the big loss?
options: She shouted at them for playing badly.
She made them run extra drills as punishment.
She told reporters the team was weak.
She encouraged the players by reminding them of their past skill and joy.
She cancelled practice for a week.
qs.why: She showed a video of their best moments and urged them to remember the fun. The extra drills were the captain’s idea, not a punishment.

title: The Wandering Fiddler
text: For twenty years, the fiddler Rosa Quintero has lived a peripatetic life, playing in a different town almost every week. She has no fixed home, only a small van and a case full of sheet music. She likes to wend her way along back roads rather than highways, stopping wherever someone will listen. Her music is lilting and gentle, like a boat rocking on water, and her singing voice is surprisingly sonorous for such a small woman, deep enough to fill a church. Many of her best moments have been serendipitous. Once, her van broke down outside a village in Ireland on the night of a wedding, and she ended up playing until dawn. “I don’t plan much,” she says, as she saunters across a market square, fiddle on her back. “The road usually knows better than I do.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “peripatetic” mean?
qs.why: She plays in a different town almost every week and has no fixed home. “Settled in one town” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “sonorous” mean?
qs.why: Her voice is “deep enough to fill a church,” which matches deep and full. It is pleasant, not harsh.

qs.q: Why does the writer mention the wedding in Ireland?
options: To show that her van is unreliable and should be replaced.
To show that she is often hired to play at weddings.
To show that she dislikes small villages.
To prove that she always plans her trips.
As an example of a lucky, unplanned event that turned out well.
To explain why she has no fixed home.
qs.why: The breakdown led by chance to a night of music, an example of her serendipitous moments. Nothing says she is usually hired for weddings.

title: The Manager's Kingdom
text: When Grant Ellison became head of the sales department, he treated it like his own fiefdom. Every decision, down to the color of the coffee mugs, had to go through him. He liked to bulldoze new rules through meetings, ignoring anyone who raised a question. His favorite underling, a young man named Corey, laughed loudly at every joke Grant made and praised every idea, however poor. The rest of the team considered Corey a sycophant, and his smarmy compliments made them cringe. Things came to a head when Grant ordered everyone to work on a holiday weekend. Nadia Petrova, the department’s best seller, simply refused. Grant called her insubordinate and threatened to report her. But when the company’s director heard the whole story, it was Grant, not Nadia, who was asked to explain himself.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “bulldoze” mean?
options: knock down buildings with a machine
discuss each rule slowly and carefully
write rules in a confusing way
force rules through with his power, ignoring objections
qs.why: He pushed rules through while “ignoring anyone who raised a question.” Here the word is about using power, not a machine.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “smarmy” mean?
qs.why: Corey praised every idea “however poor” to please his boss, so his compliments were fake. The team cringed because they were not honest.

qs.q: What does the ending suggest?
options: Nadia lost her job for refusing.
The director saw Grant’s behavior as the real problem.
Corey was put in charge of the department.
The team worked through the holiday weekend.
Grant’s power in the company grew stronger.
The director agreed that Nadia had been disobedient.
qs.why: Grant, not Nadia, had to explain himself, which suggests the director blamed him. Nothing says Nadia was punished.

title: The Miracle Tonic
text: In the late 1800s, wagons selling “miracle” medicines were a common sight in small American towns. In this story, a seller named Professor Crane arrives in the town of Millbrook with a nostrum he claims will cure everything from headaches to heartbreak. His speech is full of scientific-sounding words, and the more credulous townspeople line up to buy. But the town pharmacist, Elena Ruiz, listens skeptically from the back. She buys one bottle, tests it in her shop, and finds nothing but sugar water and a little alcohol. She has a reputation for unimpeachable honesty, so when she posts her results in the window, people believe her. By morning, Professor Crane’s wagon is gone. “He tried to bamboozle the whole town,” Elena says, “but quackery doesn’t survive a simple test.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “nostrum” mean?
options: a supposed cure that probably does not work
qs.why: Crane claims it cures everything, but it is only sugar water and alcohol. It is the opposite of a proven medicine.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “unimpeachable” mean?
options: so reliable that no one can doubt it
qs.why: Because her honesty could not be doubted, people believed her results. The word has nothing to do with removing someone from office here.

qs.q: Why did the townspeople believe Elena’s results?
options: She was known to be completely honest, and she had actually tested the tonic.
She shouted louder than Professor Crane.
She was selling a cheaper medicine of her own.
Professor Crane admitted that he had lied.
The tonic made many people sick.
She was the mayor of Millbrook.
qs.why: The passage links her well-known honesty and her test to the town’s trust. Crane simply left; he never admitted anything.

title: A Year Without a Queen
text: When the old queen of Veloria, an imaginary island nation, died without naming an heir, a tense interregnum began. For fourteen months no one sat on the throne, and the country’s neighbors watched hungrily. Into this gap stepped Chancellor Imani Torres, a quiet woman with decades of experience in statecraft. She knew that speeches about honor would not protect the island. Instead she practiced realpolitik, making deals even with countries she did not trust, as long as the deals kept Veloria safe. She shrewdly played two powerful neighbors against each other, so that neither dared to invade. Each month she welcomed a foreign dignitary to the palace with music and fine food. Looking back, the island’s historians agree that Veloria came perilously close to war that year, but Torres kept it from going over the edge.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “interregnum” mean?
options: a celebration for a new queen
a period between one ruler and the next
qs.why: It began when the queen died with no heir and lasted while “no one sat on the throne.” It was a gap in leadership, not a war.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “realpolitik” mean?
options: politics based on honor and moral rules
refusing to deal with other countries
politics based on practical goals rather than ideals
qs.why: She made deals even with untrusted countries because it kept the island safe, choosing results over ideals. “Honor and moral rules” is the opposite.

qs.q: How did Torres keep the neighbors from invading?
options: She built a large new army.
She quickly crowned a new queen.
She set two strong neighbors against each other so neither dared to attack.
She gave stirring speeches about honor.
She refused to let any foreign visitors in.
She attacked first to scare them.
qs.why: The passage says she “played two powerful neighbors against each other.” She avoided speeches about honor and welcomed visitors.

title: Reading the Sky
text: The fishermen of Puerto Azul can read the sky the way others read a newspaper. That afternoon, dark clouds began to billow over the hills, rising like smoke from a giant fire. Old Mateo pointed at a baleful green light at the edge of the sky and said only, “Not today.” Everyone knew what such a sky could portend: a storm strong enough to sink boats. The harbor water had already turned turbid, brown with mud stirred up from the bottom. The boats stayed tied up. That night the wind came in fitful bursts, roaring for a minute, then falling silent, then roaring again, so that nobody slept well. By morning the storm had passed. The village cat, bedraggled and furious, crept out from under a porch, and the fishermen went down to count what the sea had left them.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “turbid” mean?
qs.why: The passage explains it: the water was “brown with mud stirred up from the bottom.” It says nothing about the size of the waves.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “fitful” mean?
options: starting and stopping again and again
qs.why: The wind roared, went silent, then roared again. That stop-and-start pattern is the meaning, not “steady.”

qs.q: Why did the boats stay in the harbor?
options: The water was too muddy to catch fish.
Mateo was too ill to sail.
Signs in the sky warned the fishermen that a dangerous storm was coming.
qs.why: The clouds and green light could “portend” a storm strong enough to sink boats. Muddy water was another sign, not the reason itself.

title: Saving the School Pond
text: At first the old pond behind Marisol’s school seemed hopeless. A thick, fetid smell of rotting leaves hung over it, and students held their noses as they walked past. Then her science class adopted it as a project. They cleared out trash, planted reeds and dug a small channel to bring in fresh water. Change came imperceptibly; week by week the water grew a little clearer, though no one could say exactly when it happened. By spring, the pond had new denizens: frogs, water beetles and a pair of ducks. The air around it now felt fresh and salubrious, and teachers began holding classes on the bank. One morning the students watched dragonflies dance above the water, a beautiful but evanescent sight that was gone in minutes. A sense of pride seemed to pervade the whole school.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “denizens” mean?
qs.why: Frogs, beetles and ducks came to live in the pond. They are residents, not visitors passing through.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “evanescent” mean?
options: lasting only a very short time
qs.why: The sight “was gone in minutes,” so it was brief. It may also have been colorful, but that is not what the word means.

qs.q: How did the pond water change?
options: All at once, the day the channel was finished.
It stayed dirty, but the smell went away.
It cleared only after the ducks arrived.
Slowly, so that the change was hard to notice at any one moment.
It became clear because of heavy rain.
It got worse for months before it improved.
qs.why: The water grew clearer “week by week” and no one could say exactly when. That gradual change is what “imperceptibly” describes.

title: Two Brothers, One Gift
text: The Okafor brothers inherited the same amount of money from their aunt, but they could hardly have used it more differently. Chidi, a lifelong spendthrift, bought a sports car, threw a huge party and took friends on expensive trips. He would fritter away hundreds on small things, like fancy coffees and gadgets he never opened, without noticing. Within two years, his profligacy had left him with almost nothing, and he was paying extortionate interest on credit card debt. His brother Emeka lived frugally. He cooked at home, repaired his own bike and put most of the money into savings. Some friends called him parsimonious, and it is true he once argued for ten minutes over a one-dollar tip. But when Chidi lost his job, it was Emeka who quietly paid his rent for three months.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “extortionate” mean?
qs.why: Credit card debt with very high interest made Chidi’s problems worse. The word describes how high the interest was, not whether it was illegal.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “parsimonious” mean?
qs.why: Arguing for ten minutes over a dollar tip shows how much he hated spending. “Generous” is the opposite, though he did help later.

qs.q: What does the last sentence show?
options: Emeka secretly spent as much as Chidi.
Chidi had finally learned to save money.
Chidi paid back everything he owed.
Emeka refused to help his brother.
Emeka’s careful saving allowed him to help his brother when it mattered.
Their aunt left more money to help Chidi.
qs.why: Because Emeka saved, he could pay Chidi’s rent after he lost his job. It shows Emeka was careful, not simply mean.

title: The Piano Teacher
text: Mrs. Kowalski has taught piano in the same small studio for forty years, and her method has never changed. She believes a teacher must inculcate good habits from the very first lesson: straight back, curved fingers, slow practice. When a neophyte sits down at her piano, she does not expect brilliance, only effort. Her newest student, an eight-year-old named Hiro, arrived full of timidity, barely pressing the keys and whispering his answers. Mrs. Kowalski never shouted. If he slouched, she would chide him gently: “Back like a tree, please.” If he skipped his practice, she would admonish him more firmly, reminding him that the piano remembers every lazy week. And she was unfailingly kind. Six months later, Hiro played a short piece at the spring concert, loudly and without a single mistake, and then grinned at her from the stage.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “inculcate” mean?
options: fix firmly in a student’s mind by repeated teaching
qs.why: She builds the same habits from the first lesson onward, so they become fixed. It is about teaching, not testing or punishing.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “neophyte” mean?
qs.why: She expects “only effort” from a neophyte, like eight-year-old Hiro at his first lessons. An expert would be the opposite.

qs.q: How did Hiro change over the six months?
options: He became rude to his teacher.
He went from shy and quiet to confident enough to play loudly on stage.
He stayed shy but played without mistakes.
He learned mostly by being shouted at.
qs.why: He began whispering and barely pressing keys, and ended by playing loudly and grinning. She never shouted at him.

title: A Novel in Letters
text: Dana Whitfield’s new novel, The Harbor Letters, is an epistolary story: it is told entirely through letters, most of them between two sisters, one in Halifax and one in Cape Town, over thirty years. The form could have felt like a trick, but the letters have real verisimilitude. They complain about the weather, forget birthdays and repeat old jokes, just as real letters do. The book has won laudatory reviews from the literati, and it is easy to see why. Not every page succeeds. A few letters from the sisters’ father are turgid, with long, stiff sentences that slow the story down. Still, the book is full of moments worth marking. My own copy is now heavily annotated, its margins crowded with my notes and question marks. I suspect many book clubs will be passing their copies around this winter.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “verisimilitude” mean?
options: the quality of seeming real and true to life
qs.why: The letters complain, forget birthdays and repeat jokes “just as real letters do,” so they feel real. The passage is not praising beauty or length.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “turgid” mean?
options: heavy, stiff and hard to read
qs.why: The father’s letters have “long, stiff sentences that slow the story down.” That is the opposite of short and clear.

qs.q: What is the reviewer’s overall opinion of the book?
options: Mostly positive, with a few weak parts.
Perfect, with no flaws at all.
The letters feel fake and forced.
qs.why: The reviewer praises the realism and expects book clubs to share it, but says the father’s letters are weak. So the view is mostly positive, not perfect.

title: The Long Silence
text: For eleven years, Hana and her older brother Daniel did not speak. A fight over the sale of their parents’ house had estranged them, and the acrimony between them was so deep that relatives stopped inviting both of them to the same events. Every conversation they tried turned into recrimination: he said she had been greedy; she said he had lied. Then, last winter, Daniel’s son fell ill. Hana heard the news from a cousin and drove six hours to the hospital without a moment’s compunction about breaking her promise never to speak to him again. She sat with Daniel in the waiting room and commiserated with him, saying little, just holding his hand. Daniel later said it was her magnanimity that moved him most: she could have stayed away, and no one would have blamed her. The boy recovered. The siblings now talk every Sunday.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “recrimination” mean?
qs.why: He accused her of greed and she accused him of lying, so each answered blame with blame. It was the opposite of an apology.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “commiserated” mean?
options: shared his sadness and showed sympathy
qs.why: She sat with him and held his hand during his son’s illness, which shows sympathy. They did not argue that day.

qs.q: What ended the long silence between Hana and Daniel?
options: A court decided who owned the house.
Daniel wrote Hana a letter of apology.
Hana chose to come and support Daniel during his son’s illness.
A cousin arranged a family meeting.
Their parents asked them to make peace.
They agreed to buy the house back together.
qs.why: Hana drove to the hospital and sat with him, and Daniel was moved by her generosity. The cousin only passed on the news.

title: The Cat in Charge
text: Our cat, Biscuit, has trained the whole family. My mother dotes on him, buying him toys he ignores and brushing his fur every evening. My father claims we coddle him too much, then sneaks him bits of chicken when he thinks no one is looking. Biscuit accepts all of this with royal nonchalance, as if it is simply what he deserves. He spends an hour each morning preening in the sunny window, licking each paw until it shines. At exactly six o’clock, he begins to meow insistently, following my mother from room to room until his dinner appears. And when he wants affection, he will nuzzle your cheek with his cold nose, purring loudly, before walking away the moment you try to pet him back. We all agree that he is the one who owns the house.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “nonchalance” mean?
options: a calm, relaxed manner showing little concern
qs.why: He accepts the attention “as if it is simply what he deserves,” without fuss. He is not thankful or excited.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “insistently” mean?
options: softly and only once in a while
firmly, in a way that will not be ignored
qs.why: He keeps meowing and follows her room to room until dinner appears. He will not stop, so it is firm and persistent.

qs.q: What does the father’s behavior reveal?
options: He is the strictest member of the family.
He feeds Biscuit only healthy food.
He thinks the mother should brush the cat more.
He spoils Biscuit too, even though he says the family spoils him.
qs.why: He says they coddle Biscuit but then sneaks him chicken. His words and actions do not match.

title: Rules of the Debate Club
text: Ms. Lindqvist, who coaches the debate club at Eastbrook High, has a few rules. First: no bombast. Students who fill their speeches with big words and grand claims but no evidence lose points. Second: no sophistry. An argument may sound clever, she tells them, but if it depends on a trick of logic, a good judge will catch it. Third: answer the question. Equivocation, she says, is the fastest way to lose a judge’s trust; if you are asked whether you support a plan, do not give a long, noncommittal reply that could mean anything. What she loves most is repartee, the quick back-and-forth when both speakers are sharp and well prepared. Last year her team’s captain, Oluwaseun, won a final with one perfect rejoinder, and the audience applauded before the judges had even finished writing.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “sophistry” mean?
qs.why: The coach describes it as an argument that sounds clever but “depends on a trick of logic.” Honest logic is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “rejoinder” mean?
options: a request to join the team
qs.why: It comes in the middle of quick back-and-forth, and one sharp answer won the final. It is not an opening speech.

qs.q: Which kind of answer would Ms. Lindqvist most likely praise?
options: A speech full of impressive words but no proof.
A vague reply that avoids taking a side.
A clever logical trick that fools the other team.
A clear answer to the question, backed by evidence.
A reply that changes the subject.
qs.why: Her rules ban empty grand words, tricks of logic and vague answers, and she says to answer the question. Each wrong choice breaks one of her rules.

title: Climbing to the Camp
text: Ama Boateng had never climbed anything taller than a city hill when she joined a trek to a high mountain camp in Nepal. The first days were gentle, but the group had to stop often to acclimate, letting their bodies get used to the thin air. Higher up, the path turned into a pile of loose rocks, and Ama had to clamber over them on her hands and knees. One afternoon the group crossed a spindly bridge of rope and wood that swayed with every step. She moved laboriously, stopping every few steps to breathe. Twice she thought about turning back, but she held on tenaciously to the goal she had set. On the ninth day she reached the camp. “I didn’t conquer the mountain,” she wrote home. “I just surmounted a few hundred small problems, one at a time.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “acclimate” mean?
options: eat and rest after a long day
let their bodies get used to new conditions
qs.why: The passage explains it right away: “letting their bodies get used to the thin air.” Resting may happen too, but that is not the meaning.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “spindly” mean?
qs.why: The bridge was rope and wood and “swayed with every step,” so it looked thin and weak. It was not made of metal.

qs.q: What does Ama mean in her message home?
options: She did not actually reach the camp.
The trek turned out to be very easy.
She plans to climb an even higher mountain.
Her group did most of the work for her.
Her success came from getting past many small difficulties, not one big victory.
She regrets going on the trip.
qs.why: She says she did not “conquer” the mountain but solved “a few hundred small problems, one at a time.” She did reach the camp on day nine.

title: The Sapphire Necklace
text: No one paid attention to the small man in the gray coat who visited the Harlow Museum every Tuesday. He would study the jewel collection, glance furtively at the guards and leave after twenty minutes. His surreptitious visits, it turned out, were part of a careful plan. The chicanery began on a Friday night, when a false fire alarm drew the guards outside. By the time they returned, a sapphire necklace had vanished. The miscreant decamped to a rented apartment across the river, where he planned to wait until the search died down. But Detective Sunita Rao noticed something strange: the museum’s security alarm had been switched off ten minutes before the fire alarm rang. That could only happen with someone’s connivance. Within a week, she had arrested both the thief and the night guard who had looked the other way.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “decamped” mean?
qs.why: He hurried off to a rented apartment to hide until the search died down. Despite the word “camp,” it has nothing to do with tents.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “connivance” mean?
options: a phone call to the police
secret agreement to let something wrong happen
qs.why: The night guard “looked the other way,” secretly allowing the theft. A clever machine would be a “contrivance,” a different word.

qs.q: What clue helped the detective solve the case?
options: The thief always wore a gray coat.
The security alarm was turned off before the fire alarm, which pointed to help from inside.
The necklace was found across the river.
The thief visited only on Fridays.
A guard saw the thief take the necklace.
The fire alarm was set off by real smoke.
qs.why: Only someone on the inside could turn off the alarm early, so Rao knew a guard was involved. The fire alarm was false, not real.

title: A Night of Fashion
text: The museum’s yearly gala is famous for its fashion. This year the guests arrived in a panoply of silk, velvet and feathers, and photographers lined the steps. Lucas Ferreira, a debonair architect in a perfectly cut gray suit, charmed everyone he met. Beside him walked the svelte dancer Mei Lin, whose simple black dress was the most admired outfit of the night. Not everyone was so graceful. One businessman ostentatiously checked his gold watch every few minutes, making sure the cameras caught it. His wife wore a huge ring that, a jeweler later whispered, was only a bauble made of glass. And a young actor spoke with an odd British accent that disappeared whenever he forgot himself, an affectation that amused the crowd more than it impressed them.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “bauble” mean?
options: a cheap, showy piece of jewelry
a hair ornament made of feathers
qs.why: The jeweler says the huge ring is “only” glass, so it is bright but cheap. A valuable diamond is what it pretended to be.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “affectation” mean?
options: fake behavior meant to impress others
qs.why: The accent vanished when he forgot himself, so it was not natural. He used it to impress, but it only amused people.

qs.q: What contrast does the passage draw?
options: Some guests showed real style, while others tried too hard to impress.
Rich guests dressed better than poor guests.
The photographers cared more about watches than dresses.
Everyone at the gala was fake.
Simple clothes were laughed at by the crowd.
qs.why: Lucas and Mei Lin are admired, while the businessman, his wife and the actor try to show off. Mei Lin’s simple dress was the most admired, not laughed at.

title: The Old Teacher's Saying
text: In the mountain village where Ji-woo grew up, everyone seems to venerate Master Cho, the old calligraphy teacher. Students bow when he enters a room, and they speak of him in reverential tones, almost as if he were a saint. Master Cho is famous for his sayings. Some are hoary old proverbs that every grandmother repeats, but a few carry real profundity. Ji-woo still remembers one: “Ink cannot be expunged, so think before you write.” The lesson stayed indelibly in her mind. Years later, working as a lawyer in Seoul, she would pause before signing any contract, hearing his slow voice. When she visited him last year, she told him the story, and he laughed. “I only said that because you wasted so much paper,” he told her. “But I am happy it became wise.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “hoary” mean?
options: very old and repeated so often they have become dull
qs.why: These are proverbs “every grandmother repeats,” set against the few with real depth. Gray or white is another use of the word, for hair, not sayings.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “expunged” mean?
qs.why: The saying warns that ink cannot be removed, so you must think before writing. Nothing is about drying or copying ink.

qs.q: What does Master Cho’s reply at the end reveal?
options: He was angry that she became a lawyer.
His famous saying began as a practical complaint, not a planned lesson in wisdom.
He thinks contracts should never be signed.
He wrote the saying in a famous book.
He no longer believes his own advice.
qs.why: He says he said it because she wasted paper, yet he is glad it became wise. He clearly remembers her, so he did not forget her.

title: Under the Moon's Shadow
text: The crowd on the hilltop had waited all morning. Children stood agog, staring at the sky through their special glasses, while their parents checked their watches expectantly. At first the moon took only a small bite out of the sun. The land fell into the penumbra, the moon’s pale outer shadow, and the light turned strange and silvery, like an old photograph. Then, all at once, the sun disappeared. Stars came out at noon. The air grew cooler, and the birds went quiet. People who had been chatting a moment before stood dumbstruck. For many, it was a reminder of the immensity of space and their own small place in it. Totality lasted just over two minutes. As the first bright edge of the sun returned, a woman named Yolanda wiped her eyes. “The transience is part of it,” she said. “You can’t keep it, so you remember it.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “penumbra” mean?
options: the partly shaded outer edge of a shadow
the darkest center of a shadow
the hottest part of the day
qs.why: The passage calls it “the moon’s pale outer shadow,” seen while the sun was only partly covered. The darkest center came later, when the sun disappeared.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “dumbstruck” mean?
qs.why: People who had been chatting suddenly went silent at the sight. That is the opposite of talking excitedly.

qs.q: What does Yolanda mean by her final words?
options: She was disappointed that the eclipse was so short.
She wished she had taken a photograph.
She thinks eclipses happen too often.
She was crying because her eyes hurt.
She plans to forget the eclipse quickly.
The eclipse feels special partly because it lasts such a short time.
qs.why: She says its short life is “part of it” and makes people remember it. She values the brevity rather than being disappointed.

title: Ahead of Her Time
text: In the historical novel The Milkmaid’s Gift, Dr. Ines Albarrán is a village doctor in the 1790s with a heterodox idea. She has noticed that milkmaids who catch a mild disease from cows seem never to get smallpox. Could she inoculate healthy children with that mild disease to protect them? The senior doctors in the city reject the idea with complete dogmatism, refusing even to look at her notes. One calls her an iconoclast who wants to destroy centuries of medical wisdom. Ines keeps working anyway, carefully recording every case. The novel is loosely based on real history: the English doctor Edward Jenner tested a similar idea in 1796. By the last chapter, Ines finally wins the approbation of the city’s medical society, and readers are left admiring her prescience. She had seen, years before others, where medicine was heading.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “heterodox” mean?
options: going against what most experts believed
qs.why: Senior doctors reject the idea as an attack on accepted medical wisdom, so it went against common belief. It turned out to be sound, not silly.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “approbation” mean?
qs.why: At the end she “finally wins” it from the medical society after years of rejection, so it is approval. Doubt was what she faced before.

qs.q: Why did the senior doctors reject Ines’s idea?
options: She had no notes or records.
The idea had already been proven wrong by Jenner.
They refused to consider anything that challenged accepted beliefs.
They thought cow diseases were more dangerous than smallpox.
She refused to show them her work.
qs.why: They rejected it “with complete dogmatism” and would not even look at her notes. She did keep careful records.

title: Trouble on Maple Court
text: Every street has a busybody, and on Maple Court it is Mr. Harrington. He knows who gets which packages, who stays out late and whose lawn needs cutting. Most neighbors put up with his meddlesome habits, but last month things went too far. Mr. Harrington left a note on the Nguyens’ door saying their new fence was “an eyesore the whole street is laughing at.” It was a tactless thing to write, and Mrs. Nguyen took umbrage. She posted the note on the neighborhood message board, and a brouhaha followed: two hundred comments, three arguments and one very long apology. In the end, the neighborhood association asked everyone to sign a short promise to avoid incivility. Mr. Harrington signed first, and for nearly a week he kept his opinions to himself.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “umbrage” mean?
qs.why: Mrs. Nguyen was insulted by the note and posted it publicly. The word sounds like “umbrella,” but it does not mean shade here.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “brouhaha” mean?
qs.why: Two hundred comments and three arguments show a noisy fuss over a small matter. It was not calm.

qs.q: What does the last sentence suggest about Mr. Harrington?
options: He moved away from Maple Court.
He refused to sign the promise.
He became the Nguyens’ closest friend.
He has never spoken his opinions since.
His change in behavior did not last very long.
He wrote the long apology himself.
qs.why: “For nearly a week” hints that he went back to his old habits soon after. He signed first, so he did not refuse.

title: A Hometown Gift
text: When the retired engineer Farida Rahimi gave two million dollars to her hometown, local leaders were stunned by her largesse. She asked for only one thing: that the money be used where it was most needed. The town council set up a small committee to apportion the gift fairly. After months of meetings, they decided to earmark half for repairing the old public library and the rest for scholarships and a free health clinic. Each group that received money had to itemize its spending every three months, listing exactly what was bought and why. The committee would disburse the funds in stages, only after the reports arrived. Farida came to the library’s reopening and sat quietly in the back row. “She is the most beneficent person I’ve ever met,” the librarian said, “and she refuses to let us put her name on anything.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “earmark” mean?
options: fold the corner of a page
set aside for a particular purpose
qs.why: Half the money was reserved for the library and the rest for other uses. Folding down a page corner is “dog-earing,” a different word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “itemize” mean?
options: list each item one by one
qs.why: The passage explains: “listing exactly what was bought and why.” A single total would be the opposite of a list of items.

qs.q: How did the committee make sure the money was used properly?
options: It let Farida decide every payment herself.
It paid out money in stages, only after receiving detailed spending reports.
It gave all the money to the library at once.
It put Farida’s name on every building.
It asked the librarian to check each purchase.
It spent the money before anyone could ask for it.
qs.why: Groups had to list their spending, and funds were paid only after the reports arrived. Farida asked to stay in the background.

title: The Talk That Woke the Room
text: Dr. Kwame Asante had flown overnight to give a talk at a medical conference in Geneva. He arrived bleary-eyed, his shirt rumpled from ten hours in an airplane seat. Things got worse: the speaker before him was indisposed, stuck in his hotel room with a fever, so the organizers asked Kwame to go on an hour early. He walked wearily to the stage. Then he noticed the audience. Some people were yawning; one man was openly asleep. The previous session, a long talk on billing codes, had been soporific. Kwame decided to put his slides away. He told a story instead, about a patient whose heart had stopped for six minutes and who walked out of the hospital a week later. Fidgety students in the front row sat still and leaned forward. When the talk ended, the applause woke the sleeping man, who clapped loudest of all.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “indisposed” mean?
options: slightly ill and unable to take part
qs.why: The speaker was stuck in his hotel room with a fever, so he was mildly ill and could not speak. He was not simply unwilling or late.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “soporific” mean?
options: so dull that it made people sleepy
qs.why: After that session people were yawning and one was asleep. A billing talk might have numbers, but the word means it made them sleepy.

qs.q: Why did Kwame put his slides away?
options: He saw that the audience was tired and wanted to hold their attention with a story.
His slides had been lost on the plane.
The organizers told him he had no time for slides.
He was too sleepy to read them.
He wanted to finish an hour early.
qs.why: He changed plans right after noticing yawning and a sleeping man. Nothing suggests the slides or projector had a problem.

title: Saturday Night Laughs
text: The Sunset Players perform comedy every Saturday in an old cinema. Their most popular sketch lampoons a television chef whose histrionic tears over every burned onion get louder each week; he throws himself across the counter and begs the oven for forgiveness. The audience starts to chortle from the first line. The group also loves pure tomfoolery: pies, rubber chickens and a running joke about a mop that falls in love with a broom. Not every night goes well. Last month a new sketch about a spy fell flat, and its writer, Benedikt, worried that he had become a laughingstock. But the director, a quiet woman named Odette, said dryly, “Well, the mop has never let us down,” and the whole cast burst out laughing. The spy sketch was cut. The mop got a new scene.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “lampoons” mean?
options: makes fun of through comic copying
qs.why: The sketch exaggerates the chef’s crying for laughs, which is mocking him. A faithful, serious copy would not be comedy.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “dryly” mean?
options: in a quietly funny way while seeming serious
qs.why: Odette is quiet, yet her calm remark about the mop made the cast burst out laughing. Her joke was hidden in a serious tone.

qs.q: Why did the cast burst out laughing?
options: The spy sketch was finally working.
Odette’s calm joke eased the tension after the failed sketch.
The audience threw pies at them.
qs.why: After Benedikt’s worry, Odette’s dry line about the reliable mop broke the tension. She was joking, not angry.

title: The Train to Nowhere
text: People in Port Garland, an imaginary harbor city, call the Harbor Monorail “the Train to Nowhere.” Planned in 2009, it has cost ten times its budget and still carries no passengers. Critics call it a classic boondoggle. City officials have taken several junkets to see monorails abroad, flying first class and staying in luxury hotels, but have returned with few useful ideas. A transport wonk named Theo Marchetti has spent years studying the project’s records, and his conclusion is blunt: the problem is not the engineers but the sclerotic officialdom that oversees them, where every small decision needs nine signatures and takes months. Other cities are watching closely. Port Garland has often been a bellwether for city planning, and if it finally fixes its system, others may copy the new approach.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “junkets” mean?
options: trips paid for by others that seem more for fun than for work
qs.why: First-class flights and luxury hotels with few useful results describe pleasure trips at public cost. They were not useful research.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “sclerotic” mean?
qs.why: Nine signatures and months for each small decision show a system too stiff to work well. The passage does not accuse anyone of dishonesty.

qs.q: According to Theo Marchetti, what is the main cause of the project’s failure?
options: A shortage of money from the start
Too few passengers wanting to ride
Other cities copying Port Garland’s plans
Slow, rule-bound officials who oversee the work
qs.why: He says the problem is “not the engineers but the sclerotic officialdom.” The trips are criticized, but he does not name them as the main cause.

title: The Spoiled Flour Case
text: Both litigants arrived early on the final day of the trial. On one side sat Ruth Abernathy, a baker who said a supplier had sold her spoiled flour; on the other sat the supplier, Victor Kane, who swore he had done nothing wrong. Kane’s lawyer tried to impugn Ruth’s character, suggesting she had invented the story to avoid paying her bills. Ruth’s lawyer answered with evidence: lab tests, photos and delivery records. Then the lab worker took the stand. In plain, unvarnished words, she described what she had found in the flour. Kane continued to aver that the flour had been fresh, but his own driver’s records showed it had sat in a hot truck for a week. Judge Okonkwo weighed the facts dispassionately, ignoring the drama in the room. In her ruling, she said that Kane’s mendacity had cost him more than the flour ever could.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “impugn” mean?
qs.why: The lawyer suggested Ruth made up the story, which attacks her honesty. Defending her would be the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “dispassionately” mean?
options: calmly and fairly, without personal feelings
with deep sympathy for one side
qs.why: She ignored the drama and judged on the facts. She was clearly interested, since she weighed the facts, so “no interest” is wrong.

qs.q: What most damaged Kane’s case?
options: His own driver’s records went against his claim that the flour was fresh.
Ruth cried in front of the judge.
He arrived late on the final day.
qs.why: The records showed the flour sat in a hot truck for a week, which contradicted him. The judge ignored drama and stayed neutral.

title: The New Office Manager
text: When Priya Raman joined the logistics firm as office manager, she arrived with a reputation as a martinet. Within a week she had sent a peremptory email ordering everyone to clear their desks by five o'clock, no exceptions. Then came the new expense forms, a rigmarole of three signatures and two scanned receipts for a ten-dollar taxi ride. Staff grumbled that she was officious, correcting the angle of chairs and the labels on folders while bigger problems went unsolved. Her deputy, Tomás, was the one who stayed unflappable. When the warehouse system crashed on a Friday afternoon and drivers began shouting into the phones, he calmly rerouted orders by hand. Later, he helped mollify the angry drivers with free coffee and an honest explanation. Priya noticed. By spring, she had dropped half her rules and asked Tomás to train the new hires.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “peremptory” mean?
options: sent early, before the real instructions
private and meant to be kept secret
carefully reasoned and fair to everyone
long, friendly and full of details
politely asking for help and suggestions
demanding instant obedience in a short, rude way that allows no discussion
qs.why: The email simply ordered everyone to clear their desks, “no exceptions,” which is a curt command allowing no discussion. It was not polite or open to suggestions.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “mollify” mean?
options: to calm someone's anger and make them less upset
to pay someone back for lost money
to dismiss someone from a job
qs.why: Tomás used free coffee and an honest explanation to calm the angry drivers. Nothing suggests he paid them back or fired them.

qs.q: Why did Priya most likely drop half her rules by spring?
options: The warehouse computer system made the rules unnecessary
The company's owners ordered her to cancel them
Tomás complained about her to the head office
She was preparing to leave the firm
The drivers went on strike until the rules were removed
She saw that Tomás's calm, practical handling of a real crisis worked better than her strict rules
qs.why: The passage says “Priya noticed” how Tomás handled the crisis, and then she relaxed her rules and gave him a training role. No order, strike or complaint is mentioned.

title: A Will and a Lesson
text: Kwame Osei grew up in penury on the edge of Accra, sharing one room with five brothers and sisters. As a young tailor he learned to scrimp, mending his own shoes and walking an hour to work to save the bus fare. Decades later he owned three shops, but he never lost the habit of counting coins. His nephew Daniel saw things differently. Daniel was openly avaricious, always asking for loans for fast cars and risky schemes, and he never once said thank you. “That boy is an ingrate,” Kwame told his lawyer. “He loves lucre, not people.” He considered changing his will to disinherit Daniel completely. In the end he chose a gentler path: Daniel would receive his share only after working two years in the shops, learning what each coin had cost.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “scrimp” mean?
options: to sew clothes neatly and quickly
to waste money on many small things
to work many extra hours for more pay
to spend as little as possible, giving up comforts, in order to save money
to hide money from the rest of the family
qs.why: Kwame mended his own shoes and walked to save the bus fare, which is cutting spending to save. Sewing is his job, but that is not what “scrimp” means.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “disinherit” mean?
options: to sell a family business to strangers
to give a relative a larger share of your property
to adopt someone into the family
to refuse ever to speak to a relative
to lend money to someone without interest
to change a will so a relative receives none of your property
qs.why: Kwame talked to his lawyer about changing his will so that Daniel would get nothing. He did not plan to give him more.

qs.q: What did Kwame finally decide about Daniel?
options: The shops would be left to Kwame's lawyer
Daniel would get nothing at all from the will
The shops would be sold and the money given away
Daniel would first have to repay all his old loans
Daniel would get his share only after working in the shops for two years
qs.why: Kwame “chose a gentler path” than cutting Daniel out: he must work two years in the shops first. He only considered leaving him nothing.

title: The Magnet Bracelet Test
text: Every autumn, Dr. Mei Lin begins her first-year science class with a bracelet. A website claims that its magnets “balance the body's energy” and cure headaches. “Is this science?” she asks. Students usually say yes, because the advertisement uses words like “frequency” and “clinical.” Then she explains why the claim is pseudoscientific. A real scientific idea must be falsifiable: there must be some test that could show it to be wrong. The bracelet company offers only uncorroborated stories from happy customers, with no careful trial and no comparison group. Not a scintilla of solid evidence supports it. “Notice their certitude,” Dr. Lin adds. “Real scientists say 'the results suggest.' Sellers of hokum say 'guaranteed.'” By the end of the lesson, students are designing their own tests, and several have already begun to doubt the bracelets their relatives swear by.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “falsifiable” mean?
options: able, at least in principle, to be shown wrong by a test
too complicated to be tested at all
able to be proven completely and forever true
based on personal stories from customers
qs.why: Dr. Lin defines it in the passage: there must be some test that could show the idea to be wrong. It does not mean the idea has already been proven false.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “uncorroborated” mean?
options: not confirmed or supported by any other evidence
qs.why: The customer stories are not backed up by a trial or comparison group, so nothing confirms them. They are unsupported, not proven false.

qs.q: What is the main lesson Dr. Lin wants her students to learn?
options: Advertisements that use technical words are usually honest
Students should never buy jewelry online
Magnets cure headaches for some people but not for others
Customer stories are the best kind of scientific evidence
A scientific claim must be testable and supported by evidence, which the bracelet claim is not
Real scientists are always completely certain of their results
qs.why: She explains falsifiability and the lack of evidence behind the bracelet. She actually says real scientists speak cautiously, not with certainty.

title: Dusk at Ash Creek
text: The best time to visit Ash Creek is not noon but the gloaming, when the sun has slipped behind the hills and the sky turns the color of ripe plums. That is when the valley wakes up. Rabbits and deer are crepuscular, so they leave their hiding places at dusk to feed. Along the bank, a rivulet of snowmelt runs over smooth stones, its water so limpid that you can count the pebbles on the bottom. Beetles skitter across the wet rocks, and in early summer the shallow pools teem with tadpoles. Ranger Aiyana Begay leads a free walk here every Thursday. She asks visitors to turn off their flashlights for five minutes and simply listen. “Most people drive past at lunchtime and think nothing lives here,” she says. “They are seeing the valley at its sleepiest hour.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “crepuscular” mean?
options: active only in the darkest part of the night
active mainly in the middle of the day
living close to rivers and streams
active mainly at dawn and dusk
qs.why: The rabbits and deer come out “at dusk to feed,” the twilight hours. Animals active only in deep night would be called nocturnal instead.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “limpid” mean?
options: slow and lazy in its movement
completely clear, so you can see through it
qs.why: You can count the pebbles on the bottom, so the water is perfectly clear. It is snowmelt, but “limpid” is about clearness, not coldness.

qs.q: Why do lunchtime visitors think nothing lives in the valley?
options: The animals have all moved to another valley
The ranger's walks only take place on Thursdays
The creek dries up by noon
Many of its animals are active around dusk, not in the middle of the day
Visitors are too noisy at lunchtime
qs.why: The animals are crepuscular and wake at dusk, so at noon the valley is at “its sleepiest hour.” Flashlights are mentioned, but only for the evening walk.

title: Losing Well
text: Few people expected Rosa Delgado to last three rounds. She was a nineteen-year-old pugilist from a small gym in Tucson, facing the regional champion, a woman who had trounced her last four opponents. From the first bell it was clear that Rosa was outclassed. The champion was taller, stronger and far more experienced, and her jab landed again and again. Yet Rosa fought gamely. Lean and sinewy from years of running hills before school, she kept moving, slipping punches with a celerity that drew gasps from the crowd. She lost the fight on points, but when the result was announced, the audience stood and cheered for her as loudly as for the winner. Her coach, Ben Abara, was already smiling. “Today she learned what the top level feels like,” he said. “Next year, she will be ready for it.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “gamely” mean?
options: bravely and willingly, trying hard even though she was likely to lose
angrily, wanting to hurt her opponent
playfully, as if the fight were only a game
cleverly, in a way that won easily
qs.why: Rosa kept fighting hard against a much better opponent. The word looks like “game,” but it means brave effort, not playfulness.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “celerity” mean?
qs.why: She slipped punches so fast that the crowd gasped. Her opponent was the stronger one, so “great strength” does not fit.

qs.q: Why did the crowd cheer for Rosa so loudly?
options: She won the fight on points
She won the fight with a knockout
She was the local favorite from the town
Her coach asked the crowd to cheer
She fought hard and skillfully against a much stronger opponent, even though she lost
qs.why: Rosa lost on points but impressed everyone with her courage and speed. The passage does not say the fight was in her hometown.

title: Dinner on Larkin Street
text: Every December, the residents of Larkin Street close the road for one evening and hold a shared dinner. Days before, children festoon the lampposts with strings of paper lanterns and tiny lights. Mrs. Adebayo, who runs the corner bakery, begins to braise ten kilos of beef in a huge covered pot, letting it cook slowly in wine and onions for six hours. Others bring rice, dumplings, curries and pies, until the long tables are crowded with a bounteous spread. Nobody is asked to pay, and nobody keeps count of who brought what. The repast lasts until long after dark, and the conviviality is what people remember most: strangers sharing recipes, old friends laughing over dessert. Even the shy new family from number twelve was soon swept into the jollity, their little boy leading a line of dancers down the middle of the street.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “braise” mean?
options: to cook slowly in a covered pot with a little liquid
to serve cold as a salad
to freeze so it can be eaten later
to fry quickly in very hot oil
to grill over an open fire
qs.why: The beef cooks slowly in a covered pot with wine and onions for six hours, which is braising. Quick frying is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “festoon” mean?
options: to build small market stalls beside
to decorate by hanging chains of lights or ornaments in loops
qs.why: The children hang strings of lanterns and lights on the lampposts. They are adding decorations, not removing them.

qs.q: According to the passage, what do people remember most about the dinner?
options: The money the dinner raises for the street
The beef that Mrs. Adebayo cooks
The friendly, cheerful atmosphere of sharing with neighbors
The paper lanterns on the lampposts
qs.why: The passage says “the conviviality is what people remember most.” The beef and lanterns are mentioned, but not as the main memory.

title: After the Earthquake
text: When the temblor struck the hill town of Valdoro at dawn, it lasted barely forty seconds. That was enough to bring down the old bell tower and crack half the houses on the main square. In the weeks that followed, the streets were pockmarked with holes where cobblestones had sunk, and the town archive, soaked by broken water pipes, was judged irretrievable. Some of its records were three hundred years old. For Lucía Ferrer, the loss was heartrending: among the ruined papers was the only letter written by her forebear, the first teacher of the town school. Yet the people of Valdoro remained unbowed. Within a month, volunteers had cleared the square, and a bakery was selling bread from a tent. “Our families have rebuilt this place before,” Lucía said. “We know how to do it again.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “unbowed” mean?
options: still proud and determined, not defeated in spirit
qs.why: The people cleared the square and reopened shops within a month, showing their spirit was not broken. It has nothing to do with standing straight.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “forebear” mean?
options: an ancestor who lived long ago
qs.why: The letter was written by the town's first teacher, someone in Lucía's family long before her. “A warning” confuses it with “forewarning.”

qs.q: What does Lucía's final remark suggest?
options: She plans to leave Valdoro for good
The town has recovered from disasters before and believes it can do so again
This was the first disaster in the town's history
Her forebear's letter has been found safe
She blames her own family for the damage
The bell tower can never be rebuilt
qs.why: “Our families have rebuilt this place before” shows past recovery and confidence now. It implies the opposite of a first-ever disaster.

title: One Quiet Sentence
text: Mr. Haddad had taught chemistry for thirty years, and he had a rule: never castigate a student in front of the class. He had seen younger teachers harangue a whole room for twenty minutes over one forgotten homework assignment, and he had watched the students simply stop listening. So when Jordan threw his pen down in a fit of petulance after failing a quiz, Mr. Haddad said nothing at first. After the bell, he asked Jordan to stay. His reproof was a single quiet sentence: “That was beneath you.” Then he nodded sagely and pulled out the quiz. “Let's see what went wrong.” They spent fifteen minutes on it. Jordan later said that conversation did more to edify him than a year of lectures. He had learned chemistry, yes, but also how to fail without falling apart.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “petulance” mean?
options: childish bad temper when you do not get your way
qs.why: Throwing a pen down after failing a quiz is a childish show of bad temper. It is not quiet sadness or polite disagreement.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “harangue” mean?
options: to lecture loudly and aggressively for a long time
to teach patiently, step by step
qs.why: The younger teachers went on for twenty minutes over one missed assignment, a long, angry lecture. Speaking quietly in private is what Mr. Haddad did instead.

qs.q: What does Mr. Haddad's approach suggest he believes?
options: Long lectures are the best way to improve students
Students should be scolded loudly so that they remember
A brief, private correction followed by real help works better than a public scolding
Jordan should have been sent to the principal
Teachers should never correct students at all
Failing a quiz does not really matter
qs.why: He avoids public scolding but still corrects Jordan with one sentence and then helps him. So he does correct students, just briefly and privately.

title: Last on the Ridge
text: Our group of twelve set out at seven, and by noon I was clearly the tenderfoot. The others had hiked these mountains for years; I had bought my boots the week before. We had to traipse for hours across rocky slopes, and my legs ached with every step. Then came the ridge: a narrow path with vertiginous drops on both sides, where I kept my eyes fixed on the boots of the person ahead. When fog rolled in, it was easy to see how a hiker might become disoriented and wander off the trail. Our guide, Farida, had an unflagging energy that amazed me. She walked to the front, then back to the end, checking on every straggler, including me, more than once. I reached the hut last, exhausted, but I have rarely felt prouder.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “tenderfoot” mean?
options: a person whose feet are sore
the leader of a hiking group
someone who is afraid of heights
a beginner with little experience of rough outdoor life
the fastest walker in a group
qs.why: The narrator had just bought boots and was the least experienced hiker. The narrator's legs ached, but the word means a beginner, not someone with sore feet.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “unflagging” mean?
options: staying strong and steady without getting tired
slowly fading as the day goes on
qs.why: Farida kept walking up and down the line all day, which amazed the tired narrator. Her energy did not fade.

qs.q: How does the narrator feel at the end of the hike?
options: Proud of being the first to reach the hut
Relieved that the hike was so easy
Proud of finishing, even though they were the least experienced and arrived last
Upset at having been lost in the fog
Angry at the guide for walking too fast
Embarrassed and determined never to hike again
qs.why: The narrator arrives last and exhausted but has “rarely felt prouder.” They were last, not first.

title: The Treasurer's Secret
text: For six years, Gordon Pratt, treasurer of the Millbrook Credit Union, seemed like the most trustworthy man in town. Then a young auditor named Anjali Rao noticed small sums moving each month into an account no one recognized. Her investigation uncovered years of skulduggery. Pratt had used his position to embezzle members' savings, and a collusive arrangement with a building contractor let the two men bilk the credit union through bills for repairs that were never done. When the questions grew sharper, Pratt tried to abscond, buying a one-way ticket to another country, but he was stopped at the airport. At trial, the contractor was warned that if he chose to perjure himself to protect his partner, his own sentence would be far worse. He told the truth. Most of the money was eventually returned to members.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “collusive” mean?
options: involving a secret, dishonest agreement between people to cheat others
made in a court of law
openly approved by the credit union's board
qs.why: Pratt and the contractor secretly worked together to charge for fake repairs. Nothing about it was open or approved.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “abscond” mean?
options: to go on a long holiday
to hide money in a bank
to leave secretly and quickly to avoid arrest
to move to a new job
qs.why: Pratt bought a one-way ticket abroad as questions grew, trying to escape. It was not a holiday, since the ticket was one-way.
