qs.q: How was the scheme first discovered?
options: An auditor noticed regular payments into an account no one recognized
The contractor confessed to the police
Pratt was caught at the airport with the money
Members complained that repairs were never done
A newspaper published a report about Pratt
Pratt boasted about it to friends
qs.why: Anjali Rao's discovery of the unknown account started the investigation. The airport arrest came later.

title: Grandmother's Winter
text: After a fall on an icy step, eighty-year-old Ruth Feldman was housebound for most of the winter. Her granddaughter Nadia, a nursing student, visited every Sunday. She was solicitous without fussing: she brought groceries, checked that Ruth was taking her pills, and rubbed an emollient cream into her grandmother's dry, cracked hands. Ruth's hip healed slowly, but her mind was entirely unimpaired; she beat Nadia at cards every week and corrected her grammar. The real problem was worry. Alone all day, Ruth became fretful, and small aches began to seem like signs of disaster. A sore knee meant a broken bone; a headache meant something worse. “It's not hypochondria if you're old,” she joked. Nadia's answer was practical: a daily phone call at noon, and a list of real warning signs taped to the fridge. The worrying eased almost at once.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “solicitous” mean?
options: showing eager, attentive care for someone's comfort and health
qs.why: Nadia brings groceries, checks the pills and cares for Ruth's hands, all signs of attentive care. The passage says she does this “without fussing,” so she is not bossy.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “unimpaired” mean?
qs.why: Ruth still wins at cards and corrects grammar, so her mind works perfectly. It was her hip, not her mind, that was weak.

qs.q: What helped reduce Ruth's worrying?
options: A visit to a hospital specialist
Moving in with Nadia for the winter
A daily phone call at noon and a list of real warning signs
Playing cards with Nadia every day
Stronger pain pills from her doctor
qs.why: Right after Nadia started the noon call and the list, “the worrying eased almost at once.” Cards were weekly, not daily, and not the cure.

title: The Fundraiser Rumor
text: In a village of four hundred people, scuttlebutt travels faster than the mail. So when a rumor spread that Hamid Karimi, the popular head of the volunteer fire service, had kept money from the summer fundraiser, half the village believed it by lunchtime. The source turned out to be Clive Dunmore, a well-known meddler who had once tried to run the fire service himself. For weeks he would badmouth Hamid to anyone who would listen. But the fundraiser's accounts had been checked by two independent volunteers, and every cent was in the bank. The story was pure calumny. The village council published the figures on the noticeboard, and Clive's attempt to besmirch his rival backfired. Hamid's reputation emerged untarnished, and at the next vote he won more support than any leader in the service's history.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “calumny” mean?
options: a false statement made on purpose to damage someone's reputation
a careful check of the money
qs.why: Clive spread a false story in an attempt to damage his rival's good name. Because it was meant to hurt Hamid, “an honest mistake” is wrong.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “besmirch” mean?
options: to damage someone's good name, often unfairly
to replace someone in a job
to demand an apology from someone
qs.why: Clive tried to ruin Hamid's reputation with a false rumor. The word can mean to make dirty, but here it is about a good name.

qs.q: Why did Hamid's reputation survive the rumor?
options: Nobody in the village believed the rumor
Independent checks showed all the money was in the bank, and the figures were made public
Hamid paid the missing money back
The council removed Clive from the village
qs.why: The volunteers' check and the council's published figures proved the story false. In fact, half the village believed the rumor at first.

title: The River Symphony
text: The first rehearsal of the Eastside Youth Orchestra was, by everyone's account, cacophonous: forty teenagers tuning, chattering and dropping music stands at once. Conductor Amara Nwosu waited, arms folded, until the noise died away. The piece they were learning was a new work by a local composer about a river. A short, rising tune, the river's leitmotif, returns each time the water appears in the story, played first by a single flute and finally by the whole orchestra. Amara loved the middle section, where the syncopation in the drums makes the rhythm stumble like water over rocks. The cellos struggled with it for weeks. By the concert, though, the hall was quiet enough to hear the flutist's dulcet opening notes, and the soloist's mellifluous voice in the final song brought some parents to tears. The next morning, a local critic wrote a rhapsodic review.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “syncopation” mean?
options: a group of singers performing together
loud, harsh noise from many instruments
all the instruments playing at the same volume
a rhythm in which strong beats fall where weak beats are expected
a short tune that keeps coming back
qs.why: The drums make the rhythm “stumble,” putting accents in unexpected places. The returning tune is the leitmotif, a different idea.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “leitmotif” mean?
options: a short tune that keeps returning and is linked with one thing in the story
the loudest part of the whole piece
the rhythm played by the drums
the composer's name written on the music
the single note that opens the concert
the final song sung by the soloist
qs.why: The rising tune returns each time the river appears, so it is tied to the river. It is played by the flute but is not just the opening note.

qs.q: How did the orchestra change between the first rehearsal and the concert?
options: It had always played well from the start
It became smaller and dropped the cellos
It went from noisy and disorganized to skilled enough to move the audience
It stopped using drums in the middle section
qs.why: The first rehearsal was chaotic, but by the concert the hall was quiet and the music brought parents to tears.

title: A Hundred Years
text: When Grandpa Ichiro turned one hundred, the local paper sent a reporter to interview the town's newest centenarian. She asked his secret. “Bad temper,” he said, and his family laughed, because it was partly true. Ichiro had always been a little crotchety in the mornings and openly curmudgeonly about loud music, cell phones and the price of bread. But nobody would say he was in his dotage. He still read two newspapers a day and managed his own savings. The family went to him with every serious decision, trusting a sagacity built from decades of farming through droughts and good years alike. Near the end of the interview, the reporter asked what he was proudest of. Ichiro said nothing. He wordlessly pointed out the window at the orchard he had planted at twenty-five, now heavy with fruit.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “dotage” mean?
options: a bad mood in the morning
the period of old age when the mind has begun to weaken
qs.why: The passage says nobody would call him that because he still reads and manages money, so it means a weakened mind in old age.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “sagacity” mean?
options: a large amount of saved money
wisdom and good judgment gained from experience
qs.why: The family trusts his judgment, built from decades of farming. His temper is mentioned, but that is not why they seek his advice.

qs.q: What does Ichiro's final gesture suggest?
options: He was angry about the question
He plans to sell the orchard soon
He wanted to show her the weather
He is proudest of the orchard, the patient work of his life
He is no longer able to speak
He wanted the reporter to leave
qs.why: Asked what he was proudest of, he points to the orchard he planted at twenty-five. He spoke earlier in the interview, so he can still talk.

title: Becalmed in the Atlantic
text: On the ninth day of her solo voyage across the Atlantic, Marit Halvorsen's boat was becalmed. The sails hung like wet laundry, and the sea was as flat as glass. For two days she drifted, perforce patient, mending ropes and saving every drop of water. She watched forlornly as a plastic crate floated past, a piece of jetsam probably thrown from a cargo ship in some distant storm. Then, on the third morning, came the wind, and too much of it. A sudden storm made the boat careen wildly from wave to wave, and a loose water barrel broke free and went over the side. Yet the timing turned out to be providential: the storm pushed her two hundred miles closer to land, and a fishing boat found her the next afternoon, with her water nearly gone.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “becalmed” mean?
options: unable to move because there was no wind
pushed along by a strong wind
tied up safely in a harbor
qs.why: The sails hung loose and the sea was flat, so the boat could not move. It describes the ship, not Marit's mood.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “perforce” mean?
options: because it could not be avoided
qs.why: With no wind, Marit had no choice but to be patient. The word contains “force,” but it means “by necessity.”

qs.q: Why does the writer say the storm's timing was lucky?
options: It gave her time to finish mending the ropes
It pushed her much closer to land just as her water was running out
It damaged the fishing boat so it stopped nearby
It ended the calm and let her sail home by herself
Its rain refilled her empty water barrels
It washed the plastic crate away
qs.why: The storm moved her two hundred miles toward land, where a fishing boat found her with little water left. She did not sail home alone.

title: Notes in the Margins
text: The used copy of an explorer's biography that Sofia Mendes bought for two dollars turned out to be more interesting than the book itself. The book was a hagiography: in four hundred pages, the author never admitted that the explorer had made a single mistake or treated anyone badly. But the margins were full of handwriting. Three different readers, over perhaps sixty years, had left marginalia in pencil, blue ink and green ink. One wrote “Not true!” beside the prefatory note that praised the explorer's honesty. Another left allusive comments, quoting poems without naming them, which Sofia spent weeks tracking down. Some notes had been erased and written over, so that each page had become a kind of palimpsest. Sofia now plans to abridge the dull biography for a class project and print the readers' comments beside it.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “hagiography” mean?
options: a book about maps and geography
a travel diary written by the explorer himself
a biography that praises its subject too much and hides their faults
qs.why: The author never admits the explorer made a single mistake, so the book is one-sided praise, not a balanced account.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “prefatory” mean?
options: coming at the beginning as an introduction
qs.why: The note that praised the explorer's honesty is the introduction at the front. The readers' notes were the later additions.

qs.q: Why does Sofia find her copy more interesting than the book itself?
options: The notes added even more praise for the explorer
Readers' notes over many years question and add to the one-sided biography
The biography was full of exciting mistakes
It was signed by the explorer
A hidden map was tucked inside
qs.why: The handwritten comments challenge the book (“Not true!”) and add poems, which the dull, flattering text lacks.

title: Where New Words Come From
text: Language changes from the bottom up, says linguist Tomasz Wójcik. “Most new words are born in demotic speech: in kitchens, playgrounds and group chats, not in dictionaries.” A neologism might begin in the argot of skateboarders or video gamers, a private code that outsiders cannot follow, and within a few years appear in newspapers. Wójcik is less cheerful about another kind of language: the gobbledygook of official letters, packed with phrases like “revenue-impacting optimization initiatives” that leave readers confused. Worse still is deliberate doublespeak, where a company calls firing hundreds of workers “rightsizing” to hide what is really happening. Not every gentle phrase is dishonest, he adds. Saying someone “passed away” is euphemistic, but its aim is kindness, not deception. “The question,” Wójcik says, “is always whether a word is helping you see or stopping you from seeing.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “argot” mean?
options: special words used by one group that outsiders find hard to understand
the everyday speech of ordinary people
qs.why: The passage calls it “a private code that outsiders cannot follow.” Everyday speech of ordinary people is “demotic,” a different word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “doublespeak” mean?
options: gentle language meant to be kind
language that deliberately hides or twists the real meaning
qs.why: Calling mass firing “rightsizing” is meant to hide the truth. The kind, gentle phrase is the euphemism, which he says is not dishonest.

qs.q: What test does Wójcik offer for judging a word or phrase?
options: Whether it is a new word
Whether it helps people understand what is real or hides it
Whether it is short and simple
Whether it appears in a dictionary
qs.why: His final line asks whether a word is “helping you see or stopping you from seeing.” He even defends some polite phrases, so politeness is not the test.

title: The Falling Pan
text: The drama club's spring play was a tragicomedy about a family restaurant on its last night of business, and director Lena Okafor had worried for weeks that she had miscast her lead. Marcus, a quiet, serious student, was playing the loud, joking father, a role that seemed made for someone else. On opening night, a pan fell off the stage set during the saddest scene. A few people in the front row began to titter nervously. Marcus paused, picked up the pan, and delivered an extemporaneous line: “Even the kitchen is leaving me.” Then the whole audience began to guffaw, and the rest of the show was uproarious, though the final scene still left many in tears. Afterward, Lena admitted she had been wrong about Marcus. “He wasn't playing a funny man,” she said. “He was playing a sad man who uses jokes.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “titter” mean?
options: to laugh very loudly and freely
qs.why: Only a few people laughed, and they did so nervously during a sad scene. The loud laughter came later, with “guffaw.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “extemporaneous” mean?
options: made up on the spot, without a script
qs.why: Marcus invented the line after the pan fell by accident, so it could not have been rehearsed.

qs.q: What did Lena come to realize about Marcus?
options: He had forgotten his lines on opening night
His serious nature helped him show the sadness beneath the father's jokes
He would make a better director than actor
He should have been given a different role
He had planned for the pan to fall
He was really a loud, funny person all along
qs.why: She says he was playing “a sad man who uses jokes,” which suited a quiet, serious actor. The pan fell by accident.

title: A Shop Finds Its Feet
text: When Chen Wei opened her bike repair shop, she had one goal: to gain a toehold in a neighborhood dominated by two big chain stores. The early months were not remunerative. Some weeks she earned less than her rent. Then came a recessionary year in which many families stopped buying new bikes and began fixing old ones instead. Business doubled. Chen learned to economize, buying parts in bulk with three other small shops and turning off the heating in the back room. Her biggest problem became a logjam of repairs: thirty bikes waiting, and only two pairs of hands. A small grant from the city's small-business fund gave the shop a welcome fillip, paying for a second mechanic. Today Chen trains teenagers in repair work every summer, and one of the chain stores across the street has closed.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “toehold” mean?
options: a bank loan for a new business
a large share of the market
a partnership with a big chain store
a small first position from which to grow
a tool for fixing bike pedals
qs.why: Chen wanted a small starting place in a market controlled by big chains. She did not begin with a large share.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “fillip” mean?
qs.why: The small grant helped by paying for a second mechanic. It was a helpful push, not a full rescue, since business was already growing.

qs.q: Why did Chen's business double during the recessionary year?
options: She cut her prices in half
Teenagers began working in the shop for free
Families repaired their old bikes instead of buying new ones
The city grant paid her customers' bills
Both chain stores closed that year
qs.why: When money was tight, families fixed old bikes rather than buying new, and business doubled. The mechanic and the closed store came later.

title: The Miracle Knife
text: The man in the shiny suit arrived at the county fair with a truck, a microphone and a “miracle” kitchen knife. He was a classic huckster. “Folks, this blade will never, ever need sharpening!” he shouted, slicing through a tin can. The ballyhoo drew a crowd of fifty. His manner was unctuous: he called every woman “madam,” praised every man's “clever face,” and laughed at his own jokes. He knew how to beguile an audience, and the most suggestible people were reaching for their wallets within minutes. My grandmother, Esperanza, was not among them. She had watched men like him hoodwink farmers for fifty years. She asked to borrow the knife, tried it on a ripe tomato, and handed it back without a word. The tomato was squashed flat. Sales stopped immediately.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “unctuous” mean?
options: too flattering and smoothly polite in a fake way
oily or greasy to the touch
qs.why: He called everyone “madam” and praised their “clever face” to win sales, which is fake flattery. The word can mean oily, but here it describes his manner.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “suggestible” mean?
options: easily influenced and quick to accept what others say
qs.why: The people most easily swayed by his talk reached for their wallets first. It does not mean they made suggestions.

qs.q: What did the grandmother's test with the tomato show?
options: Tin cans are harder to cut than tomatoes
The tomato she chose was not ripe
The knife was not nearly as sharp as the seller claimed
The knife was too sharp to use on tomatoes
She was an old friend of the seller
She secretly wanted to buy the knife
qs.why: A truly sharp knife slices a ripe tomato easily, but this one squashed it flat, and the crowd stopped buying.

title: The Debating Final
text: At the national schools debating final, the motion was “Cities should ban cars from their centers.” Aditi Sharma, speaking against the motion, had a difficult job. Her opponent had opened with a tendentious set of figures, choosing only the cities where bans had worked and ignoring the rest. Aditi did not shout. She calmly pointed out that the figures were contestable, since they came from a group that campaigned for bans. Then she offered her counterargument: that a ban without better buses would hurt workers who lived far from the center. She supported it with an apposite example from her own family, whose bakery delivers bread before the buses start running. The judges praised her for arguing lucidly. “A good disputation,” the head judge said, “is not won by volume, but by clarity.” Aditi's team won by one point.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “tendentious” mean?
options: one-sided, chosen to support a particular view
qs.why: The opponent picked only the cities where bans worked and ignored the rest, a biased selection. That is the opposite of balanced.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “apposite” mean?
options: opposite to what was said before
highly relevant and well suited to the point
qs.why: The bakery example fits her point about workers exactly. The word sounds like “opposite,” but it means fitting.

qs.q: Why did the judges favor Aditi?
options: She spoke louder than her opponent
She presented more statistics than anyone else
She argued calmly and clearly, questioned her opponent's sources and used relevant evidence
Her family owns a well-known bakery
The head judge was her teacher
She agreed with her opponent in the end
qs.why: The judges praised her clarity and calm, and the head judge said debates are won “by clarity,” not volume. The bakery was only her example.

title: The Night Visitor
text: The trouble at the Nakamura house began with small things. A cookie vanished from the counter. Then a sock, a pencil, a shiny earring. Hana's younger brother was blamed at first for trying to pilfer snacks, but he swore he was innocent. Whoever was doing it seemed to filch only shiny or tasty objects, and always at night. One morning the family found the pantry ransacked: cereal boxes torn open, flour across the floor. The thief was finally caught on Hana's phone camera: a young raccoon squeezing through a loose vent. A wildlife officer removed it and sealed the vent, and the house was later fumigated to deal with the fleas it had left behind. Mice had long been Mrs. Nakamura's personal bugaboo, but she now admits the raccoon was worse. Within a week the pantry was shipshape again.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “filch” mean?
options: to steal something small quickly and secretly
to hide something in a safe place
qs.why: Small shiny or tasty things disappeared at night without anyone seeing, which is quiet, secret stealing.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “bugaboo” mean?
options: something a person fears or worries about, often too much
qs.why: Mice were Mrs. Nakamura's long-standing fear, until the raccoon proved worse. It is not a type of insect.

qs.q: Who was taking things from the house?
options: A young raccoon coming in through a loose vent
qs.why: Hana's phone camera caught a raccoon squeezing through a loose vent. The brother was only blamed at first.

title: Two Kinds of Roommate
text: When Jonah moved into the student apartment, his three roommates had one question: would he help? Their last roommate, Felix, had been a famous freeloader. He ate their food, used their shampoo, and never paid his share of the internet bill. Felix's indolence was legendary; he once spent an entire weekend on the sofa while the kitchen sink overflowed with dishes. “He wasn't evil,” said Grace, “just slothful and a bit shiftless, with no plans beyond the next video game.” Jonah turned out to have a different problem. He was a procrastinator. He did his share of the cleaning, but always at midnight on the day it was due, and he would dawdle over breakfast while essays waited unwritten. Still, the roommates agreed: a late helper was far better than none.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “freeloader” mean?
options: someone who takes food, money or a place to stay without paying back
someone who works without being paid
qs.why: Felix ate others' food and never paid his share of the bill. Being messy is true of him too, but that is not what the word means.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “procrastinator” mean?
options: someone who refuses to do any work at all
someone who takes other people's food
someone who likes cleaning at night
someone who keeps putting off tasks until later
someone who always gets up early
qs.why: Jonah does his share but always at the last moment. Refusing to work at all describes Felix, not Jonah.

qs.q: How is Jonah different from Felix?
options: Jonah refuses to pay any bills
There is no real difference between them
Jonah does his share but leaves it late, while Felix did not help at all
Jonah is even lazier than Felix
qs.why: Felix took without giving, while Jonah helps, just late. That is why the roommates say “a late helper was far better than none.”

title: A Quiet Chapel
text: Theo Marchetti is an aesthete who has visited more than two hundred art museums, and he is famous among friends for his flamboyance: purple velvet jackets, bright orange scarves, rings on every finger. Yet he insists that his favorite room in the world is plain and silent. It is a small chapel in the hills, its single window covered by a diaphanous white curtain. In the late afternoon, light passes through the thin cloth and falls across a simple painting of a woman's face, her expression calm and beatific. Theo, who is not religious, struggles to explain the feeling. “It is numinous,” he says, “as if something holy were standing just behind you.” He compares the sublimity of that moment to seeing the ocean for the first time. “Great beauty does not need to shout,” he says, adjusting his orange scarf, and smiling at himself.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “diaphanous” mean?
options: so thin and delicate that you can almost see through it
qs.why: Light passes through the “thin cloth,” so the curtain is nearly see-through. Velvet belongs to Theo's jackets, not the curtain.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “flamboyance” mean?
options: a bold, colorful style meant to attract attention
qs.why: Purple velvet, orange scarves and many rings are a showy, eye-catching style. His love of quiet places is the contrast in the story.

qs.q: Why does Theo smile at himself at the end?
options: He painted the woman's face himself
He praises quiet beauty while dressing in a loud, attention-grabbing style
He prefers busy museums after all
He has just admitted that he is religious
He has never actually seen the ocean
qs.why: Saying “great beauty does not need to shout” while fixing a bright orange scarf shows he sees the contrast with his own style.

title: The Queen Sacrifice
text: Before the final of the city chess championship, Viktor Sorokin was cocksure. He told reporters he would beat “the schoolgirl” in under thirty moves. His opponent, fifteen-year-old Zainab Musa, said nothing. During the game Viktor tried every kind of gamesmanship allowed by the rules: he spent ages over the simplest moves and took long walks around the hall, all to make her wait and lose focus. Zainab remained imperturbable. She sat with an unblinking gaze fixed on the board, as if he were not even there. On move twenty-two, she offered her queen. It looked like a blunder, and Viktor grabbed it at once. Six moves later, his king was trapped. She had managed to outmaneuver him completely, and he left the hall ignominiously, ignoring the reporters he had spoken to so proudly the day before.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “gamesmanship” mean?
options: playing many games at the same time
fair and generous behavior toward an opponent
using tactics that are allowed but questionable to gain an advantage
qs.why: Stalling over easy moves and wandering the hall were within the rules but meant to unsettle her. They were not illegal moves.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “cocksure” mean?
options: certain because of careful study of the facts
far too sure of himself, in a proud and annoying way
qs.why: He boasted he would win in under thirty moves and lost. His confidence was arrogant, not based on facts.

qs.q: Why did Viktor take Zainab's queen?
options: The rules forced him to take it
He wanted to make her wait longer
Zainab asked him to take it
It looked like a mistake, but it was a trap that led to his defeat
He was running out of time
qs.why: The queen offer “looked like a blunder,” and six moves later his king was trapped. Taking it lost him the game.

title: A Scathing Review
text: Food critic Marguerite Okonjo is known for writing scathingly about restaurants that charge too much, and her review of the Silver Peacock last week was no exception. The service, she wrote, was “abysmally slow”: forty minutes for a glass of water. The waiter was insufferably smug, correcting her pronunciation of the menu twice. The soup was execrable, cold and tasting faintly of soap, and the “famous” dessert arrived looking like a slapdash pile of cream tossed together in a hurry. Most risible of all, she noted, was the bill: ninety dollars per person, plus a “presentation fee.” Not every review she writes is negative. The following week she praised a tiny noodle shop run by two sisters, where lunch cost eleven dollars and every bowl was, in her words, “made with patience.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “risible” mean?
options: so ridiculous that it deserves to be laughed at
qs.why: Charging ninety dollars plus a “presentation fee” for such a poor meal is laughable. She clearly did not find it fair.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “slapdash” mean?
qs.why: The dessert was “tossed together in a hurry,” which describes careless work. It was made of cream, but the word is about the care taken.

qs.q: What does the noodle shop review show about Okonjo?
options: She cares more about fast service than taste
She only enjoys very cheap food
She changed her mind about the Silver Peacock
She was paid by the two sisters
She praises good value and care, so she is not simply negative about everything
qs.why: The passage says “not every review she writes is negative” and shows her praising a modest, careful shop. Nothing says she likes only cheap food.

title: Summer Camp, Day One
text: Every summer, my aunt Leilani runs a small day camp on her farm, and every summer it begins the same way. By ten o'clock on the first morning, at least one camper has become a ragamuffin, covered in mud, with a torn shirt and grass in his hair. This year it was Mateo, a gawky eleven-year-old who seemed to be all elbows and knees. The horseplay started near the hay bales: pushing, wrestling and a lot of shrieking. Aunt Leilani appeared, arms akimbo, and the noise stopped. Mateo looked up at her quizzically, as if wondering whether he was in trouble. “Lunch,” she said. “Wash first.” Then she smiled. A small girl named Ivy peeked out coyly from behind the barn door, pretending to be shy, though she had started the whole thing.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “akimbo” mean?
options: with hands on the hips and elbows pointing outward
qs.why: Arms akimbo means hands on hips with elbows out, a stance that silenced the campers. Folded arms would be a different position.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “quizzically” mean?
options: in a puzzled way, as if asking a question
in a testing way, like a teacher giving a quiz
qs.why: Mateo looked “as if wondering whether he was in trouble,” a puzzled, questioning look. It is not about giving a quiz.

qs.q: What does the passage suggest about Ivy?
options: She was the camper covered in mud
She told Aunt Leilani about Mateo
She started the horseplay but pretended to be innocent and shy
She was hurt during the horseplay
qs.why: She was “pretending to be shy, though she had started the whole thing.” Mateo, not Ivy, was the muddy one.

title: New in Town
text: When the Okoye family moved from Lagos to a small mountain town, they found the neighbors standoffish at first. People nodded but rarely spoke, and some seemed mistrustful of newcomers who asked questions about the town's history. Mrs. Okoye, a teacher, saw it as insularity rather than hostility: the town had been cut off for generations by bad roads and long winters, and few outsiders ever stayed. She also noticed a mild ethnocentrism in comments like “Do you even have proper food where you come from?” Instead of arguing, she invited the whole street for jollof rice and taught the local children a clapping game. She tried to stay nonjudgmental, remembering that the questions were usually more curious than cruel. Slowly, things changed. A year later, the festival committee asked her, as an unprejudiced newcomer who now knew everyone, to help judge the cooking contest.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “insularity” mean?
options: the fact of living on an island
a narrow, inward-looking attitude that ignores outsiders
qs.why: Mrs. Okoye explains it as the habit of a town long cut off from outsiders, “rather than hostility.” So it is not open hatred.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “ethnocentrism” mean?
options: interest in learning about other cultures
living in the center of town
judging other cultures by your own, believing yours is better
qs.why: Asking whether her country has “proper food” judges another culture by local standards. It shows the opposite of interest in other cultures.

qs.q: How did Mrs. Okoye respond to the town's coolness?
options: By refusing to speak to anyone
With patience and friendly gestures instead of arguments
By complaining to the town council
qs.why: She invited the street to a meal and taught the children a game, choosing “instead of arguing” to stay friendly and open.

title: The Newsroom Rule
text: When Ana Lima joined the newsroom at twenty-two, she was a complete greenhorn. She did not know how to check a source, write a headline, or say no to an editor. She was assigned to Ruth Abernathy, a reporter with forty years' experience, and became her first mentee in a decade. Ruth's worldliness was obvious within a day: she could tell from a single phone call when someone was lying, and nothing seemed to surprise her. Yet she valued what Ana brought too. “Your questions are artless,” she said, “and that's a gift. People tell you things because you're not trying to trick them.” Deadlines and angry callers did not daunt Ruth, and slowly they stopped frightening Ana as well. Ten years later, Ana runs the newsroom, and Ruth's rule remains her lodestar: “Check it twice, then tell it plainly.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “artless” mean?
options: natural and sincere, without any tricks
qs.why: Ruth explains that people open up because Ana is “not trying to trick them.” It has nothing to do with skill at art.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “lodestar” mean?
options: a heavy burden she must carry
a bright star in the night sky
a principle that guides and inspires her
qs.why: Ruth's rule still guides Ana ten years later. A lodestar was once a guiding star, but here it is a guiding principle.

qs.q: Why does Ruth value Ana's questions?
options: Because they are bold and rude
Because they are extremely clever and complex
Because they are honest and not tricky, people trust Ana and tell her things
qs.why: Ruth says people talk to Ana “because you're not trying to trick them.” The worldliness belongs to Ruth, not Ana.

title: My Father's Old Machines
text: My father calls himself a proud troglodyte. He still writes paper checks, keeps phone numbers in a notebook, and owns a television so antediluvian that it has a dial. When my sister gave him a smart speaker for his birthday, he unplugged it within a week. “I don't need a machine listening to me,” he said. But there is a practical side to his resistance. He runs a printing shop, and he has watched expensive gadgetry come and go every few years, each new machine making the last one obsolescent before it had paid for itself. In the corner sits a superannuated fax machine that nobody has used in years. But his most reliable press, built in 1978, still handles the shop's workaday jobs: menus, wedding invitations, posters for lost cats. “Fashion changes,” he says. “A good machine just keeps working.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “obsolescent” mean?
options: becoming out of date and starting to go out of use
qs.why: Each new machine makes the last one old-fashioned before it has paid for itself. The older machine still works, so it is not broken.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “workaday” mean?
qs.why: Menus, invitations and lost-cat posters are the shop's normal, everyday jobs, not special ones.

qs.q: What is the father's practical reason for keeping old machines?
options: He is angry with his sister
He does not know how to use modern devices
He cannot afford to buy any new machines
He has seen new technology lose its value quickly, while a good old machine keeps working
qs.why: He watched new gadgets become outdated before paying for themselves, while his 1978 press still works. Nothing says he cannot afford new machines.
